    Contents

    Playwright + Python QA Automation¶

    A self-paced course for the experienced engineer who wants to understand, not just operate. By the end you will be able to design, build, and defend a production-grade Playwright + Python test framework.

    Who this is for¶

    Perhaps you have written browser automation before — for example Playwright in TypeScript or another tool — and can read code fluently. Perhaps you are newer to it. Either way, what this course offers is the why behind each decision, the Python-specific idioms explained from scratch, and the architecture that separates a throwaway script from a framework a team can live with for years.

    This course assumes you are comfortable with general programming and HTML/CSS. It does not assume Python fluency, deep OOP design experience, or prior exposure to pytest, fixtures, the Page Object Model, or XPath. Those are taught from first principles.

    What you will be able to do¶

    • Read and write idiomatic Python, including the parts that trip up people arriving from TypeScript (self, dataclasses, comprehensions, Protocol, context managers, Decimal).
    • Explain Playwright's execution model — browser, context, page — and why its auto-waiting locator model makes time.sleep() an anti-pattern.
    • Choose the right locator strategy every time, and write XPath when (and only when) it is the right tool.
    • Use pytest the way professionals do: fixtures as dependency injection, parametrization for data-driven tests, markers, parallelism, and the pytest-playwright plugin.
    • Design a layered framework — components → services → tests — that honors SOLID and the Single Responsibility Principle.
    • Build configuration and environment handling that is data-driven and secret-safe.
    • Diagnose flakiness with the trace viewer, produce Allure reports, and wire up GitHub Actions CI.
    • Critically review AI-generated test code and articulate exactly what is wrong with it.

    The mental model you are building¶

    Keep this diagram in your head; the whole course fills it in.

            ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │  tests/        what to verify (assertions)   │
        └─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                              │ calls
                              ▼
        ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │  services/     business flows (the "how")    │
        └─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                              │ composes
                              ▼
        ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │  components/   one UI region each (the POM)  │
        └─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                              │ drives
                              ▼
        ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │  Playwright    browser / context / page      │
        └─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    Each layer has exactly one job. Tests assert. Services orchestrate. Components know markup. Playwright drives the browser. The discipline of keeping these separate is the single most important thing this course teaches — it is what an interviewer is testing when they ask "walk me through your architecture."

    Interview lens

    Throughout the book, callouts like this one tell you what an interviewer is actually probing for behind a question. Read every one twice.

    Ready? Start with Part I, Chapter 1 — Setup & tooling.

    Part I — Python for Automation Engineers

    Chapter 1 — Setup & Tooling¶

    Before we write a single test, we need to understand the machinery a Python project sits on: the interpreter, virtual environments, the package manager, and the project manifest. This is not busywork. Two of the most common ways a newcomer gets stuck — "it works on my machine but not in CI" and "I installed the package but Python can't find it" — are tooling problems, not code problems. Spend twenty minutes here and you will save hours later, and you will be able to answer the very first question many interviewers ask: "How do you manage your project's dependencies?"

    We will build up the picture one layer at a time, and nothing below assumes you have used Python's tooling before.

    1.1 What "running Python" actually means¶

    When you run a Python program, a piece of software called the interpreter reads your .py file and executes it line by line. The interpreter is itself a program installed on your computer, usually reachable as python or python3:

    python3 --version
# Python 3.12.3

    So far so simple. The complication is packages. Almost no real program is written from scratch — you install libraries other people wrote (Playwright, pytest, and so on). When you install a package, it gets copied into a special folder that the interpreter searches when your code says import playwright. That folder is called site-packages.

    Here is the problem. If every project on your computer shares one site-packages folder (the one belonging to the system's Python), then every project shares one version of every library. Picture two projects:

    • Project A was written last year and depends on Playwright 1.40.
    • Project B is brand new and needs Playwright 1.50, which changed how a function behaves.

    You cannot have both 1.40 and 1.50 installed in the same site-packages at once. Fix one project and you break the other. This is the famous "dependency hell," and beginners hit it constantly because the obvious move — pip install straight into the system Python — is exactly the thing that causes it.

    Key idea

    Installing packages into the single, shared system Python couples every project to one set of library versions. We need a way to give each project its own private set of packages. That mechanism is the virtual environment.

    1.2 Virtual environments: a private sandbox per project¶

    A virtual environment ("venv") is, quite literally, a folder. Inside it lives a private copy (or link) of the Python interpreter and a private, empty-to-start site-packages. When a venv is "active," the names python and pip point at that folder's interpreter and that folder's packages instead of the system ones.

    You can see this with your own eyes. Without a venv:

    which python3
# /usr/bin/python3          ← the system interpreter, shared by everything

    Create and activate a venv, and the same command points somewhere else:

    python3 -m venv .venv          # create a venv in a folder called .venv
source .venv/bin/activate      # "activate" it (Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate)
which python
# /home/you/project/.venv/bin/python   ← now it's the PRIVATE one

    Anything you pip install now lands in .venv/, visible only to this project. Delete the .venv folder and the project's packages vanish with it, the system untouched. Project A and Project B each get their own .venv, each with the Playwright version they need, and they never collide.

    From TypeScript

    A venv is conceptually like node_modules plus a pinned copy of Node itself, bundled in one folder you "step into." Node resolves node_modules implicitly from the nearest parent folder; a venv instead changes what python means once you activate it. The payoff is identical: per-project isolation.

    This works, but managing venvs by hand (python -m venv, source activate, pip install, remembering to activate every time, keeping versions in sync across a team) is fiddly. That is the gap the next tool fills.

    1.3 uv: one tool that manages all of it¶

    uv is a modern, extremely fast project manager for Python (written in Rust). It rolls the jobs of several older tools — venv, pip, virtualenv, pip-tools — into one. Crucially, it creates and manages the venv for you, so you rarely activate anything by hand.

    Install it once:

    curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh    # macOS / Linux

    The single command you will use most is uv run. It means: "make sure this project's venv exists and has exactly the right packages installed, then run the following command inside it."

    uv run pytest          # runs pytest inside the project's managed venv
uv run python script.py
uv run playwright install chromium

    Notice you never typed source activate. uv run handles the venv transparently. That is why every command in this course is prefixed uv run — it guarantees the command executes against the correct, isolated set of packages.

    If you come from the Node world, this table is the Rosetta Stone:

    Task npm / Node uv
    Install everything the project declares npm install uv sync
    Add a runtime dependency npm install playwright uv add playwright
    Add a development-only dependency npm install -D pytest uv add --dev pytest
    Run a tool inside the project npx tool uv run tool
    Run a tool you don't want to install npx tool uvx tool
    The lockfile (see §1.5) package-lock.json uv.lock

    Interview lens

    A common opener is "How do you set up and manage a Python project?" A confident answer: "I use uv — it manages the virtual environment and dependencies and runs everything with uv run, so the environment is reproducible and I never pollute the system Python. Dependencies and tool config live in pyproject.toml, pinned by a uv.lock lockfile." You have just signalled that you understand isolation, reproducibility, and modern tooling — in two sentences.

    1.4 pyproject.toml: the project's single manifest¶

    Modern Python projects describe themselves in one file: pyproject.toml. (TOML is a simple, readable configuration format — think of it as a tidier .ini file. Values are grouped under headings in [square brackets] called tables.) This file is the Python equivalent of package.json.

    Here is a representative manifest, annotated. Read the numbered notes below it:

    [project]                       # (1)
name = "ebay-automation"
version = "0.1.0"
requires-python = ">=3.11"      # (2)
dependencies = [                # (3)
    "playwright>=1.44.0",
    "pyyaml>=6.0",
]

[dependency-groups]             # (4)
dev = [
    "pytest>=8.2.0",
    "pytest-playwright>=0.5.0",
    "ruff>=0.4.7",
    "black>=24.4.2",
]

[tool.pytest.ini_options]       # (5)
addopts = "--tracing=retain-on-failure"
testpaths = ["tests"]
markers = [
    "smoke: fast critical-path tests",
    "regression: full regression suite",
]
    1. [project] holds the project's identity — its name, version, and metadata.
    2. requires-python declares which Python versions are acceptable. >=3.11 means "3.11 or newer." Tools refuse to install the project on an older interpreter, catching a whole class of "works on my machine" surprises early.
    3. dependencies are the libraries the shipped code needs to run. The >=1.44.0 is a version constraint: "at least 1.44.0." Without these, your import statements would fail.
    4. [dependency-groups] → dev are libraries needed only while developing — the test runner, the linter, the formatter. A person who merely uses your package doesn't need pytest; a person working on it does. Separating the two keeps the shipped artifact lean.
    5. [tool.*] tables configure your tools, all in this one file. Instead of a scattered .pytest.ini, .ruffrc, and .flake8, everything lives under [tool.pytest...], [tool.ruff], and so on. One file, one place to look.

    Interview lens

    "Why pyproject.toml instead of a requirements.txt?" → "pyproject.toml is the modern, standardized (PEP 621) manifest. It captures project metadata, separates runtime from dev dependencies, and centralizes tool configuration — and it pairs with a lockfile for reproducible installs. A requirements.txt is just a flat list of packages with none of that." Mentioning PEP 621 by name signals you keep up with the ecosystem.

    1.5 The lockfile: making installs reproducible¶

    dependencies lists constraints (playwright>=1.44.0), not exact versions. That flexibility is good when adding packages, but dangerous for reproducibility: if you install today and a teammate installs next month, you might silently get different versions, and "works on my machine" creeps back in.

    The lockfile (uv.lock) solves this. When you run uv sync or uv add, uv resolves your constraints into one exact set of versions — including the versions of your dependencies' dependencies — and records every one in uv.lock. Commit that file, and everyone (and CI) installs the byte-for-byte same versions.

    uv sync     # reads pyproject.toml + uv.lock, installs the EXACT locked versions

    From TypeScript

    uv.lock is exactly package-lock.json / yarn.lock: the manifest says "roughly these versions," the lockfile says "precisely these versions." Commit the lockfile for applications; the reasoning is identical in both ecosystems.

    1.6 Installing the browsers (a separate step)¶

    Here is a subtlety unique to Playwright that trips up almost everyone on their first run. Installing the playwright package (via uv add/uv sync) gives you the Python API — the code you call. It does not download the actual browser programs. Those are large binaries fetched separately:

    uv run playwright install chromium               # download Chromium
uv run playwright install --with-deps chromium   # ...plus required OS libraries

    --with-deps additionally installs the operating-system-level shared libraries that headless Chromium needs (fonts, graphics libraries, etc.). On your laptop you usually already have them; on a fresh, bare Linux machine — like a CI runner — you do not, which is why CI scripts always add --with-deps.

    Gotcha — the most common first-run error

    If you install the package but forget playwright install, your first test fails with a confusing message like "Executable doesn't exist at .../chrome-linux/chrome. Looks like Playwright was just installed... run playwright install." It is not a code bug. It means the browser binaries were never downloaded. Run the install command and it disappears.

    1.7 A professional project layout¶

    Here is the directory shape this course uses, and that you should reach for in real work:

    ebay-automation/
├── pyproject.toml            # manifest + tool config (§1.4)
├── uv.lock                   # pinned, reproducible versions (§1.5)
├── .env.example              # documents which secrets are needed (committed)
├── .env                      # the actual secret VALUES (gitignored — never committed)
├── src/
│   └── ebay_automation/      # the importable package — your framework code
│       ├── components/       # Page Object Model layer
│       ├── services/         # business-flow layer
│       ├── db/               # config / test-data loading
│       └── utils/            # small helpers (logging, price parsing, screenshots)
└── tests/
    ├── conftest.py           # shared pytest fixtures
    ├── unit/                 # fast tests with no browser
    └── test_*.py             # end-to-end tests

    Two conventions here are worth understanding rather than just copying.

    The src/ layout. Notice the package lives under src/, not at the repo root. Why the extra folder? Because of a sneaky bug it prevents. If your package sat at the root, Python could import ebay_automation directly from your working directory even when the package was never properly installed. Everything would seem fine on your machine — and then break for a teammate or in CI, because the "it just happened to be importable from the current folder" trick doesn't hold there. Putting the code under src/ makes that shortcut impossible, which forces you to install the package properly (uv sync does this automatically, in "editable" mode — see the note). Your tests then import the package the exact same way a real user would, so a packaging mistake fails immediately and locally, not later and remotely.

    tests/ is a sibling of src/, not inside it. Test code is not part of the shipped product, so keeping it out of the package keeps the published artifact clean.

    From TypeScript

    The src/ layout is like keeping src/ and test/ as siblings with a build step that only emits src/. "Editable install" is like npm link-ing your own package into itself: your code edits are picked up live, with no rebuild between change and test run.

    1.8 Secrets versus structural configuration¶

    There are two kinds of "configuration," and conflating them is a classic, sometimes serious, mistake.

    • Secrets — passwords, API keys, tokens. These differ per person or machine, must never be committed to git, and live in a file called .env that is listed in .gitignore. To document which secrets a project needs without revealing their values, you commit a .env.example template with the keys but blank/placeholder values.
    • Structural configuration — base URLs, timeouts, which region or currency to test, how many pages to paginate. These are not secret, are shared by the whole team, and should be committed — ideally in a typed, queryable form (we build exactly this in Chapter 21).
    # .env.example  (committed — a template, no real values)
EBAY_USERNAME=
EBAY_PASSWORD=

# .env          (gitignored — the real values, only on your machine)
EBAY_USERNAME=alice@example.com
EBAY_PASSWORD=hunter2

    Gotcha

    Two failure modes, mirror images of each other: putting a base URL in .env (now every teammate must invent their own, and there is no shared source of truth), and putting a password in committed config (now your secret is in git history forever — a genuine security incident). The rule is simple: secrets in .env, everything else in committed config.

    Interview lens

    "Where do you keep configuration?" Always split the answer in two: "Secrets in a gitignored .env, documented by a committed .env.example. Structural, non-secret config — base URLs, profiles, timeouts — in a committed, typed file." This shows security awareness and maintainability instinct in one breath.

    1.9 Putting it together: a first run from scratch¶

    Let's assemble everything above into a real, working setup you can type out now.

    # 1. Create and enter a project folder
mkdir hello-playwright && cd hello-playwright

# 2. Initialise a uv project (writes a starter pyproject.toml)
uv init

# 3. Add the dependencies we need
uv add playwright
uv add --dev pytest pytest-playwright

# 4. Download the browser binaries
uv run playwright install chromium

# 5. Write the smallest possible test
mkdir tests
cat > tests/test_first.py <<'PY'
def test_title(page):
    page.goto("https://playwright.dev/")
    assert "Playwright" in page.title()
PY

# 6. Run it
uv run pytest

    You should see one passing test. Pause on something subtle: your test function took an argument called page, yet you never created a page anywhere. Where did it come from? It was supplied by the pytest-playwright plugin through a mechanism called a fixture — pytest saw the parameter named page, found a provider for it, created a fresh browser page, and handed it in. That is dependency injection, and it is one of the most important ideas in the whole course. We unpack it thoroughly in Chapter 13; for now, just notice that something gave you a working browser tab for free.

    1.10 Exercises¶

    Exercise 1.1 — see the isolation

    In an empty folder, run which python3. Then python3 -m venv .venv and source .venv/bin/activate (or .venv\Scripts\activate on Windows), and run which python again. Confirm the path changed from a system location to one inside .venv/. Run deactivate and confirm it changes back. You have now seen what a virtual environment does.

    Exercise 1.2 — a project from nothing

    Follow §1.9 end to end on your own machine. Then deliberately skip step 4 (playwright install) in a fresh project and run the test — read the error message carefully so you'll recognise it instantly the next time it appears in a colleague's screen-share.

    Exercise 1.3 — read a manifest

    Open the pyproject.toml uv init generated and add a dev dependency with uv add --dev ruff. Watch how both pyproject.toml and uv.lock change. Explain to yourself, in one sentence each, what each file now records.

    Key idea

    The interpreter runs your code; a virtual environment gives each project its own private packages; uv creates that environment and runs everything with uv run; pyproject.toml is the single manifest and the uv.lock lockfile pins exact versions for reproducibility; browsers install separately from the Playwright package; the src/ layout forces correct installs; and secrets and structural config live in different places for different reasons.

    Chapter 2 — Python Essentials for the Working Programmer¶

    This chapter teaches the Python you need for everything that follows. It assumes you can already program — you know what a variable, a loop, and a function are — but it assumes nothing about Python specifically. Every idiom is explained from the ground up, with several examples, because the small syntactic and semantic differences between Python and other languages are exactly where bugs hide.

    If you happen to know TypeScript or JavaScript, the From TypeScript notes connect each idea to something you already know. If you don't, skip them — the main text stands on its own.

    2.1 The shape of Python code¶

    Let's start with a complete, ordinary function and dissect every part of it:

    def greet(name: str, loud: bool = False) -> str:
    message = f"Hello, {name}"
    if loud:
        message = message.upper()
    return message

    Walking through the unfamiliar pieces, one at a time:

    Blocks are defined by indentation, not braces. There are no { } around the function body or the if body. Instead, the indentation itself — four spaces by convention — tells Python what belongs to what. The colon : at the end of def …: and if …: opens a new indented block. This is not a style preference you can ignore; mis-indenting is a syntax error that stops the program from running.

    if loud:
    message = message.upper()   # indented → inside the if
print(message)                  # not indented → runs always

    Variables are not declared. There is no let, const, or var, and no type keyword in front. You simply assign: message = "Hello". The variable springs into existence on first assignment.

    Type hints are written name: type. In the signature, name: str says "name is expected to be a string," and -> str says "this function returns a string." Hold on to a crucial fact we'll expand in §2.7: Python does not enforce these at run time. They are documentation for humans and tools.

    f"...{expr}..." is an f-string — a string with embedded expressions. Anything in { } is evaluated and inserted: f"Hello, {name}" with name = "Sam" produces "Hello, Sam". You can put any expression inside: f"{2 + 2}" → "4".

    Naming conventions are cultural but near-universal. Functions and variables use snake_case (lowercase with underscores). Classes use PascalCase. Constants use UPPER_SNAKE_CASE. Linters will nag you if you deviate, and other Python programmers will read snake_case as "this is a function or variable" automatically.

    From TypeScript

    No braces (indentation instead); no let/const (just assign); types written after a colon and — unlike TS — not checked at compile time (§2.7). f"{x}" is a template literal `${x}`. snake_case where you'd write camelCase.

    Gotcha — tabs vs spaces

    Mixing tabs and spaces for indentation is a syntax error in Python 3. Configure your editor to insert 4 spaces when you press Tab. Almost every Python editor does this by default, but if you ever see a baffling TabError, this is why.

    2.2 None, truthiness, and the two kinds of equality¶

    Python has a single value representing "nothing here": None. There is no separate null and undefined — just None.

    result = None

    Testing for None: use is¶

    Python has two comparison operators that look similar but mean different things:

    • == asks "are these two values equal?"
    • is asks "are these two the exact same object in memory?" (identity)

    For almost everything, you want ==. The one place you use is is comparing against None, True, and False, because there is only ever one None object in a running program, so identity is the precise, idiomatic check:

    if result is None:        # idiomatic
    ...
if result is not None:    # the negation
    ...

    Truthiness: what counts as "empty"¶

    In a boolean context (if x:, while x:), Python treats certain values as falsy: None, False, 0, 0.0, "" (empty string), [] (empty list), {} (empty dict), and set() (empty set). Everything else is truthy. This enables a very common, readable idiom:

    urls = []
if not urls:              # reads as "if urls is empty"
    print("no results")

if urls:                  # reads as "if urls has anything in it"
    process(urls)

    You will see if not items: continue and return value or default throughout test code, and now you can read them at a glance.

    Gotcha — if x: is NOT if x is not None:

    These two checks are not the same, and confusing them causes real bugs. If x could legitimately be 0 or "", then if x: is False for those values, but if x is not None: is True. Concretely: a price of 0 is a valid price, but if price: would treat it as "missing" and skip it. When zero or empty is a legitimate value, always test is None explicitly. This single distinction separates code that handles edge cases from code that quietly mishandles them.

    From TypeScript

    None ≈ null and undefined merged into one. Python == does not do JavaScript-style type coercion, so it behaves like JS === for primitives. is has no everyday JS equivalent — it's reference identity, closest to Object.is.

    2.3 The four collection types¶

    Python has four built-in containers. You will use all of them.

    List — an ordered, growable sequence¶

    nums = [10, 20, 30]
nums.append(40)        # → [10, 20, 30, 40]
len(nums)              # 4
nums[0]                # 10  (first; zero-indexed)
nums[-1]               # 40  (last; negative counts from the end)
nums[1:3]              # [20, 30]  (a "slice": from index 1 up to, not including, 3)

    The two things most likely to surprise you: negative indices count from the end (nums[-1] is the last element, nums[-2] the second-to-last), and slicing nums[start:stop] returns a new list from start up to but not including stop.

    Dict — key/value pairs¶

    config = {"region": "US", "headless": True}
config["region"]            # "US"
config["currency"] = "USD"  # add or overwrite a key
config.get("missing")       # None  (instead of raising)
config.get("missing", "?")  # "?"   (a default if the key is absent)
"region" in config          # True  (membership test on keys)

    The important nicety: indexing a missing key (config["nope"]) raises an error, whereas config.get("nope") returns None (or a default you supply). Reach for .get() when a key might legitimately be absent.

    Tuple — a fixed, unchangeable sequence¶

    point = (40.7, -74.0)       # parentheses; cannot be modified after creation
point[0]                    # 40.7

    Tuples are used for fixed-size records and for returning several values from a function at once: return ("ok", 200).

    Set — unique members, fast membership¶

    tags = {"smoke", "regression"}   # curly braces, but no key:value → it's a set
"smoke" in tags                  # True  (very fast)
tags.add("smoke")                # no effect; sets ignore duplicates

    Sets shine for "does this collection contain X?" and for de-duplicating.

    Unpacking (destructuring)¶

    Any sequence can be "unpacked" into variables in one line:

    lat, lon = point                 # lat = 40.7, lon = -74.0
first, *rest = [1, 2, 3, 4]      # first = 1, rest = [2, 3, 4]

    From TypeScript

    list ≈ Array; dict ≈ Object/Map (with explicit keys); tuple ≈ a fixed-length readonly tuple; set ≈ Set. nums[-1] and nums[1:3] have no JS syntax equivalent (arr.at(-1) and arr.slice(1,3) are the closest). lat, lon = point is array destructuring [lat, lon] = point.

    2.4 Loops and the all-important comprehension¶

    Python's for loop iterates directly over the items of a collection — there is no C-style for (i = 0; i < n; i++):

    for url in urls:           # `url` takes each value in turn
    print(url)

for i in range(3):         # range(3) yields 0, 1, 2
    print(i)

for i, url in enumerate(urls):    # index AND value together
    print(i, url)

    range(n) produces the numbers 0 to n-1. enumerate(seq) pairs each item with its index — use it instead of manually maintaining a counter.

    The comprehension¶

    This is the single most important Python idiom to be able to read, because well-written Python uses it constantly. A list comprehension builds a new list from an existing iterable, optionally filtering, in one expression:

    labels = ["small", "", "large", ""]
result = [label.upper() for label in labels if label]
# result == ["SMALL", "LARGE"]

    Read it left to right as an English sentence:

    [  label.upper()    for label in labels    if label  ]
   ▲ what to keep    ▲ the loop              ▲ the filter (optional)

    "Take label.upper(), for each label in labels, but only where label is truthy (non-empty)." Let's build one up in stages so the structure is unmistakable:

    [x for x in nums]                 # every element, unchanged → a copy
[x * 2 for x in nums]             # every element, doubled
[x for x in nums if x > 10]       # only elements greater than 10
[x * 2 for x in nums if x > 10]   # doubled, but only the ones over 10

    There are dict and set comprehensions too, with the same structure:

    {s.id: s for s in scenarios}      # dict comprehension: {id → object}
{card.url() for card in cards}    # set comprehension: unique URLs (dedupes)

    Why does Python prefer this over a for loop with .append()? Because it is one self-contained expression, it is faster, and — once you can read it — it states the intent ("a list of the upper-cased non-empty labels") more directly than three lines of loop-and-append.

    From TypeScript

    A comprehension is a fused .filter().map(): [x*2 for x in nums if x>10] ≈ nums.filter(x => x > 10).map(x => x * 2). Python folds both into one expression and considers it the idiomatic default.

    Exercise 2.1 — read and write comprehensions

    First, predict the output of [n for n in range(6) if n % 2 == 0]. Then rewrite this loop as a single comprehension: 

    out = []
for c in cards:
    if not c.is_sponsored():
        out.append(c.url())
    Answers First: [0, 2, 4] (the even numbers under 6). Second: out = [c.url() for c in cards if not c.is_sponsored()].

    2.5 The walrus operator :=¶

    You will meet := ("the walrus," for its eyes-and-tusks shape) in resilient list-building code. Normal assignment with = is a statement and produces no value. The walrus := is an expression: it assigns and hands back the assigned value, so you can both store something and test it in the same breath.

    The motivating example: collect each link's href, but keep only the ones that actually have an href, without fetching it twice:

    return [
    href
    for i in range(links.count())
    if (href := links.nth(i).get_attribute("href"))
]

    Trace what happens for each i: links.nth(i).get_attribute("href") is called once; its result is stored in href; the if then tests whether href is truthy; and if so, that same href is what the comprehension keeps. Without the walrus you would have to call get_attribute once in the if and again in the output expression — slower and easy to get subtly wrong.

    From TypeScript

    No clean equivalent. The closest feel is assigning inside a condition — if ((href = el.getAttribute("href"))) { ... } — which JS allows but lint rules usually forbid. Python deliberately introduced := to make exactly the comprehension pattern above both possible and readable.

    2.6 Functions: defaults, keyword arguments, and variadics¶

    def search(query: str, max_price, limit: int = 5) -> list[str]:
    ...

    Default values. limit: int = 5 gives limit a default, so callers may omit it. Keyword arguments. Any parameter can be passed by name at the call site, which makes calls self-documenting:

    search("shoes", 220)               # limit defaults to 5
search("shoes", 220, 3)            # positional: 3 is `limit` (you must know the order)
search("shoes", 220, limit=3)      # keyword: unmistakable
apply_price_range(max_value=price) # the name tells the reader what `price` is for

    Keyword-only arguments. A bare * in the signature forces everything after it to be passed by name. This prevents a caller from accidentally passing a flag positionally:

    def capture(self, step: str, *, full_page: bool = True):
    ...
capture("cart", full_page=False)   # OK
capture("cart", False)             # TypeError — `full_page` must be named

    Variadic parameters. *args collects extra positional arguments into a tuple, and **kwargs collects extra keyword arguments into a dict. You'll see these most in wrapper functions and decorators (Appendix A):

    def f(*args, **kwargs):
    print(args)      # a tuple of positionals
    print(kwargs)    # a dict of named arguments
f(1, 2, x=3)         # args == (1, 2);  kwargs == {"x": 3}

    Gotcha — never use a mutable default argument

    This is one of Python's most infamous traps: 

    def add(item, items=[]):     # BUG: the default [] is created ONCE, ever
    items.append(item)
    return items
add(1)   # [1]
add(2)   # [1, 2]  ← the SAME list persisted between calls!
    The default list is created a single time when the function is defined, then shared across every call, so it silently accumulates state. The fix is the standard idiom: 
    def add(item, items=None):
    items = items if items is not None else []
    items.append(item)
    return items

    From TypeScript

    limit=5 ≈ a default parameter limit = 5. Keyword arguments are like passing an options object but built into the language. *args/**kwargs ≈ rest parameters (...args) plus an options bag. The mutable-default trap has no TS equivalent — it's a genuinely Python-specific thing to memorize.

    2.7 Type hints are advisory, not enforced¶

    This is the single biggest mental adjustment for programmers arriving from a compiled, statically-typed language, so we'll be explicit about it.

    def price_text(self) -> str:
    return 42        # annotated to return str, actually returns int

    Python will run this happily. The -> str is never checked at run time. The annotations exist for three audiences: human readers, your editor (autocomplete and inline warnings), and optional external type-checkers. To actually verify the hints, you run a separate tool — mypy or pyright — typically as a CI step:

    uv run mypy src/      # reports type mismatches WITHOUT running the program

    So type hints are not worthless — far from it. They make code self-documenting, power your editor, and catch real bugs when you run the checker. But by default they are advice, not law.

    From TypeScript

    In TypeScript, tsc refuses to compile mismatched types and the types vanish at run time. In Python, the types also vanish at run time and are never checked at all unless you opt in with mypy/pyright. So treat hints like JSDoc types that a separate tool can verify if you ask it to — valuable, but advisory by default.

    2.8 Modules, packages, and imports¶

    A single .py file is a module. A folder of modules is a package. You bring names from one module into another with import:

    from ebay_automation.components.home import HomePage   # one specific name
from decimal import Decimal                             # one name from a stdlib module
import re                                               # the whole module; use re.compile(...)
    • from X import Y brings the single name Y into scope.
    • import X brings the whole module; you then access its contents as X.thing.
    • Imports are resolved by package path (dotted names like ebay_automation.db.client), not by relative file path like ../db/client.

    A folder becomes an importable package when it contains an __init__.py file (which may be empty). That file is what lets components/ be imported as ebay_automation.components.

    Finally, you will see this guard at the bottom of runnable scripts:

    if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

    It means "only run main() when this file is executed directly, not when it is imported by something else." Library modules omit it; scripts you run from the command line include it.

    From TypeScript

    from x import y ≈ import { y } from "x"; import x ≈ import * as x from "x". There is no default export — every import is named. if __name__ == "__main__": is the rough analogue of checking whether a module is the entry point.

    2.9 Exceptions and error handling¶

    Python signals errors by raising exceptions, which you catch with try/except:

    try:
    price = parse_price(text)
except ValueError:
    log.debug("unparseable price; skipping this card")
    return None
finally:
    tab.close()        # runs no matter what — success OR exception
    • raise ValueError("message") throws an exception.
    • except SomeError: catches a specific type. Catch the narrowest type you can — except ValueError: catches only value errors; the catch-all except Exception: hides bugs you didn't anticipate and should be rare.
    • finally: always executes, whether the try body succeeded, raised, or returned. It's the classic place for cleanup like closing a browser tab. (Often a with block, covered in Chapter 5, expresses this even more cleanly.)

    A small but important design point lives in that example: parse_price raises when it can't make sense of the text, and the caller decides what to do about it (here: skip this one card and move on). The function that detects the problem doesn't decide the policy; the caller does. We'll return to this "separate the mechanism from the policy" idea repeatedly.

    Interview lens

    "How would you handle a listing whose price can't be parsed?" → "The parser raises a ValueError rather than guessing a number; the caller catches it, logs at debug level, and skips that single listing instead of failing the whole run. That keeps how to parse and what to do when parsing fails in separate places." This answer quietly demonstrates that you think about error policy, not just error handling.

    Exercise 2.2 — exceptions

    Write a function safe_divide(a, b) that returns a / b, but returns None (and logs a message) if b is 0, using try/except ZeroDivisionError. Then call it with safe_divide(10, 0) and confirm it returns None rather than crashing.

    Key idea

    Indentation defines blocks; None with is; truthiness powers if not items; the comprehension ([expr for x in xs if cond]) is the core idiom to master; := assigns-and-returns inside an expression; keyword arguments make calls self-documenting (and never use a mutable default); type hints are advisory unless you run mypy; imports are by package path; and exceptions separate detecting a problem from deciding what to do about it.

    Chapter 3 — Object-Oriented Python¶

    The Page Object Model — the architecture at the heart of this course — is applied object-oriented programming. If classes feel shaky, POM will feel like magic incantations. So this chapter builds classes up slowly and concretely, with enough examples that by the end the later architecture chapters read as common sense rather than mystery. We assume you've seen the idea of objects before, but not how Python specifically expresses them.

    3.1 What a class is, and why we want one¶

    A class is a template that bundles together some data (called attributes or fields) and the functions that operate on that data (called methods). An object (or instance) is one concrete thing built from that template.

    Why bundle data and behavior? Because it keeps related things together. Imagine automating a search box. Without a class you'd have a loose selector string here, a "fill the box" function there, a "click submit" function somewhere else — all referring to the same UI element but scattered. A class gathers them into one named unit:

    class HeaderComponent:
    _SEL_SEARCH_NAME = "Search for anything"   # (1) class attribute (shared)

    def __init__(self, page):                  # (2) the constructor
        self.page = page                       # (3) instance attribute (per-object)

    def search(self, query):                   # (4) a method
        self.page.fill(self._SEL_SEARCH_NAME, query)

    Let's name each part, because these four ideas recur on every component you'll write:

    1. A class attribute is defined directly under the class line and is shared by every instance of the class. We use these to hold selector strings — the constant that identifies the search box is the same for every HeaderComponent. (Think of it as a static field.)
    2. __init__ is the constructor: a special method Python runs automatically when you create an instance. ("Dunder" is shorthand for "double underscore"; names like __init__ are special hooks Python calls for you — more in Appendix C.)
    3. self.page = page stores the value passed in as an instance attribute — data that belongs to this particular object. Until you assign something to self.something, it's just a local variable that disappears when __init__ ends.
    4. A method is a function defined inside the class. Its first parameter is always self (explained in §3.2).

    You create and use an instance like this — note there is no new keyword:

    header = HeaderComponent(page)   # this CALLS __init__(self=header, page=page)
header.search("shoes")           # this CALLS search(self=header, query="shoes")

    So HeaderComponent(page) builds an object, runs __init__ to set it up, and hands you back the ready-to-use instance stored in header.

    From TypeScript

    __init__ ≈ constructor. A class attribute ≈ a static readonly field. An instance attribute (self.page) ≈ this.page. The biggest surface difference: Python has no new — you "call the class" directly, HeaderComponent(page).

    3.2 self: the explicit "this"¶

    Every method's first parameter is, by strong convention, named self, and it refers to the specific instance the method was called on. Here is the part that surprises newcomers: you write self in the definition, but you never pass it at the call site — Python supplies it automatically.

    class HeaderComponent:
    def search(self, query):          # you DECLARE self...
        self.page.fill("...", query)

header = HeaderComponent(page)
header.search("shoes")                # ...but you pass only "shoes"; Python sends `header` as self

    When you write header.search("shoes"), Python rewrites it internally as HeaderComponent.search(header, "shoes") — the object before the dot becomes self. That's the whole rule. Inside the method, self.page means "the page belonging to whichever instance this was called on."

    From TypeScript

    self ≈ this, with three improvements: (a) you always declare it explicitly as the first parameter, so there's no ambiguity about where it comes from; (b) you never pass it manually; and (c) it can never be silently rebound the way JavaScript this can when you detach a method — so the entire family of "lost this" bugs simply doesn't exist in Python.

    Gotcha — forgetting self

    If you write def search(query): (no self) and then call header.search("x"), Python raises TypeError: search() takes 1 positional argument but 2 were given. The "2" is confusing until you realise Python passed the instance as a hidden first argument and your signature had no slot for it. Whenever you see that exact error, you forgot self.

    3.3 "Private" by convention: the leading underscore¶

    Python has no private or public keywords. Instead it uses a convention: a name beginning with a single underscore is understood to be internal — "this is an implementation detail; please don't depend on it from outside."

    class HeaderComponent:
    _SEL_SEARCH_NAME = "Search for anything"   # internal: a selector detail
    def search(self, query): ...               # public: part of the API
    def _build_query(self, raw): ...           # internal helper
    • name — public API, safe for others to use.
    • _name — internal; may change without warning; don't rely on it from outside.
    • __name (two underscores) — name-mangled to avoid clashes in subclasses; rarely needed in practice.

    Nothing enforces this — Python won't stop you touching a _name from outside — but every Python programmer and every linter reads the underscore as "hands off." It's a social contract that works remarkably well.

    From TypeScript

    _name ≈ private name, but advisory rather than compiler-enforced. Python's guiding philosophy here is "we're all consenting adults": the underscore signals intent; if you reach past it anyway, you accept the consequences.

    3.4 Inheritance: building on a base class¶

    Inheritance lets one class build on another, reusing its attributes and methods. The classic use in this course is a thin shared base that every UI component extends:

    class BaseComponent:
    def __init__(self, page, root=None):
        self.page = page
        self.root = root if root is not None else page.locator("body")
        self.log = get_logger(self.__class__.__name__)

class ResultCardComponent(BaseComponent):       # (1) inherit from BaseComponent
    def __init__(self, page, root):
        super().__init__(page, root)             # (2) run the base constructor
        # ...any extra setup specific to a result card...
    1. class ResultCardComponent(BaseComponent): declares that a ResultCardComponent is a BaseComponent. It automatically gains everything the base defines — self.page, self.root, self.log — without re-declaring them.
    2. super().__init__(page, root) calls the parent's constructor so the base's setup actually runs. This is easy to forget and important: if you override __init__ in the child and don't call super().__init__(...), then self.page, self.root, and self.log are never set, and the object is half-built. A frequent beginner bug.

    That self.__class__.__name__ line is a small, professional flourish: self.__class__ is the actual runtime class of the object, and .__name__ is its name as a string. So when a ResultCardComponent is running, the base creates a logger labelled "ResultCardComponent" — log lines automatically say which component produced them, with no per-class boilerplate.

    From TypeScript

    class Child(Parent): ≈ class Child extends Parent. super().__init__() ≈ calling super(...) in a constructor. Methods are "virtual" by default — a child method with the same name simply replaces the parent's, with no override keyword needed.

    3.5 Composition: building with parts (usually the better default)¶

    Inheritance models an is-a relationship ("a result card is a component"). Composition models a has-a relationship ("a home page has a header") and is usually the better tool for assembling behaviour. Real pages use both, deliberately:

    class HomePage(BaseComponent):                      # IS-A component (inheritance)
    def __init__(self, page):
        super().__init__(page)
        self.header = HeaderComponent(page)         # HAS-A header (composition)
        self.cookie_banner = CookieBannerComponent(page)  # HAS-A cookie banner

    HomePage is a BaseComponent, so it gets logging and the scoped-locator helper for free. And it has a HeaderComponent and a CookieBannerComponent, so you can write:

    home = HomePage(page)
home.header.search("shoes")        # reach into the composed header
home.cookie_banner.accept()        # reach into the composed banner

    This mirrors how a real page is actually built: a page is made of regions. Composition lets the same HeaderComponent be reused on the home page, the search-results page, the item page — written once, plugged in everywhere.

    Interview lens

    "Inheritance or composition for page objects?" → "Inherit from a thin base for shared plumbing — logging, a scoped-locator helper — and compose sub-components for the page's regions. Deep inheritance between pages is a smell, because pages don't have a clean is-a relationship with each other, but they clearly have regions. So: inherit the plumbing, compose the parts." Knowing when to prefer composition is a senior-level signal; reciting "inheritance good" is not.

    3.6 @property: a method that reads like an attribute¶

    Sometimes you want a value that is computed on demand but reads like a plain field. The @property decorator turns a method into exactly that — a read-only, computed attribute accessed without parentheses:

    class SearchResultsPage(BaseComponent):
    @property
    def cards(self):
        return self.page.locator("ul.srp-results > li.s-item")

results = SearchResultsPage(page)
results.cards          # NO () — looks like a field, but runs the method each time
results.cards.first    # chain straight onto the result

    Without @property you'd write results.cards() with parentheses; with it, the access reads as a noun — results.cards, header.search_input — which is how we think about these things. The method still runs fresh on every access, so the locator is always current.

    (@property is a decorator. We give decorators their own thorough treatment in §3.7 and Appendix A; for now, just read @property as "make this method behave like a getter.")

    From TypeScript

    @property ≈ a get cards() getter: accessed without (), computed behind the scenes.

    3.7 Decorators — the short version¶

    A decorator is a function that wraps another function or class to add behaviour, written with @name on the line directly above a def or class:

    @property                 # turns a method into a getter
def cards(self): ...

@dataclass(frozen=True)   # auto-generates a constructor, equality, immutability
class Scenario: ...

@pytest.fixture           # marks a function as a test-dependency provider
def db(): ...

    The mental shortcut: @thing above a definition means "pass this definition through thing and use whatever comes back." You will use decorators long before you ever write one, and that's perfectly fine. Because they come up so often — and because "explain a decorator" is a classic interview question — they get a full, build-it-from- scratch treatment in Appendix A — Decorators, which you should read after Part I.

    From TypeScript

    Python decorators resemble TS decorators (@Component, @Injectable), and the @pytest.fixture dependency-injection pattern will feel a lot like Angular/NestJS providers — though Python decorators are just plain functions, simpler than TS's.

    3.8 @dataclass: typed records without the boilerplate¶

    Storing a few fields on an object normally means writing a repetitive __init__ (self.id = id, self.query = query, …). A dataclass writes that constructor for you — plus equality and a readable string form — from nothing more than typed field declarations:

    from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from decimal import Decimal

@dataclass(frozen=True)            # (1)
class Scenario:
    id: str
    query: str
    max_price: Decimal
    limit: int
    allow_partial: bool
    min_results: int = 1                            # (2) field with a default
    tags: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)   # (3) mutable default — special!
    1. frozen=True makes instances immutable: after construction, scenario.limit = 9 raises an error. This is perfect for configuration and test data that should never change mid-run — it turns "someone accidentally mutated the config" into an immediate, loud failure.
    2. Fields with defaults must come after fields without them (the same rule as function parameters).
    3. For a mutable default like a list or dict, you must use field(default_factory=list) rather than a bare = []. This is the exact same trap as the mutable-default-argument gotcha from Chapter 2: a bare [] would be created once and silently shared across every instance. default_factory=list instead creates a fresh empty list per instance.

    What you get for those few lines:

    s = Scenario(id="x", query="shoes", max_price=Decimal("220"),
             limit=5, allow_partial=True)
s.query                    # "shoes"
s.tags                     # []  (its own fresh list)
print(s)                   # Scenario(id='x', query='shoes', ...)  ← readable repr
s == Scenario(id="x", ...) # value equality, generated for you

    The auto-generated __repr__ (the readable form) is a real gift in test output: when an assertion fails, the failure log prints the whole object legibly instead of <Scenario object at 0x7f…>.

    From TypeScript

    @dataclass(frozen=True) ≈ a readonly interface plus an auto-generated constructor and structural equality. It's what you reach for instead of hand-writing a class with five this.x = x lines — "a class that behaves like a typed record."

    Interview lens

    "How do you model test data or configuration?" → "Frozen dataclasses. They give me typed fields, immutability so config can't be mutated mid-run, value equality, and a readable repr in failure logs — all without boilerplate. And I parse fields like money into Decimal at load time (Chapter 21) so the rest of the code is type-safe."

    Exercise 3.1 — write a small class

    Write a class Cart whose __init__ stores an empty list self.items. Give it an add(self, name, price) method that appends a (name, price) tuple, and a total(self) method that returns the sum of the prices. Create one, add two items, and print the total. (You've now written instance state and behaviour.)

    Exercise 3.2 — inheritance and super()

    Make a BaseThing with __init__(self, name) that sets self.name. Make a Widget(BaseThing) whose __init__(self, name, size) calls super().__init__(name) and then sets self.size. Create a Widget and print both attributes. Then delete the super().__init__(name) line and observe the AttributeError when you access self.name — that's the "forgot to call super" bug, made visible.

    Key idea

    A class bundles state (self.x, set in __init__) with behaviour (methods, whose first parameter is the explicit self). Inherit a thin base for shared plumbing; compose sub-objects for a page's regions. A leading underscore marks "internal." @property makes a computed getter; @dataclass(frozen=True) makes an immutable typed record. These are the entire structural vocabulary of the Page Object Model.

    Chapter 4 — Typing, Generics & Protocols¶

    Chapter 2 established that type hints in Python are advisory — documentation that a separate tool can check, not rules the interpreter enforces. This chapter goes deeper: how to write hints for the situations that actually come up in test code, and one idea — Protocol — that is genuinely powerful, that underpins a beautifully decoupled piece of the reference project, and that comes up in senior interviews. We build everything from the notation up; no prior typing experience is assumed.

    4.1 The notation, reviewed and extended¶

    A type hint is written after a colon for variables and parameters, and after an arrow for return values:

    name: str = "shoes"               # a variable, hinted as a string
prices: list[Decimal] = []        # a list of Decimals
config: dict[str, int] = {}       # a dict mapping strings to ints

def search(query: str, max_price: Decimal, limit: int = 5) -> list[str]:
    ...                           # takes those types; returns a list of strings

    The bracket syntax describes containers and what's inside them:

    Hint Meaning
    list[str] a list whose elements are strings
    dict[str, int] a dict with string keys and int values
    tuple[str, int] a 2-tuple of a string then an int
    set[str] a set of strings
    list[Decimal] a list of Decimal values

    On Python 3.11+ you use the lowercase built-in names (list, dict, tuple, set) directly. Older code imports capitalised versions (List, Dict) from a module called typing; you may see those, but prefer the lowercase forms in new code.

    4.2 Optional values: X | None¶

    Constantly in test code, a lookup might find nothing — an element with no href, a config key that's absent. The type for "an X, or nothing" is written X | None:

    def url(self) -> str | None:        # might find an href, might not
    href = self.root.get_by_role("link").first.get_attribute("href")
    return href or None             # return the href, or None if it was empty/missing

    The | reads as "or," so str | None is "a string or None." This shows up most often in two places:

    # 1. Return types of lookups that can come up empty:
def find_price(self) -> Decimal | None: ...

# 2. Optional parameters that default to "nothing":
def __init__(self, page: Page, root: Locator | None = None) -> None:
    ...

    That second line is the signature of every component in the reference project: "you may hand me a root locator to scope me, or omit it (in which case root is None and I fall back to a default)." We'll see exactly how that's used in Chapter 19.

    From TypeScript

    str | None is identical to TS string | null. Locator | None = None ≈ root: Locator | null = null. Older Python wrote Optional[str] (imported from typing); str | None is the modern, equivalent spelling — prefer it.

    4.3 Generics: code that works for any type while remembering which¶

    Sometimes a function should work for any element type but still report the right type back. Consider a "give me the first element" helper. It should work on a list of ints (returning an int) or a list of strings (returning a string). A generic expresses "whatever type goes in, that same type comes out."

    In Python you introduce a type variable with TypeVar, then use it as a stand-in type:

    from typing import TypeVar

T = TypeVar("T")                  # T is a placeholder for "some type"

def first(items: list[T]) -> T:   # takes a list of T, returns one T
    return items[0]

first([1, 2, 3])        # T is inferred as int  → returns an int
first(["a", "b"])       # T is inferred as str  → returns a str

    The single T ties the input and output together: whatever element type the list has, that's what first returns. A type-checker now knows first([1,2,3]) is an int, catching mistakes like first([1,2,3]).upper() (you can't .upper() an int).

    The reference project's paginator is generic over the type of thing it collects:

    def collect_until(..., collect_fn: Callable[[_Pageable], list[T]], ...) -> list[T]:

    It accumulates a list[T] and returns a list[T], where T is whatever the collector function produces — here, str URLs, but it could be anything. So one paginator works for collecting URLs, or product objects, or rows of a table, with no changes. (Callable and _Pageable are explained next.)

    From TypeScript

    T = TypeVar("T") then using T ≈ declaring a generic <T> on a function. Python spells the type parameter as a module-level variable instead of inline angle brackets, but the meaning is the same: "preserve whatever type the caller used."

    4.4 Callable: typing a function you pass around¶

    In Python, functions are values you can pass as arguments (we saw this in Chapter 2 and it's the basis of decorators). When a function accepts another function, you type that parameter with Callable:

    from typing import Callable

# "a function that takes a SearchResultsPage and returns a list of strings":
collect_fn: Callable[[SearchResultsPage], list[str]]

    The shape is Callable[[ArgType1, ArgType2, ...], ReturnType] — a list of the argument types, then the return type. Passing functions as values is what lets the paginator stay ignorant of what it's collecting: the caller hands it a small function describing how to gather one page's worth of items.

    Those small inline functions are often written as a lambda — an anonymous, single-expression function:

    collect_fn=lambda r: self._collect_card_urls(r, max_price)
#          ▲ parameter  ▲ the single expression it returns

    lambda r: <expr> is a function taking r and returning <expr>. It's used for short, throwaway functions where a full def would be overkill.

    From TypeScript

    Callable[[Arg], Ret] ≈ a function type (arg: Arg) => Ret. A lambda r: expr ≈ an arrow function (r) => expr. Same concepts, different spelling.

    4.5 Protocol: the star of the chapter (structural typing)¶

    This is the idea worth real attention. It's what makes the paginator elegant, and being able to explain it cleanly is a strong interview signal.

    Two ways a type can "match"¶

    There are two philosophies for deciding whether some object satisfies a type:

    • Nominal typing (Python's classic default): an object matches a type only if its class explicitly says it does — e.g. by inheriting from it. The name of the relationship is what counts.
    • Structural typing: an object matches a type if it has the right shape — the right methods and attributes — regardless of what it inherits from. "If it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, it's a duck."

    Protocol brings structural typing to Python. You declare a Protocol describing the shape you need, and any object with that shape satisfies it — no inheritance required.

    A worked example¶

    The paginator needs to "advance through pages." It doesn't care what it's paging — a search-results page, an orders list, anything — only that the thing can tell it whether there's a next page and can go to it. So we describe exactly that capability:

    from typing import Protocol

class _Pageable(Protocol):
    def has_next_page(self) -> bool: ...      # "...": no body needed; this is just a shape
    def go_to_next_page(self) -> None: ...

def collect_until(component: _Pageable, ...):
    ...
    if not component.has_next_page():
        break
    component.go_to_next_page()

    Now look at SearchResultsPage. It happens to have both methods:

    class SearchResultsPage(BaseComponent):
    def has_next_page(self) -> bool: ...
    def go_to_next_page(self) -> None: ...

    Crucially, SearchResultsPage does not inherit from _Pageable and never mentions it. But because it has the right shape — both required methods, with matching signatures — a type-checker accepts it anywhere a _Pageable is expected. That's structural typing in action.

    Pictured, the relationship looks like this — note the dashed arrow, signalling that SearchResultsPage matches _Pageable by shape, not by inheritance:

    flowchart LR
    P["_Pageable (Protocol)<br/>• has_next_page()<br/>• go_to_next_page()"]
    S["SearchResultsPage<br/>• has_next_page() ✓<br/>• go_to_next_page() ✓<br/>(does NOT inherit from _Pageable)"]
    C["collect_until()<br/>(the paginator)"]
    S -. matches by shape .-> P
    C -- depends on --> P

    Why this is good design, not just clever¶

    • The paginator depends on a capability, not a class. It knows nothing about SearchResultsPage, eBay, or search results — only "something I can ask for a next page and tell to advance." That's a tiny, honest dependency.
    • Future pages satisfy it for free. A reviews list, an order-history page — any class that grows those two methods works with the paginator instantly, with zero changes to the paginator.
    • It is the Dependency Inversion Principle (the "D" of SOLID, Chapter 17) captured in one small construct: the high-level paginator and the low-level page both depend on an abstraction (_Pageable), not on each other.

    From TypeScript

    Protocol ≈ a TypeScript interface used structurally. In TS, an object satisfies an interface just by having the right members — you don't write implements. SearchResultsPage "implements" _Pageable exactly that way: by shape, not by declaration. If you've ever passed a plain object to a function expecting an interface in TS, you already understand Protocol.

    Interview lens

    Being able to say "the paginator accepts a Protocol, so it's decoupled from any concrete page — that's dependency inversion" demonstrates three things at once: you understand Python's typing, you know SOLID, and you design for reuse. It's a genuinely senior sentence — understand it well enough to say it in your own words.

    4.6 Making the hints real: running a type-checker¶

    Because hints do nothing at run time, they only catch bugs if you run a checker. The two common ones are mypy and pyright:

    uv run mypy src/      # analyses types statically, reports mismatches, runs nothing

    Wire this into CI and a whole class of bugs — passing the wrong type, forgetting a None check, returning the wrong shape — is caught before code merges. A common, pragmatic policy is to type-check src/ strictly and be more relaxed in tests.

    Exercise 4.1 — write a Protocol

    Define a Protocol named Closable with a single method close(self) -> None. Write a function close_all(items: list[Closable]) -> None that calls .close() on each. Then create two unrelated classes — File and Connection — each with a close method, put instances of both in one list, and pass it to close_all. Note that neither class inherits from Closable, yet both satisfy it by shape. You've just used structural typing.

    Key idea

    Use X | None for "maybe nothing"; TypeVar + list[T] for generics that preserve the caller's type; Callable[[A], R] for function parameters (often supplied as a lambda); and — the centrepiece — Protocol for structural typing, which lets a utility like the paginator depend on a shape rather than a concrete class. That decoupling is the Dependency Inversion Principle you can point to in real code.

    Chapter 5 — Decimal, Money & Context Managers¶

    Two compact topics that punch far above their weight — in real bugs and in interviews. The first is why money must never be a floating-point number, and how to handle it correctly. The second is the with statement, the mechanism Playwright and the reporting tools lean on to manage resources safely. Both are explained from scratch.

    5.1 Why floating-point numbers corrupt money¶

    Computers store ordinary decimals like 0.1 using a format called floating point (IEEE 754), which represents numbers in binary (base 2). The trouble is that many perfectly ordinary base-10 fractions have no exact representation in base 2 — just as 1/3 has no exact representation in base 10 (0.3333… forever). So the computer stores the closest binary approximation, and the tiny error leaks out:

    >>> 0.1 + 0.2
0.30000000000000004
>>> 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3
False

    Read that again: in Python (and JavaScript, and most languages), 0.1 + 0.2 is not equal to 0.3. It's 0.30000000000000004. The error is microscopic, but it is real, and it is exactly the kind of thing that wrecks a test that compares money.

    Picture the reference project's core assertion: "the cart subtotal must not exceed the budget." If budgets and prices are floats, you can get:

    • a subtotal of $0.30 that compares as greater than a budget computed as 0.1 + 0.2, failing a test that should pass; or
    • a $220.01 total that rounds its way to comparing as ≤ 220.0 and passes a test that should fail.

    Money bugs are the bugs that destroy trust, because the numbers are almost right.

    5.2 Decimal: exact base-10 arithmetic¶

    Python's standard library provides Decimal, which stores numbers in base 10, exactly as written — no binary approximation:

    from decimal import Decimal

Decimal("0.1") + Decimal("0.2")              # Decimal('0.3')  — exact
Decimal("0.1") + Decimal("0.2") == Decimal("0.3")   # True

    Decimal supports all the arithmetic and comparisons you'd expect, and it never silently turns back into a float, so an entire money pipeline — parse, multiply, compare — stays exact end to end.

    But there is one rule you must never break:

    Decimal("25.00")     # CORRECT — construct from a STRING
Decimal(25.00)       # WRONG — the float 25.00 may already be imprecise
Decimal(0.1)         # Decimal('0.1000000000000000055511151231257827021181583404541015625')

    Look at that last line. Decimal(0.1) is a disaster, because 0.1 was already a lossy binary float before Decimal ever saw it — and Decimal faithfully preserves the error. Decimal("0.1"), built from the string "0.1", is exactly one-tenth.

    The cardinal rule of money in Python

    Always build a Decimal from a string, never from a float. The instant a value passes through float, the damage is done and Decimal can only preserve it. This is precisely why prices are stored as quoted strings in YAML (max_price: "220.00") and parsed with Decimal(str(value)) — the value goes string → Decimal and never touches float.

    Multiplication and comparison stay exact, which is all the budget check needs:

    budget = budget_per_item * items_count    # Decimal * int → Decimal, still exact
if subtotal > budget:                      # exact comparison
    raise AssertionError("over budget")

    From TypeScript

    JavaScript has only IEEE floats (the number type), which is why serious JS money code reaches for integer cents, BigInt, or libraries like decimal.js/dinero.js. Python's Decimal is the batteries-included equivalent of decimal.js. The trap Decimal(0.1) vs Decimal("0.1") is identical to new Decimal(0.1) vs new Decimal("0.1") in those libraries.

    Interview lens

    "Why use Decimal instead of float for prices?" is a classic question that sorts juniors from seniors. A full answer: "Floats are binary and can't represent most decimal fractions exactly, so 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3. For budget comparisons that causes false passes and false failures. Decimal is exact base-10 — but only if you construct it from a string, never a float, which is why I store prices as quoted strings." Explaining the binary representation root cause is what makes the answer complete.

    5.3 Parsing a messy price string safely¶

    Real prices on a page arrive as messy text: "$25.00", "US $1,234.56", "$25.00 to $30.00", even "Subtotal (3 items) $50.00". We need to extract the number reliably. A robust parser anchors on the $ sign and refuses to guess when there's no price:

    import re
from decimal import Decimal

_DOLLAR_AMOUNT = re.compile(r"\$\s*(-?\d{1,3}(?:,\d{3})*(?:\.\d+)?)")

def parse_price(text: str) -> Decimal:
    match = _DOLLAR_AMOUNT.search(text)
    if match is None:
        raise ValueError(f"no numeric value found in price text: {text!r}")
    return Decimal(match.group(1).replace(",", ""))

    Don't worry about mastering the regular expression itself yet — that's the subject of Appendix B. What matters here are the two design decisions baked into this tiny function, because both are reusable principles:

    1. Anchor on intent ($), not on position. The pattern requires a literal $, so in "Subtotal (3 items) $50.00" the 3 from "(3 items)" can never be mistaken for the price — the parser locks onto $50.00. A naive "grab the first number" parser would return 3, and every budget comparison downstream would silently use the item count as the price. Anchoring on the meaningful symbol prevents an entire category of subtle bug.

    2. Fail loudly on ambiguity. When there's no $-anchored number at all ("Auction ended", "Time left: 3d 4h"), the function raises ValueError rather than returning 0 or None. Why? Because a parser that invents 0 for garbage spreads a wrong number into your assertions, where it's almost impossible to trace. Raising puts the decision back where the context lives — the caller decides whether to skip that listing or fail the test. (This is the "separate mechanism from policy" idea from Chapter 2, made concrete.)

    Here's the parser working across the formats it must survive:

    parse_price("$25.00")                     # Decimal('25.00')
parse_price("US $1,234.56")               # Decimal('1234.56')   (strips the comma)
parse_price("$25.00 to $30.00")           # Decimal('25.00')     (lower bound of a range)
parse_price("Subtotal (3 items) $50.00")  # Decimal('50.00')     ($ wins over the "3")
parse_price("Time left: 3d 4h")           # raises ValueError     (refuses to guess)

    Interview lens

    Reviewers love this function because it is pure — input text in, Decimal out, no browser, no I/O. "I extracted price parsing into a pure function so I could unit-test 20+ formats in milliseconds without launching a browser" is a strong thing to say. It's also why Chapter 16 on unit testing exists — pure functions are the part of a suite you can test exhaustively and instantly.

    5.4 Context managers: the with statement¶

    The second topic. A context manager is an object that guarantees some setup happens before a block of code and some cleanup happens after it — even if the block raises an exception. You use one with the with keyword, and you'll encounter it in three places in this stack:

    with sync_playwright() as p:        # SETUP: starts the Playwright runtime...
    browser = p.chromium.launch()
    page = browser.new_page()
    page.goto("https://example.com")
# ...CLEANUP: stops the runtime here, automatically — even if something above failed

with allure.step("SEARCH"):         # SETUP: opens a labelled report step...
    urls = search.search_items_by_name_under_price(...)
# ...CLEANUP: closes the step here

with open("file.txt") as f:         # SETUP: opens the file...
    data = f.read()
# ...CLEANUP: closes the file handle here, guaranteed

    How it works under the hood: the object after with defines two special methods — __enter__ (run on entry; its return value is what as name captures) and __exit__ (run on the way out, guaranteed, whether the block finished normally or threw). Python calls them for you. (Those are dunder methods again; see Appendix C.)

    Why prefer with over manually cleaning up? Compare:

    # Manual — you must remember the cleanup, and get it right even on exceptions:
f = open("file.txt")
try:
    data = f.read()
finally:
    f.close()        # easy to forget; must be in `finally` to survive exceptions

# Context manager — the resource owns its own cleanup; you cannot forget it:
with open("file.txt") as f:
    data = f.read()

    The with version is shorter, and — more importantly — the cleanup is defined once by the resource itself, not re-typed correctly at every call site. You literally cannot forget it.

    From TypeScript

    with has no long-standing JavaScript equivalent (the newer using declaration is the emerging analogue). Today's JS pattern is try { ... } finally { resource.close(); }. with sync_playwright() as p: is that try/finally, but with the cleanup defined by the resource rather than rewritten at each use.

    Gotcha — a real bug this prevents

    A common mistake (you'll dissect it in Chapter 26) is calling sync_playwright().start() and then never calling .stop(), which leaks a background process. Repeated in CI, the runner eventually exhausts its handles and starts failing mysteriously. Wrapping the runtime in with sync_playwright() as p: fixes the leak by construction — the __exit__ calls .stop() for you, every time, even on error. This is a concrete reason context managers matter for test stability, not just tidiness.

    Exercise 5.1 — feel the float bug, then fix it

    In a Python REPL, evaluate 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 (it's False). Now evaluate Decimal("0.1") + Decimal("0.2") == Decimal("0.3") (it's True). Finally, evaluate Decimal(0.1) and read the long imprecise result — that's the float error preserved. Internalise: strings into Decimal, never floats.

    Exercise 5.2 — write a context manager user

    Use with open("notes.txt", "w") as f: to write a line to a file, then read it back with another with open(...). Confirm you never called f.close() yet the file was properly written and closed both times.

    Key idea

    Money is Decimal, and a Decimal is always built from a string, never a float (binary floats can't represent most decimal fractions exactly). Parse prices by anchoring on the meaningful symbol ($) and raising on ambiguity so the caller sets policy. And with (context managers) guarantees setup and cleanup around a block even on exceptions — use it for the Playwright runtime, files, and report steps so cleanup can never be forgotten.

    Part II — Playwright Core

    Chapter 6 — How Playwright Is Built¶

    Playwright has a small, clean object model. Once it clicks, the rest of the library follows naturally, and you can answer the common interview opener "walk me through Playwright's architecture" with confidence. We'll build the model from the outside in, explaining each layer and why it exists, then cover the one decision that's specific to Python (sync vs async) and the single most important idea in the whole library (lazy locators).

    6.1 The four objects: Playwright, Browser, Context, Page¶

    Everything you do flows through a hierarchy of four objects:

    Playwright (the runtime)
└── Browser              one launched browser process (Chromium, Firefox, or WebKit)
    └── BrowserContext   an isolated, incognito-like session
        └── Page         a single tab
            └── Frame    (an <iframe> embedded within a page)

    The same picture, drawn to highlight why one browser hosts many isolated contexts (the isolation/parallelism boundary), each holding its own tabs:

    flowchart TD
    PW["Playwright runtime"]
    B["Browser — ONE process, expensive"]
    C1["Context A — isolated session<br/>(own cookies, storage)"]
    C2["Context B — isolated session<br/>(own cookies, storage)"]
    P1["Page (tab)"]
    P2["Page (tab)"]
    P3["Page (tab)"]
    PW --> B
    B --> C1
    B --> C2
    C1 --> P1
    C1 --> P2
    C2 --> P3

    Let's understand each, because the differences between them are what matter.

    The Playwright runtime is the engine. You rarely interact with it directly beyond starting and stopping it — and even that is usually handled for you (§6.3).

    A Browser is an actual launched browser process. Launching one is expensive — it takes a few hundred milliseconds and consumes real memory — so the rule is: launch a browser once and reuse it across many tests.

    A BrowserContext is the key concept. Think of it as a fresh incognito window: it has its own cookies, its own localStorage, its own cache, its own permissions, all completely isolated from every other context. Two contexts in the same browser cannot see each other's data. And creating a context is cheap — near-instant. This combination (one expensive browser, many cheap isolated contexts) is the foundation of two things you care about deeply: test isolation and parallelism.

    A Page is a single tab inside a context. One context can hold several pages — which is exactly what happens when the cart flow opens each product in its own tab while keeping the search-results tab around.

    A Frame is the document inside an <iframe>. Most pages have just the one main frame; you only think about frames when content is embedded (payment widgets, some consent banners) — covered in Chapter 11.

    Key idea — the isolation boundary is the CONTEXT, not the browser

    Each test gets its own fresh context: a clean cookie jar and clean storage, while sharing the already-launched (expensive) browser. This is why one test's login or cart state never leaks into the next, and why tests can run in parallel safely. If you remember one thing from this chapter, remember that the context is the unit of isolation.

    From TypeScript
