    The model is identical across languages: chromium.launch() → browser.newContext() → context.newPage(). The only surface differences in Python are snake_case (new_page() not newPage()) and the absence of await (next section).

    6.2 Two APIs: sync and async (and why this course uses sync)¶

    Playwright for Python ships two versions of its API. They do the same things; they differ in how you call them.

    from playwright.sync_api import sync_playwright

with sync_playwright() as p:
    browser = p.chromium.launch()
    page = browser.new_page()
    page.goto("https://playwright.dev")
    print(page.title())          # this line BLOCKS until the title is ready
    browser.close()

    import asyncio
from playwright.async_api import async_playwright

async def main():
    async with async_playwright() as p:
        browser = await p.chromium.launch()
        page = await browser.new_page()
        await page.goto("https://playwright.dev")
        print(await page.title())     # note the `await` on every call
        await browser.close()

asyncio.run(main())

    In the synchronous API, each call runs to completion and returns its result directly — no await, no async def, no event loop to manage. This is the right choice for test suites, for three reasons: tests are inherently step-by-step ("do this, then assert that"); pytest is built around ordinary synchronous functions; and the code reads straight down the page. The asynchronous API only earns its extra ceremony when you need genuine concurrency — driving many pages at once within a single process — which test suites almost never do. (When suites want speed, they parallelise across processes with pytest-xdist, covered in Chapter 15, not across async tasks.)

    From TypeScript

    JavaScript has only the async API — every Playwright call is awaited, because JS is single-threaded and built on an event loop. Python's sync API is a real convenience JS can't offer: the same calls, no await. Mentally, take any TS Playwright snippet and delete every await. (Under the hood, the sync API runs the async engine on a background thread and blocks for you — but you never see that.)

    Gotcha — don't mix the two APIs

    Importing from both playwright.sync_api and playwright.async_api in one flow, or putting await in front of a sync call, produces confusing errors. Choose the sync API for a pytest suite and stay entirely within it.

    6.3 Who creates these objects?¶

    In a quick standalone script, you create them — that's the with sync_playwright() as p: block in §6.2, where you call launch(), new_page(), and close() yourself.

    In a pytest suite, you almost never do. The pytest-playwright plugin provides ready-made browser, context, and page objects and manages their entire lifecycle — launching the browser once, giving each test a fresh context, and tearing everything down afterwards. You simply request a page by naming it as a function argument:

    def test_home(page):                 # the plugin creates and injects a fresh page
    page.goto("https://www.ebay.com")

    That "request it by naming it" mechanism is a fixture ( Chapter 13). For now the rule to hold onto is: manual lifecycle management is for scripts; fixtures are for suites. Mixing them up — manually launching Playwright inside a pytest test — throws away everything the plugin gives you and is one of the bugs you'll dissect in Chapter 26.

    6.4 Headless vs headed, and slow-motion¶

    When you launch a browser you can choose whether it's visible and how fast it moves:

    browser = p.chromium.launch(
    headless=False,    # show a real browser window
    slow_mo=100,       # pause 100ms before each action so a human can follow along
)
    • Headless (no visible window) is the default and the right choice for CI: it's faster and needs no display attached to the machine.
    • Headed (headless=False) is for development — you watch the browser drive itself, which is invaluable when something isn't working.
    • slow_mo inserts a small delay before each action. It is purely a human-watching aid. It is not a synchronisation tool — you never use slow_mo to "wait for the page," because Playwright already waits automatically (the entire next chapter). Reaching for slow_mo to fix a timing problem is the same mistake as time.sleep.

    These two settings map directly onto the reference project's environment profiles (Chapter 21): the dev profile runs headed with slow_mo=100 for watchability; the ci profile runs headless with slow_mo=0 for speed. Same code, different configuration.

    6.5 The single most important concept: locators are lazy¶

    This idea is the hinge the whole library turns on, so we'll be deliberate about it.

    When you write this:

    search_box = page.locator("#search")   # creates a LOCATOR — finds nothing yet

    …you have not found an element. Nothing has been queried in the page. A Locator is not an element — it is a recipe for finding an element, a stored description that gets re-evaluated every time you act on it:

    search_box.fill("shoes")    # NOW Playwright runs the recipe, finds the element, and types

    Why does this laziness matter so much? Because web pages are dynamic — elements appear, disappear, and get re-rendered as JavaScript runs. If a locator captured a specific element the moment you created it, that reference would go stale the instant the page re-rendered (the classic "stale element" error from older tools). Because a Playwright locator re-runs its recipe at the moment of each action, it always finds the current element. This laziness is exactly what makes the auto-waiting in the next chapter possible — and it's why the same locator can be created early and used safely much later.

    Interview lens

    A model answer to "walk me through Playwright's object model": "One expensive browser, reused across tests; many cheap, isolated contexts — the context is the unit of test isolation and what makes parallelism safe; and pages (tabs) within a context. In a suite, the pytest-playwright fixtures own that whole lifecycle and hand each test a fresh context. And a locator is a lazy recipe, re-evaluated on every action, not a captured element — which is why it never goes stale and why auto-waiting works." That's complete, accurate, and senior.

    Exercise 6.1 — see laziness in action

    In a script, write box = page.locator("#search") before calling page.goto(...). Then page.goto(...) and only afterwards box.fill("hi"). It works — even though the locator was created before the page existed — because the locator didn't look for anything until .fill() ran. Now try the same with an old-style page.query_selector("#search") before navigation and watch it fail or return nothing: that's the difference between a lazy locator and an eager element handle.

    Key idea

    Browser (expensive, shared) → Context (cheap, isolated — the test/parallelism boundary) → Page (tab). Use the sync API in suites and let fixtures own the lifecycle. And a Locator is a lazy, re-evaluated recipe, never a captured element — the foundation everything else rests on.

    Chapter 7 — Locators & Auto-Waiting¶

    If you internalise one chapter in this book, make it this one. Auto-waiting is the reason Playwright exists and the single biggest source of reliability in a modern suite. Understanding it deeply will eliminate the great majority of "flaky test" problems before they ever start — and "how does Playwright handle waiting?" is one of the most common interview questions there is.

    7.1 The problem: pages are asynchronous, and naive automation races them¶

    Modern web pages don't finish loading all at once. You click a button, a network request fires, and the results appear in the page some unpredictable number of milliseconds later. A naive automation tool acts the instant you tell it to — and so it often acts before the page is ready, and fails.

    The old, broken way people "fixed" this was to sleep for a fixed time and hope:

    page.click(".submit")
time.sleep(3)                 # cross your fingers that 3 seconds is enough
results = page.query_selector_all(".result")

    This is wrong in two opposite directions at once:

    • It's too slow. If the results actually appear in 200ms, you still sit there for the full 3 seconds. Multiply that waste across hundreds of tests and you've turned a two-minute suite into a twenty-minute one.
    • It's too flaky. If a busy CI machine takes 3.2 seconds one morning, the test fails — even though the application worked perfectly. The usual "fix" is to bump the sleep to 5 seconds, then 8, and now the suite is both slow and still occasionally flaky.

    There is no good fixed number, because the right amount of waiting is however long it actually takes this time, which varies. Sleeping for a constant can never be that.

    7.2 The solution: actions auto-wait for "actionability"¶

    Here is Playwright's central trick. Every action on a locator — click, fill, check, and so on — does not fire immediately. First it waits, retrying continuously, until the target element is genuinely ready to be acted upon, or until a timeout (30 seconds by default) elapses. "Ready" is defined by a precise set of actionability checks. For a click, the element must be:

    1. Attached — present in the page's DOM.
    2. Visible — it has a non-empty size and isn't hidden via display:none or visibility:hidden.
    3. Stable — not currently animating; its bounding box is the same across two consecutive animation frames.
    4. Receiving events — not covered by some overlay or other element at the point where the click would land.
    5. Enabled — not a disabled control.

    So this single line:

    page.get_by_role("button", name="Search").click()

    …actually means: "Keep checking — is the Search button attached? visible? stable? clickable at its centre? enabled? — and the moment all of those are true, click it. If 30 seconds pass and they're never all true, raise a clear timeout error explaining which check failed."

    You write the intent ("click Search") and Playwright handles the timing. For the common case, you never wait manually and you never sleep.

    Pictured, that retry loop looks like this:

    flowchart TD
    Start(["loc.click() called"]) --> A{attached?}
    A -- yes --> V{visible?}
    V -- yes --> St{stable?}
    St -- yes --> H{receives<br/>events?}
    H -- yes --> E{enabled?}
    E -- yes --> Do(["click fires"])
    A -- no --> Wait((wait briefly<br/>& retry))
    V -- no --> Wait
    St -- no --> Wait
    H -- no --> Wait
    E -- no --> Wait
    Wait --> T{timeout<br/>reached?}
    T -- no --> A
    T -- yes --> Fail(["raise: clear timeout<br/>naming which check failed"])

    Key idea

    Actions auto-wait for actionability. The instant you feel the urge to "wait here for the page to be ready," the correct response is almost never time.sleep — it's either "do nothing, the action already waits" or "assert the state you're waiting for" (next section).

    From TypeScript

    Auto-waiting is engine-level, not language-level, so it behaves identically in TS. If you ever reached for await page.waitForTimeout(3000) out of habit in TypeScript, this chapter is for you too — that's the same anti-pattern as time.sleep.

    7.3 Web-first assertions: expect() that retries¶

    Actions auto-wait. But what about checking something — that a heading appeared, that a list has five items, that the URL changed? For that, Playwright gives you expect(), whose assertions automatically retry until they pass or time out. This is how you wait for a state without sleeping:

    from playwright.sync_api import expect

expect(page.get_by_role("heading")).to_be_visible()      # waits until it's visible
expect(results).to_have_count(5)                          # retries until exactly 5 (or fails)
expect(page).to_have_url(re.compile(r".*/sch/.*"))        # waits for navigation to happen
expect(price_node).to_have_text("$25.00")                 # waits until the text matches

    Each of these polls the page repeatedly. expect(results).to_have_count(5) doesn't check "are there 5 right now?" once — it keeps checking as items stream in, and succeeds the moment there are five (or fails with a clear message after the timeout).

    Contrast this with a plain Python assert, which checks exactly once, immediately:

    assert results.count() > 0          # checks ONCE, right now — flaky if still loading
expect(results.first).to_be_visible()   # retries until visible — robust

    The rule of thumb, which we'll repeat in Chapter 10: use expect() for anything the page is still settling into, and plain assert only for values you've already finished computing in Python (a parsed Decimal, a list length you've finished building).

    Gotcha — a locator is not its matches

    This trips up nearly everyone once: 

    results = page.locator(".result-item")
assert results              # ALWAYS true! `results` is a Locator object, not a count
    A Locator is always a truthy object regardless of whether it matches anything. To actually assert presence you must act on it: expect(results.first).to_be_visible() or check results.count(). The buggy code in Chapter 26 makes exactly this mistake — it builds a locator and then asserts nothing real.

    7.4 Strict mode: ambiguity is an error, on purpose¶

    What happens if your locator matches more than one element?

    page.get_by_role("button").click()
# playwright._impl._errors.Error: strict mode violation:
#   get_by_role("button") resolved to 12 elements

    Rather than silently clicking the first match (or a random one), an action on an ambiguous locator raises a strict-mode violation. This is a deliberate, valuable feature. An ambiguous locator is a latent bug: "click the button" is meaningless if there are twelve buttons. Playwright surfaces that immediately and loudly, instead of letting it manifest later as an intermittent "it clicked the wrong thing" failure that's miserable to debug.

    When you hit a strict-mode violation, the fix is to be more specific — and the ways to do that, best to worst:

    page.get_by_role("button", name="Search")   # 1. BEST: disambiguate by accessible name
page.get_by_role("button").first            # 2. take the first — only if you're SURE
page.locator("#search-btn")                 # 3. a uniquely-identifying selector

    Interview lens

    "What is strict mode?" → "If a locator matches more than one element, Playwright throws on the action instead of guessing. It converts 'silently clicked the wrong element' — an intermittent, awful-to-debug failure — into an immediate, explicit error. I treat a strict-mode violation as a signal that my locator isn't specific enough, and I fix it by adding an accessible name, not by reflexively slapping .first on the end." That last sentence shows judgment, not just knowledge.

    7.5 Locator vs ElementHandle: use locators, always¶

    You will occasionally see an older style. It's worth knowing why to avoid it.

    Locator (use this) ElementHandle (legacy — avoid)
    Created by page.locator(...), page.get_by_*(...) page.query_selector(...)
    What it is a lazy recipe, re-resolved on each use a captured pointer to one specific DOM node
    Auto-waits? yes no
    Survives a re-render? yes (it re-finds the element) no (the pointer goes "stale")

    ElementHandle is a holdover from the Selenium/Puppeteer era. Because it grabs a specific DOM node at creation time, it becomes invalid the moment the page re-renders — the source of the dreaded StaleElementReferenceException that plagued older suites. Locators don't go stale, because they re-find the element every time you use them (§6.5). Modern Playwright is locators-only; if you see query_selector in code, that's a smell.

    7.6 Composing locators: chaining and scoping¶

    Locators combine. You take a broad locator and narrow it by chaining .locator(...) or .get_by_*(...) onto it — each step searches within the previous result:

    card = page.locator("li.s-item").first        # one result card
card.get_by_role("link").first                 # the link INSIDE that card
card.locator(".s-item__price")                 # the price INSIDE that card

    This scoping is the mechanical foundation of the component objects you'll build in Chapter 19. A component is handed a root locator and finds everything relative to it, so a ResultCardComponent scoped to one card's <li> can never accidentally grab a different card's price — even though fifty cards on the page all use the same .s-item__price class. The base component's helper is exactly this idea in one method:

    def locator(self, selector: str) -> Locator:
    return self.root.locator(selector)   # always searches within THIS component's root

    7.7 Selecting among many matches: filter and nth¶

    When a locator legitimately matches many elements and you want a specific one, prefer selecting by content over fragile position:

    rows = page.get_by_role("listitem")

rows.filter(has_text="In stock")                          # only rows containing that text
rows.filter(has=page.get_by_role("button", name="Buy"))   # only rows containing a Buy button
rows.nth(2)                                                # the third match (0-indexed)
rows.first                                                 # the first; rows.last for the last

    filter() lets you say "the row that contains X," which survives reordering and ad injection. nth(i) selects by index when you genuinely need a positional one (note: Playwright's nth is 0-indexed, unlike XPath's 1-indexing — a difference worth remembering).

    Exercise 7.1 — auto-waiting and strict mode, hands on

    On https://playwright.dev: (a) get the "Get started" link with get_by_role and click it — note you never had to wait for the page to finish loading. (b) Assert the page title contains "Playwright" using expect(page).to_have_title(...). (c) Deliberately write page.get_by_role("link").click() to trigger a strict-mode violation, read how many elements it reports, then fix it by adding a name=. You've now seen auto-waiting, web-first assertions, and strict mode.

    Exercise 7.2 — feel the difference

    Find any page with results that load after a click. Assert presence first with assert loc.is_visible() (a non-waiting snapshot) and run it ten times — note the occasional failure. Replace it with expect(loc).to_be_visible() and run ten more — note it's now rock-solid. That's the value of a retrying assertion.

    Key idea

    Actions auto-wait for actionability (attached, visible, stable, hittable, enabled), so you never time.sleep. expect() retries assertions, so you wait for state without sleeping. Ambiguity throws a strict-mode error on purpose. Use Locator (lazy, never stale), never ElementHandle. Narrow locators by chaining from a root, and select among many by content (filter) rather than position. With these habits, flakiness mostly disappears.

    Chapter 8 — Choosing the Right Locator¶

    The previous chapter made acting on elements robust. This chapter is about finding them robustly. The locator you choose decides whether a test quietly keeps working after a site redesign, or shatters the moment a CSS class is renamed. There's a clear priority order and — more importantly — a clear principle behind it, and getting this right is a large part of what evaluators mean by "smart locators."

    8.1 The guiding principle¶

    Here is the one idea that generates the entire priority order below:

    Key idea

    Locate elements the way a user perceives the page, not the way a developer built it. A user looks for "the Search button" — they neither know nor care that it has the class .btn-prim-2 or sits third in some <div>. Class names and DOM positions are implementation details that change on a whim; the things a user perceives — roles, labels, visible text — are the contract the page makes with everyone (humans and assistive technology alike), and they're far more stable.

    Everything that follows is just this principle applied.

    8.2 The priority order¶

    Reach for the highest strategy on this list that uniquely identifies your element:

    1. get_by_role(role, name=...) — first choice for almost everything.
    2. get_by_label(...) — for form inputs that have a visible label.
    3. get_by_placeholder(...), get_by_text(...), get_by_alt_text(...) — for content-anchored elements.
    4. get_by_test_id(...) — when the application deliberately exposes a test hook.
    5. CSS selector — a fallback, when no semantic anchor exists.
    6. XPath — the last resort, for things CSS genuinely cannot express (covered fully in Chapter 9).

    We'll go through each, with examples.

    8.3 Role-based locators and the accessibility tree¶

    To understand why roles are the gold standard, you need to know about the accessibility tree. As the browser parses your HTML, it builds — alongside the visual page — a second structure describing the page semantically, the way a screen reader would announce it. In that tree, each meaningful element has:

    • a role — what kind of thing it is: button, link, heading, textbox, combobox, checkbox, listitem, and so on; and
    • an accessible name — its label, usually its visible text or an aria-label.

    get_by_role queries that semantic tree:

    page.get_by_role("button", name="Search")        # the button labelled "Search"
page.get_by_role("link", name="Get started")      # the link labelled "Get started"
page.get_by_role("heading", level=1)               # the <h1>
page.get_by_role("textbox", name="Email")          # the input labelled "Email"
page.get_by_role("combobox", name="Search for anything")   # eBay's search box

    Why this is the best default:

    • It's stable. Roles survive cosmetic refactors. If a designer rebuilds a <div class="btn"> as a proper <button>, the visual styling changes but the role stays button, so your locator keeps working.
    • It's self-documenting. get_by_role("button", name="Add to cart") tells the next reader exactly what's being clicked. Compare that to .locator(".x7g").
    • It double-checks accessibility. If your role locator can't find a button that's clearly on the page, it often means the application has an accessibility bug (a clickable <div> with no role). Your tests quietly become an accessibility smoke check.

    The name argument matches the accessible name, and it accepts either a plain string or a regular expression for fuzzy matching when the label has a dynamic part:

    import re
page.get_by_role("link", name=re.compile(r"^Cart"))   # matches "Cart", "Cart (3)", ...

    From TypeScript

    Identical API (getByRole). If you've used Testing Library (@testing-library/*), this is the very same philosophy — Playwright's locators were directly inspired by it. "Find by role, label, and text; not by class" is the shared creed.

    8.4 Labels, placeholders, and text¶

    For form fields, the right tool is get_by_label, which follows the HTML association between a <label> and its input — exactly how a sighted user reads the form:

    page.get_by_label("Maximum Value").fill("220")    # the input whose visible label is "Maximum Value"

    For other content-anchored elements, match their text or attributes:

    page.get_by_placeholder("Search")                 # by the input's placeholder text
page.get_by_text("SPONSORED")                       # by visible text content
page.get_by_text(re.compile(r"^Subtotal"))         # text that starts with "Subtotal"
page.get_by_alt_text("Company logo")               # an <img> by its alt text

    A useful distinction: use get_by_text for static, copy-anchored things — a "Sponsored" badge, the "Subtotal" line — but prefer get_by_role for anything clickable (those have roles like button or link). Text can change with copy edits; roles are more stable for interactive controls.

    8.5 Test IDs¶

    Some applications deliberately add data-testid attributes as stable hooks for testing:

    page.get_by_test_id("x-price-primary")    # matches an element with data-testid="x-price-primary"

    These are excellent when they exist: stable by contract (the team agrees not to break them), invisible to users, and decoupled from styling. The catch with a public site you don't control (like eBay) is that test IDs appear only sporadically — so you can't rely on them everywhere, but where one does exist (eBay's price node has one) it beats a fragile structural CSS selector.

    8.6 CSS selectors — the principled fallback¶

    When there is no role, label, text, or test ID — for example a price <span> that carries only a class — drop to a CSS selector, preferring the most stable anchors available:

    page.locator("ul.srp-results > li.s-item")          # eBay result cards
page.locator('[data-testid="x-price-primary"], .x-price-primary')  # price, with fallback

    A few CSS habits worth knowing:

    • Prefer IDs (#srp-results) and data-* attributes over deep structural chains.
    • The comma is "OR": '[data-testid="x"], .x-class' tries the test ID first, and falls back to the class if it's absent. This one trick absorbs a whole category of "the site rolled out a new markup variant" failures — it's cheap insurance on volatile pages.
    • > means "direct child"; a space means "any descendant," however deep.

    Gotcha — never locate by position

    Avoid :nth-child(3), div > div > span:last-child, and similar position-based selectors. Real sites reorder elements, inject ads mid-list, and A/B-test layouts per visitor, so "the third card" is not a stable identity. Always locate by what the element is, never by where it happens to sit. This is the same lesson as §8.1, and it's worth repeating because positional selectors are the most common source of "worked yesterday, broke today" flakiness.

    8.7 Centralise selectors as _SEL_ constants¶

    Inside a component class, store selector strings as class-level constants with a _SEL_ prefix, and reference them from the methods:

    class HeaderComponent(BaseComponent):
    _SEL_SEARCH_INPUT_NAME = "Search for anything"
    _SEL_SEARCH_SUBMIT_NAME = "Search"

    def search(self, query: str) -> None:
        self.root.get_by_role("combobox", name=self._SEL_SEARCH_INPUT_NAME).fill(query)
        self.root.get_by_role("button", name=self._SEL_SEARCH_SUBMIT_NAME).click()

    The payoff of this small discipline:

    • One place to change when the markup shifts. You can grep for _SEL_ to audit every selector in the whole suite.
    • Intent is collected at the top of the class; the methods read as actions.
    • No "magic strings" scattered through method bodies.

    It's a minor habit, but reviewers read it as "this person has maintained a suite before, not just written one."

    Interview lens

    "How do you decide which locator to use?" → Recite the priority order and the why: "Role and label first, because they mirror how a user and assistive tech perceive the page and survive restyling. Test IDs when the app provides them. CSS only when there's no semantic anchor, preferring data-* over structural chains, and using comma fallbacks for volatile markup. XPath strictly last. And I never locate by position, because sites reorder elements." That one answer covers most of what "smart locators" means in an evaluation.

    Exercise 8.1 — climb the priority order

    Pick any real web form (a login page, a search page). For one input and one button, write a locator at each feasible level: get_by_role/get_by_label, then a CSS selector, then (peeking ahead to Chapter 9) an XPath. Reload the page a few times and notice which ones would survive a class rename and which wouldn't. Keep the highest one that uniquely identifies the element.

    Key idea

    Locate by perception (role, label, text), not construction (class, position). Climb down the priority order only as far as you must: role/label → text/test-id → CSS (with comma fallbacks) → XPath last. Never use positional selectors. Centralise every selector as a _SEL_ constant so there's exactly one place to fix when markup changes.

    Chapter 9 — XPath, Properly Understood¶

    XPath is a tool many automation engineers have used for years without ever really understanding it. By the end of this chapter you will understand it well enough to write it, read it, and explain why you usually shouldn't reach for it. That last part is what interviewers most want to hear.

    9.1 What XPath actually is¶

    XPath (XML Path Language) is a query language for navigating a tree of nodes. HTML, once parsed, is a tree (the DOM), so XPath can address any element by describing a path through that tree — much like a filesystem path addresses a file through directories.

    /html/body/div/ul/li/a        ← an absolute path, like /home/user/file.txt

    CSS selectors can also find elements, and for most jobs they're shorter and faster. XPath's distinguishing powers are:

    1. It can match on an element's text content (contains(text(), "Add")).
    2. It can walk upward and sideways (to a parent, ancestor, or sibling), not just downward.

    Those two abilities are the only reasons to choose XPath over CSS. If you need neither, use CSS.

    9.2 The anatomy of an XPath expression¶

    //ul[contains(@class, 'srp-results')]/li[contains(@class, 's-item')]//a
└┬┘└┬┘└──────────┬───────────────┘└┬┘└─┬─┘└────────┬──────────┘└┬┘└┬┘
 │  │            │                 │  │            │            │  │
 │ node         predicate         sep node     predicate       sep node
 axis          (a filter)              (a filter)

    Piece by piece:

    Axis / separators: / and //¶

    • / — direct child. ul/li = an li that is an immediate child of ul. (Same as CSS >.)
    • // — any descendant, at any depth. //a = any <a> anywhere below. (Same as CSS descendant — a space.)
    • A leading / means absolute from the document root; a leading // means relative — match anywhere. You almost always want // (relative); absolute paths from <html> are the most brittle locators in existence.

    Node test¶

    The element name: ul, li, a, div. Use * to match any element: //*[@id='main'] = any element with that id.

    Predicate: [ ... ]¶

    A filter in square brackets, applied to the node before it. This is where XPath's power lives:

    //li[@class='s-item']                  element whose class attribute EQUALS 's-item'
//li[contains(@class, 's-item')]       class attribute CONTAINS 's-item' (substring)
//button[text()='Add to cart']         element whose text EQUALS 'Add to cart'
//button[contains(text(), 'Add')]      text CONTAINS 'Add'
//a[@href]                             any <a> that HAS an href attribute
//li[3]                                the THIRD <li> (XPath is 1-indexed!)
//div[@id='cart'][@data-open='true']   two predicates = AND
    • @name reads an attribute (@class, @href, @id, @data-testid).
    • = is exact match; contains(haystack, needle) is substring match.
    • text() is the element's text node.
    • [n] selects by position, 1-indexed (XPath counts from 1, unlike almost everything else in programming).
    • Stacking [..][..] means logical AND.

    Gotcha — 1-indexed and = vs contains

    Two traps for newcomers: (1) //li[1] is the first item, not the second — XPath counts from 1. (2) [@class='s-item'] requires the class attribute to be exactly s-item; if the real markup is class="s-item s-item--large", that exact match fails. Use contains(@class, 's-item') for elements that carry multiple classes — which is most of them.

    Useful functions¶

    contains(@class, 'x')          substring match on an attribute
starts-with(@id, 'item-')      prefix match
normalize-space(text())        text with leading/trailing/collapsed whitespace removed
text()                         the text node
last()                         the last positional index: //li[last()]
not(@disabled)                 negation: //option[not(@disabled)]

    normalize-space() is the professional touch — raw text() includes stray whitespace and newlines from HTML formatting, so text()='Add to cart' can fail where normalize-space(text())='Add to cart' succeeds.

    9.3 Axes — XPath's superpower (walking up and sideways)¶

    CSS can only go down the tree (with limited recent exceptions). XPath can go anywhere via axes:

    //span[text()='$25.00']/parent::div            the element's direct parent
//span[@class='price']/ancestor::li            the nearest <li> ancestor
//label[text()='Size']/following-sibling::select   the <select> after that <label>
//td[text()='Total']/following::td[1]          the next <td> in document order

    The killer use case: "find the price that lives in the same card as this title." You locate the title by its text, then walk up to the shared <li> ancestor, then back down to the price. CSS cannot express "go up to my container" — this is the one job XPath is uniquely good at.

    //a[contains(text(), 'Nike Air')]/ancestor::li[contains(@class,'s-item')]//span[@class='s-item__price']
└─────────── find the title ──────────┘└──── walk up to its card ────┘└──── then down to price ────┘

    9.4 Using XPath in Playwright¶

    Prefix the selector with xpath=:

    page.locator("xpath=//ul[contains(@class,'srp-results')]//a[contains(@class,'s-item__link')]")

# A leading // is auto-detected as XPath, so this also works:
page.locator("//button[text()='Add to cart']")

    Auto-waiting and strict mode (Chapter 7) apply to XPath locators exactly as they do to any other — XPath only changes how you describe the element, not how Playwright acts on it.

    9.5 CSS ⇄ XPath translation table¶

    Goal CSS XPath
    Element by tag li //li
    Direct child ul > li //ul/li
    Any descendant ul li //ul//li
    By id #main //*[@id='main']
    By class (exact) .s-item //*[@class='s-item']
    By class (contains) [class~='s-item'] //*[contains(@class,'s-item')]
    By attribute [href] //*[@href]
    nth match li:nth-of-type(3) //li[3]
    By text (not possible) //button[text()='Buy']
    Parent (not possible) //span/parent::div
    Ancestor (not possible) //span/ancestor::li

    The bottom three rows are XPath's reason to exist. Everything above them, prefer CSS.

    9.6 Why we avoid XPath by default¶

    Given XPath is more powerful, why is it last in the priority order?

    • Brittleness. XPath tempts you into long positional chains (/div[2]/div/ul/li[3]/a) that break on any DOM edit. CSS discourages this (it has no clean ancestor axis, so you don't write 8-level paths).
    • Readability. get_by_role("button", name="Add to cart") states intent; //div[3]//button[1] states structure. The next maintainer can read the first and must reverse-engineer the second.
    • Performance. XPath evaluation is generally slower than CSS, and noticeably so on large pages with // (full-tree) scans.
    • No accessibility signal. A role locator doubles as an a11y check; an XPath positional chain tells you nothing about whether the page is usable.

    Key idea

    Use XPath only for its two unique powers — matching by text and walking to a parent/ancestor/sibling. For everything else CSS is shorter, faster, and less brittle, and role/label locators beat both. Never write positional XPath chains.

    9.7 A worked case: when a spec demands XPath¶

    Sometimes a specification (or an interviewer) explicitly requires XPath — for example, "retrieve the items using XPath." That creates a tension with the priority order you just learned. The reference project resolves it the senior way: role/CSS is the default everywhere, and there is one documented XPath method that satisfies the requirement:

    _SEL_CARD_LINKS_XPATH = (
    "//ul[contains(@class, 'srp-results')]"      # the results list (descendant)
    "/li[contains(@class, 's-item')]"            # each card (direct child)
    "//a[contains(@class, 's-item__link')]"      # the link within (descendant)
)

def card_links_via_xpath(self) -> list[str]:
    links = self.page.locator(f"xpath={self._SEL_CARD_LINKS_XPATH}")
    return [
        href
        for i in range(links.count())
        if (href := links.nth(i).get_attribute("href"))
    ]

    Notice the deliberate choices that make this good XPath rather than typical bad XPath:

    • // and / mixed intentionally, not a blind //a.
    • contains(@class, …), not @class='…', because eBay cards carry several classes.
    • No positional [n] anywhere — eBay shuffles result order per visitor, so position-based XPath would be flaky. We match by what the element is.
    • The walrus := keeps only links that actually have an href (Chapter 2.5).

    Interview lens — a model answer

    "My default is role/CSS locators because they survive restyling and read as intent. When a spec asks specifically for XPath, I add one documented XPath retrieval path — and I write it carefully: relative //, contains(@class,…) rather than exact match because the cards have multiple classes, and crucially no positional indices, since eBay reorders results per visitor. So it demonstrates I can write XPath and that I know its failure modes." This answer turns the one apparent rule-break in the repo into evidence of judgment.

    Exercise 9

    On any e-commerce page, open DevTools → Console and test XPath live with $x("//a[contains(@class,'product')]") (Chrome's $x() helper runs XPath). Then: (a) select an element by its visible text, (b) from that element, walk up to its containing card with ancestor::, (c) deliberately write a positional path and then a class-based one, and observe which survives if you delete a sibling node in the Elements panel.

    Chapter 10 — Actions & Assertions¶

    This chapter is the practical vocabulary of Playwright: the verbs that do things to a page, the methods that read state back out, and the assertions that check it. None of it is hard, but several pairs of methods look almost identical and behave differently, and those subtle differences cause real bugs. We'll go slowly through each one and show which to reach for and why.

    10.1 Input actions: making things happen¶

    These are the actions that simulate a user interacting with the page. Remember from Chapter 7 that every one of them auto-waits for the element to be actionable before it fires — you never precede them with a sleep.

    loc.fill("shoes")            # clear the field, then type this value (the usual choice)
loc.click()                  # click it (after auto-waiting)
loc.dblclick()               # double-click
loc.check()                  # tick a checkbox/radio (no-op if already ticked)
loc.uncheck()                # untick it
loc.select_option(label="Large")     # choose an <option> in a <select> by its visible text
loc.select_option(value="lg")        # ...or by the option's `value` attribute
loc.select_option(index=2)           # ...or by position
loc.hover()                  # move the mouse over it
loc.press("Enter")           # press a keyboard key while it's focused
loc.set_input_files("path/to/file.png")   # choose a file for a file <input>

    The one pair to be careful about is fill versus the older type:

    Gotcha — fill vs type (now press_sequentially)

    fill() sets the field's value in one atomic step (clearing any existing text first). It's what you want about 99% of the time. The older type() — renamed press_sequentially() — emits a separate key event for every character, which is slower and only necessary when the page reacts to individual keystrokes (an autocomplete that filters as you type, for instance). Defaulting to type everywhere makes tests needlessly slow and occasionally flaky. Use fill unless you have a specific reason not to.

    select_option is exactly how the variant service picks a size or colour:

    combo.select_option(label=random.choice(valid_labels))

    10.2 Reading state out of the page¶

    These methods read information rather than change it. Two pairs here are easy to mix up and worth dwelling on.

    loc.inner_text()          # the VISIBLE, rendered text (respects CSS, collapses whitespace)
loc.text_content()        # the RAW text content of the node (includes hidden text)
loc.get_attribute("href") # an attribute's value, or None if the attribute is absent
loc.input_value()         # the current value of an <input>/<textarea>/<select>
loc.is_visible()          # a boolean — is it visible RIGHT NOW? (does NOT wait)
loc.is_enabled()          # similarly, a right-now boolean
loc.count()               # how many elements this locator currently matches
loc.all_text_contents()   # a list of the text of EVERY matched element

    inner_text vs text_content. This distinction bites people:

    Gotcha — inner_text vs text_content

    inner_text returns what a user actually sees: visible text, with whitespace collapsed the way the browser renders it. text_content returns the raw text in the DOM, including text that's hidden with display:none and with all the original newlines and indentation. For a price you want inner_text() (giving a clean "$25.00"); for scraping a hidden data field you might want text_content(). Mixing them up yields surprising values — stray "Sale!" text that's visually hidden, or uncollapsed newlines. The reference components consistently use .inner_text().strip().

    is_visible() does not wait. This is the second trap:

    Gotcha — is_visible() is a snapshot, not a wait

    is_visible() answers "is it visible at this instant?" and returns immediately. It is not a wait. If you write assert loc.is_visible() while the element is still loading, you'll get intermittent failures. To wait for visibility, use expect(loc).to_be_visible() (§10.4). Reserve is_visible() for genuine branching — "is there a cookie banner present at all, yes or no?" — which is precisely how CookieBannerComponent decides whether to click.

    10.3 Iterating over many matched elements¶

    A locator can stand for many elements. To act on each in turn, get the count and index with nth(i):

    links = page.locator("a.s-item__link")
count = links.count()
for i in range(count):
    href = links.nth(i).get_attribute("href")
    print(href)

    nth(i) returns a locator for the i-th match, 0-indexed (the first is nth(0)). This is the exact pattern behind the reference project's "wrap each result card as its own component" factory (Chapter 19).

    When you just need the text of all matches at once, all_text_contents() does it in a single call — used by the variant service to read every dropdown option's label:

    labels = combo.locator("option:not([disabled])").all_text_contents()
# e.g. ["Small", "Medium", "Large"]

    10.4 Web-first assertions: the expect() matchers¶

    Chapter 7 introduced expect() as the retrying assertion. Here is its matcher vocabulary — each one polls the page until it passes or the timeout elapses, then fails with a clear, diffed message:

    from playwright.sync_api import expect

expect(loc).to_be_visible()
expect(loc).to_be_hidden()
expect(loc).to_be_enabled()
expect(loc).to_be_disabled()
expect(loc).to_be_checked()
expect(loc).to_have_text("Exact text")              # the full text equals this
expect(loc).to_contain_text("partial")               # the text contains this
expect(loc).to_have_value("shoes")                   # an input's current value
expect(loc).to_have_attribute("href", re.compile(r"/itm/"))
expect(loc).to_have_count(5)                          # exactly five matches
expect(loc).to_have_class(re.compile(r"active"))

expect(page).to_have_url(re.compile(r".*/sch/.*"))    # the page's URL
expect(page).to_have_title(re.compile(r"eBay"))       # the page's <title>

    Negate any of them with .not_:

    expect(loc).not_.to_be_visible()      # waits until it is NOT visible

    10.5 The decision: expect() versus plain assert¶

    This is the rule that, once internalised, keeps re-introduced flakiness out of an otherwise good suite:

    # The PAGE is still settling → use expect() (it retries / waits):
expect(results.first).to_be_visible()
expect(page).to_have_url(re.compile(r"/sch/"))

# A value you've ALREADY finished computing in Python → plain assert is fine:
urls = search.search_items_by_name_under_price("shoes", Decimal("220"), 5)
assert len(urls) > 0                  # `urls` is a finished list; nothing to wait for

subtotal = cart.subtotal()            # a Decimal you've already parsed out
assert subtotal <= budget

    Say it as a slogan: expect() for page state, plain assert for in-memory values. The most common way flakiness creeps back into a mature suite is someone writing assert loc.is_visible() (a one-shot snapshot) where the page hasn't finished rendering — use expect() there instead.

    Interview lens

    A frequent screening question: "What's the difference between assert x.is_visible() and expect(x).to_be_visible()?" → "is_visible() is a non-waiting boolean snapshot, so asserting on it is flaky if the element is still appearing. expect(...) .to_be_visible() retries until the timeout, so it actually waits for the state. I use expect for anything the page is still settling into, and plain assert only for values I've already finished computing." Crisp, correct, and shows you understand why.

    Exercise 10.1 — the two assertion styles

    On any site with a search box that loads results after submitting: (a) submit a query, (b) assert the results container expect(...).to_be_visible(), (c) assert the first result expect(...).to_contain_text(<your query>). Then deliberately replace one expect with assert loc.is_visible() and run the test ten times — observe the occasional failure, and understand exactly why it happens.

    Exercise 10.2 — read vs. see

    Find an element that contains some visually-hidden text (or add one with style="display:none"). Print both loc.inner_text() and loc.text_content() and compare. You've now seen why the distinction matters.

    Key idea

    Prefer fill over type; know inner_text (visible) vs text_content (raw); remember is_visible() is a non-waiting snapshot (use it for branching, not waiting); iterate matches with nth(i) (0-indexed). Assert page state with the retrying expect() matchers, and already-computed in-memory values with plain assert.

    Chapter 11 — Navigation, Network, Tabs & Cookies¶

    This chapter covers the mechanics of getting around: loading pages, building URLs safely, juggling multiple tabs, seeding session state with cookies, and handling the occasional dialog or iframe. These are the capabilities the authentication and cart flows are built on, and they round out your working knowledge of the page.

    11.1 Navigating to a page¶

    page.goto("https://www.ebay.com")                  # an absolute URL
page.goto("/sch/i.html?_nkw=shoes")                # a relative path (resolves against base_url)
page.goto(url, wait_until="domcontentloaded")      # navigate and wait for a specific load stage

    goto does two things: it navigates, and it waits for a load milestone before returning. Which milestone is controlled by wait_until:

    wait_until value Returns when… When to use
    "load" (default) the load event fires (all resources, images included) ordinary pages
    "domcontentloaded" the HTML is parsed, before images/CSS finish faster; good for heavy or SPA pages
    "commit" the server response is received rarely needed
    "networkidle" no network requests for 500ms discouraged on sites with polling/ads

    For most pages the default is fine. On a heavy site like eBay, "domcontentloaded" plus auto-waiting on the specific element you need next is both faster and more robust than waiting for every tracking pixel to load.

    Gotcha — avoid networkidle

    networkidle waits for the network to go quiet for half a second. On a real commercial site — full of analytics beacons, ads, and background polling — the network may never go quiet, so networkidle can hang until timeout or fluctuate run to run. Wait for the element you care about, not for the network to fall silent.

    base_url is what lets you navigate with short paths instead of full URLs — and it's the key to keeping hardcoded URLs out of your code (Chapter 21). You set it once on the context, then navigate by path:

    context = browser.new_context(base_url="https://www.ebay.com")
page.goto("/sch/i.html?_nkw=shoes")     # → https://www.ebay.com/sch/i.html?_nkw=shoes

    11.2 Building URLs safely¶

    Never assemble a query string by gluing strings together — special characters (spaces, &, =, non-ASCII) will break it or, worse, silently corrupt it. Use the standard library's urlencode, which escapes everything correctly:

    from urllib.parse import urlencode

qs = urlencode({"_nkw": "vintage camera"})    # "_nkw=vintage+camera"  (space encoded)
page.goto(f"/sch/i.html?{qs}")

    This is the same instinct as never building HTML or SQL by hand-concatenation: let a purpose-built function handle the escaping so an unusual input can't break — or exploit — your code.

    11.3 Working with multiple tabs¶

    A context can hold many tabs (pages). The cart flow opens each product in its own new tab, so the search-results tab stays exactly where it was:

    tab = context.new_page()       # a fresh tab in the SAME context (shares cookies, cart, session)
try:
    tab.goto(url)
    item = ItemPage(tab)
    item.add_to_cart()
finally:
    tab.close()                # always close it, even if add_to_cart raised

    Two properties of this pattern matter:

    • The new tab shares the context's session. Because context.new_page() creates the tab inside the same context, it shares cookies and the cart. That's essential — an item added in the new tab really does appear in the cart you later assert against. (A tab in a different context would be a separate session and wouldn't share the cart.)
    • try/finally guarantees cleanup. The tab is closed whether the body succeeded or threw, so a long run doesn't leak dozens of tabs. (This is the manual form of the context-manager idea from Chapter 5.)

    When the site itself opens a tab — say, clicking a link with target="_blank" — you capture the new page like this:

    with context.expect_page() as new_page_info:
    page.get_by_role("link", name="Open in new tab").click()
new_tab = new_page_info.value      # the page the site just opened

    11.4 Cookies and seeding session state¶

    You can write cookies straight into a context before navigating. This is how the authentication flow pins region and currency without going through a login form:

    context.add_cookies([
    {"name": "ebay_region",   "value": "US",  "domain": ".ebay.com", "path": "/"},
    {"name": "ebay_currency", "value": "USD", "domain": ".ebay.com", "path": "/"},
])

    Each cookie needs at least a name, a value, and either a url or a domain + path.

    For real authentication, the professional pattern is storage state: log in once, save the entire session (cookies plus localStorage) to a file, and load that file into every test's context so each test starts already logged in — no repeated logins:

    # Once (e.g. in a setup step), after logging in:
context.storage_state(path="auth.json")            # save the whole session to a file

# Then, in every test:
context = browser.new_context(storage_state="auth.json")   # start ALREADY authenticated

    Interview lens

    "How would you handle login without doing it in every single test?" → "storageState: authenticate once, persist cookies and localStorage to a file, and load it into each test's context, so every test starts authenticated in milliseconds — no repeated logins, no rate-limit risk. For a site whose login is gated by captcha, or where the flow under test is fully reachable as a guest, I might skip login entirely and just seed the cookies I need." This shows you know the real-world pattern and when it isn't necessary.

    11.5 Dialogs (alert, confirm, prompt)¶

    Native browser dialogs block the page until dismissed. Register a handler before the action that triggers one:

    page.on("dialog", lambda dialog: dialog.accept())   # auto-accept any dialog
# (or dialog.dismiss(), or dialog.accept("typed text") to answer a prompt)
page.get_by_role("button", name="Delete").click()

    If you don't register a handler, Playwright auto-dismisses dialogs by default — which is usually what you want for stray "are you sure you want to leave?" prompts.

    11.6 Frames (iframes)¶

    Content inside an <iframe> is a separate document; an ordinary page.locator(...) won't see into it. You enter the frame first, then locate within it:

    frame = page.frame_locator("iframe#checkout")
frame.get_by_role("button", name="Pay").click()

    frame_locator returns a scope you chain locators onto, just like a component's root. Embedded payment widgets, maps, and some consent banners live in iframes — so if a locator "can't find" an element you can clearly see on the page, suspect an iframe.

    11.7 Waiting explicitly — the rare legitimate cases¶

    Auto-waiting (Chapter 7) handles almost everything. But occasionally you must wait on a condition that isn't "an element became actionable" — and there are proper tools for that, none of which is time.sleep:

    page.wait_for_url(re.compile(r"/cart"))            # wait for the URL to change
page.wait_for_load_state("domcontentloaded")       # wait for a load milestone
page.wait_for_response(lambda r: "/api/cart" in r.url and r.status == 200)  # a network response
loc.wait_for(state="visible", timeout=2000)         # an element state, with a custom timeout

    The cookie-banner component uses that last one as a bounded probe:

    def is_visible(self) -> bool:
    try:
        self._accept_button().wait_for(state="visible", timeout=2000)
    except PlaywrightTimeoutError:
        return False        # not here within 2s → there's no banner
    return True

    This is a legitimate explicit wait: a bounded "is it here within 2 seconds? if not, there isn't one" probe followed by a branch — completely different from a blind sleep.

    Gotcha — these are NOT time.sleep

    Every method above waits for a named condition — a URL, a response, an element state — and returns the instant that condition is met. time.sleep(n) waits for the clock, regardless of whether anything is ready. If you ever feel the urge to sleep, identify the condition you're actually waiting for and wait for that instead.

    Exercise 11.1 — tabs share a session

    In a script, create a context, open page = context.new_page(), set a cookie via context.add_cookies([...]), then open a second tab tab = context.new_page() and navigate it to a page that reads cookies. Confirm the second tab sees the cookie — that is the shared session that makes the cart flow work.

    Key idea

    goto with a sensible wait_until (avoid networkidle on busy sites); build URLs with urlencode; new tabs from the same context share the session (so the cart persists) and should be closed in finally; seed sessions with add_cookies or storage_state; handle dialogs with a pre-registered handler and iframe content via frame_locator; and when you must wait explicitly, wait for a named condition, never the clock.

    Part III — pytest & Test Engineering

    Chapter 12 — pytest Fundamentals¶

    pytest is the test runner the Python world has standardised on. Its philosophy is refreshingly minimal: a test is just a function, and an assertion is just Python's assert keyword. On top of that simple base sits a powerful system called fixtures (the next chapter). This chapter covers the simple base thoroughly, so the fixtures chapter has solid ground to build on.

    12.1 A test is a function whose name starts with test_¶

    That's the entire rule for the simplest case:

    # tests/test_example.py
def test_addition():
    assert 1 + 1 == 2

    You run your tests with the pytest command (here, through uv run so it uses the project's environment):

    uv run pytest                       # find and run every test in the project
uv run pytest tests/test_example.py # run just one file
uv run pytest tests/test_example.py::test_addition   # run one specific test
uv run pytest -k "addition"         # run tests whose name matches "addition"
uv run pytest -v                    # verbose: print one line per test
uv run pytest -x                    # stop at the first failure
uv run pytest -ra                   # print a summary of skips and failures at the end

    -k and -v and -x are the flags you'll reach for daily: filter by name, see each test individually, and fail fast while debugging.

    12.2 How pytest finds tests (discovery by convention)¶

    You never register a test or list it in a manifest. pytest discovers tests by following naming conventions:

    • in files named test_*.py or *_test.py,
    • located within the paths you configure (the reference project sets testpaths = ["tests"] in pyproject.toml),
    • it collects functions named test_*,
    • and methods named test_* inside classes named Test*.

    That convention-over-configuration approach is why you can drop a new test_whatever.py into tests/ and it just runs.

    Gotcha — a non-test class named Test...

    Because pytest collects classes named Test*, a perfectly ordinary class that happens to start with "Test" gets mistaken for a test class. The reference project has a TestDatabase class (a data loader, not tests) and silences this by setting a class attribute: __test__ = False. If you ever name a non-test class Test... and see pytest emit a warning about it, that attribute is the fix.

    12.3 Plain assert — and why pytest's is special¶

    pytest does not give you a matcher library like some frameworks (no expect(x).toBe(y)). You use Python's built-in assert statement. What makes pytest's special is assertion rewriting: pytest inspects your assert and, on failure, prints a rich, introspected breakdown of why it failed — for free:

    def test_list():
    urls = ["a", "b"]
    assert len(urls) == 3

    >       assert len(urls) == 3
E       assert 2 == 3
E        +  where 2 = len(['a', 'b'])

    Notice you didn't ask for any of that detail — pytest shows the operands, the comparison, and even what produced the left-hand value. You can add a custom message after a comma, which is good practice for assertions whose failure isn't self-explanatory:

    assert len(urls) >= scenario.min_results, (
    f"scenario {scenario.id}: expected at least {scenario.min_results}, got {len(urls)}"
)

    From TypeScript

    Jest/Mocha give you a matcher DSL (expect(x).toEqual(y)). pytest instead uses the plain language assert plus compiler-level rewriting for good messages — fewer APIs to learn, and the language itself is the assertion library. (Don't confuse this with Playwright's expect() from Chapter 10, which is a separate thing, used only for page state.)

    12.4 Testing that something raises an exception¶

    Often the correct behaviour is to raise — and you want to assert that it does. Use pytest.raises as a context manager:

    import pytest

def test_parser_rejects_garbage():
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="no numeric value"):
        parse_price("Time left: 3d 4h")

    This asserts two things: that the block raises a ValueError, and (via match, a regex) that its message contains "no numeric value". If the block doesn't raise, or raises a different type, the test fails. This is exactly how the price parser's "refuses to guess" behaviour is pinned down (Chapter 16).

    12.5 Setup and teardown — and why fixtures replace them¶

    Tests usually need something set up first — a database connection, a browser page, some data. Older testing frameworks use setUp/tearDown methods that run before and after each test. pytest can do that, but its real mechanism is far more flexible: fixtures — functions that produce the things a test needs, which a test receives simply by naming them as parameters:

    def test_search_returns_results(page):     # "page" is a fixture, supplied by pytest
    page.goto("https://www.ebay.com")
    ...

    You didn't create page. You requested it by putting it in the parameter list, and pytest supplied a ready-made one. That is dependency injection, and it is the single most important pytest concept — important enough to get its own chapter next. For now, just register the shape: a test names what it needs, and pytest provides it.

    12.6 Skipping tests and marking expected failures¶

    Sometimes a test shouldn't run, or is known to fail. Say so explicitly, with a reason:

    @pytest.mark.skip(reason="login is gated by captcha — out of scope")
def test_login(): ...

@pytest.mark.skipif(sys.platform == "win32", reason="POSIX-only behaviour")
def test_unix_thing(): ...

@pytest.mark.xfail(reason="known bug TICKET-123; remove this mark when fixed")
def test_known_bug(): ...
    • skip — never run this test.
    • skipif(condition, ...) — run it only when the condition is false.
    • xfail — "expected to fail." It runs, but a failure is expected and doesn't fail the suite; and crucially, if it unexpectedly passes, pytest flags it ("xpassed") so you remember to remove the mark. This lets you track a known bug without a permanently red build.

    Interview lens

    "How do you handle a test for a feature that's temporarily broken or out of scope?" → "skip with a reason string, so the report records why it didn't run; or xfail for a known bug, so a future fix surfaces as an unexpected pass that prompts me to remove the marker. I never silently comment a test out — that destroys the signal and loses the reason." Emphasising the reason string is what signals discipline here.

    Exercise 12.1 — write three tests

    Create tests/test_math.py with: one passing test; one failing test with a custom assert message (run it and read pytest's introspected output); and one using pytest.raises to confirm 1 / 0 raises ZeroDivisionError. Run with -v, then with -x, and observe the difference.

    Key idea

    A test is a test_* function, discovered by convention. Assertions are plain assert, with rich rewritten failure messages for free. pytest.raises tests error paths. skip/skipif/xfail (always with a reason) preserve the signal for tests that can't or shouldn't pass right now. And dependencies arrive through fixtures — the subject of the next chapter.

    Chapter 13 — Fixtures & Dependency Injection¶

    Fixtures are pytest's defining feature and the concept interviewers probe hardest. They're also the thing that makes conftest.py look like magic until it clicks. This chapter takes fixtures from "I copied this and it worked" to "I understand exactly what pytest is doing and why." We build up slowly, with examples at each step.

    13.1 What a fixture is¶

    A fixture is a function that produces something a test needs. You mark it with the @pytest.fixture decorator. A test then requests that thing by listing the fixture's name as one of its parameters:

    import pytest

@pytest.fixture
def db():                          # a fixture named "db" that produces a TestDatabase
    return TestDatabase("db")

def test_scenarios_load(db):       # this test REQUESTS "db" by naming it as a parameter
    assert len(db.scenarios.all()) > 0

    Here is exactly what pytest does when it runs test_scenarios_load:

    1. It looks at the test's parameters and sees one named db.
    2. It searches for a fixture named db — and finds the function above.
    3. It calls that fixture function.
    4. It passes the return value into the test as the db argument.

    So you never write db = TestDatabase("db") inside your test. You declare a need ("I need a db") and pytest fulfils it. That separation — the test says what it needs, the fixture system handles how to build it — is called dependency injection.

    From TypeScript

    This is precisely Angular/NestJS constructor injection, or any DI container resolving providers — except keyed by parameter name rather than by type. If you've written constructor(private db: Database) and let the framework supply the instance, you already understand fixtures. The page fixture from pytest-playwright is a provider you didn't write, resolved the same way.

    13.2 Fixtures can request other fixtures (a dependency graph)¶

    This is where the power appears. A fixture can itself request other fixtures, and pytest resolves the whole chain for you, top to bottom:

    @pytest.fixture
def profile():
    return os.getenv("PROFILE", "dev")        # depends on nothing

@pytest.fixture
def db():
    return TestDatabase("db")                 # depends on nothing

@pytest.fixture
def env(db, profile):                         # depends on db AND profile
    return db.environments.get(profile)

@pytest.fixture
def search_service(page, env):                # depends on `page` (from the plugin) AND env
    return SearchService(page, env)

def test_x(search_service):                   # the test needs only ONE thing
    ...

    When test_x requests search_service, pytest must first build search_service's dependencies (page and env), and to build env it must first build db and profile. It works all of this out automatically and assembles a fully-wired SearchService — and the test simply lists search_service. This is exactly how the reference project's conftest.py constructs its services: each service fixture pulls in the page/context/env it needs, and tests just ask for search_service, cart_service, and so on.

    Pictured, pytest resolves the graph from the test downward, building each dependency in turn:

    flowchart TD
    T["test_x(search_service)"]
    SS["search_service"]
    PG["page<br/>(from pytest-playwright)"]
    EN["env"]
    DB["db"]
    PR["profile"]
    T --> SS
    SS --> PG
    SS --> EN
    EN --> DB
    EN --> PR

    Interview lens

    "How are your page objects and services instantiated in tests?" → "Constructor injection via pytest fixtures. Each service has a fixture that pulls in the page/context/env it needs; fixtures form a dependency graph pytest resolves automatically, so a test just lists search_service as a parameter and receives a fully-wired instance. No new scattered through tests, no globals — and because the wiring is in fixtures, I can swap a real dependency for a fake in one place." That last clause hints you understand testability, which lands well.

    13.3 Scope: how often a fixture is built¶

    By default, a fixture runs once per test (this is called function scope). You can widen the scope so one instance is shared across more tests — trading isolation for speed:

    @pytest.fixture(scope="session")    # built ONCE for the entire test run
def db():
    return TestDatabase("db")

@pytest.fixture(scope="function")   # the default — rebuilt fresh for every test
def search_service(page, env):
    ...
    Scope Built Good for
    function (default) once per test anything stateful or mutable; the page
    class once per test class shared setup for a group of tests
    module once per file expensive read-only setup used across a file
    session once for the whole run immutable config, the loaded database, the browser

    The governing principle: the more state a fixture shares across tests, the more opportunities for one test to corrupt another. Use a wide scope like session only for things that are immutable or genuinely safe to share — configuration, the loaded data, the launched browser. Use the default function scope for anything a test might change. In the reference project, db/env/profile are session-scoped (read-only config) while page/context and the services are function-scoped (fresh and isolated per test).

    Gotcha — shared mutable state via wide scope

    A session-scoped fixture that holds mutable state leaks that state between tests: one test's changes bleed into the next, producing failures that depend on the order tests ran in — among the most miserable bugs to track down. When in doubt, default to function scope; only widen it when you're sure the thing is safe to share.

    13.4 Setup and teardown with yield¶

    Many fixtures need to clean up after the test. A fixture that uses yield instead of return splits naturally into setup (before yield), the value handed to the test (the yielded value), and teardown (after yield) — and the teardown is guaranteed to run, even if the test fails:

    @pytest.fixture
def temp_cart(context):
    cart = create_cart(context)         # ← SETUP runs before the test
    yield cart                          # ← the test runs here, receiving `cart`
    cart.empty()                        # ← TEARDOWN runs after the test, always

def test_with_cart(temp_cart):
    ...                                 # uses temp_cart; when it ends, control returns
                                        # to the fixture and cart.empty() fires

    Trace the flow: pytest runs the fixture up to yield, hands the yielded cart to the test, the test runs, and when it finishes (pass or fail) execution resumes after the yield to do cleanup.

    From TypeScript

    A yield-style fixture is beforeEach and afterEach fused into one function, with the setup and its matching teardown sitting right next to each other so they can't drift apart. Everything before yield is beforeEach; everything after is afterEach.

    13.5 conftest.py: shared fixtures with no imports¶

    Where do you put fixtures that many test files need? In a specially-named file: conftest.py. Fixtures defined there are automatically available to every test in that directory and all subdirectories — you never import them. It is pytest's convention for "shared test infrastructure."

    tests/
├── conftest.py        # fixtures here are visible to EVERY test below — no imports needed
├── test_smoke.py      # can use db, env, page, search_service, ... just by naming them
└── unit/
    └── test_x.py      # also sees tests/conftest.py's fixtures

    This is why the reference project's tests can request search_service with no visible import — it's defined in tests/conftest.py. conftest.py is also where you put plugin-configuration hooks and overrides (the next two sections, and Chapter 15).

    13.6 autouse: fixtures that run without being requested¶

    Occasionally you want some setup to apply to every test automatically, without each test listing it. Set autouse=True:

    @pytest.fixture(autouse=True)
def _set_region_cookies(request, env):
    if not _uses_browser(request):     # skip for unit tests that have no browser
        yield
        return
    context = request.getfixturevalue("context")
    context.add_cookies([...])         # seed cookies before EVERY browser-based test
    yield

    autouse=True means "apply to every test in scope, requested or not." Use it sparingly, for genuinely cross-cutting setup like seeding cookies, configuring logging, or writing a report file. Notice the reference project's version guards itself: it checks whether the test actually uses a browser (via request.fixturenames) and does nothing for unit tests, so the fast no-browser tests don't get saddled with browser setup. That guard is a thoughtful detail worth being able to point at.

    Gotcha — unguarded autouse fixtures

    An autouse fixture runs for every test in its directory tree, including ones that don't need it. An unguarded autouse fixture that, say, launches a browser would force your fast unit tests to spin up Chromium for no reason. Always ask "does every test in scope truly need this?" — and if not, guard it (as above) or move it to a narrower location.

    13.7 The request object¶

    request is a built-in fixture that gives a fixture (or test) metadata about the test currently running:

    @pytest.fixture
def screenshots(page, request):
    return ScreenshotManager(page, test_id=request.node.nodeid)   # name files after the test

# Commonly used members:
request.fixturenames                 # the names of all fixtures this test uses
request.getfixturevalue("context")   # fetch a fixture by name, at runtime
request.node.nodeid                  # e.g. "tests/test_search.py::test_full[param]"

    request.getfixturevalue("context") lazily resolves a fixture by name — which is exactly how the autouse cookie fixture in §13.6 pulls in context only when a browser test actually needs it, rather than declaring it as a parameter (which would force it on every test).

    Exercise 13.1 — build a dependency graph

    Write three fixtures: raw_config (returns a dict), setting (depends on raw_config, returns one key from it), and a test that requests only setting. Confirm it works — you've built a two-level dependency graph and let pytest resolve it. Then add a fourth fixture using yield that prints "setup" before and "teardown" after; request it in the test and watch the order of the printed lines.

    Key idea

    Fixtures are dependency injection by parameter name; they compose into a graph pytest resolves automatically. Scope trades isolation for speed (default function; reserve session for immutable or shared things). yield fuses setup with guaranteed teardown. conftest.py shares fixtures with no imports. autouse applies cross-cutting setup (always guard it). Together these are the entire backbone of a real conftest.py.

    Chapter 14 — Data-Driven Testing¶

    "Data-driven" testing is a standard requirement of professional suites and a common point of evaluation. The core idea is simple and powerful: separate the test logic from the test data. Write the test body once, then run it against many sets of inputs — ideally inputs that live in an external file so they can be edited without touching code. This chapter builds from the basic tool up to loading scenarios from a YAML file.

    14.1 @pytest.mark.parametrize: one body, many cases¶

    The foundational tool is the parametrize marker. It generates several separate tests from a single function, one per row of data you supply:

    import pytest
from decimal import Decimal

@pytest.mark.parametrize(
    "text, expected",                       # (1) the parameter names
    [                                        # (2) a list of value tuples
        ("$25.00", Decimal("25.00")),
        ("US $1,234.56", Decimal("1234.56")),
        ("$25.00 to $30.00", Decimal("25.00")),
        ("Subtotal (3 items) $50.00", Decimal("50.00")),
    ],
)
def test_parse_price(text, expected):       # (3) parameters match the names in (1)
    assert parse_price(text) == expected
    1. The first argument is a string naming the parameters ("text, expected").
    2. The second is a list of tuples — each tuple supplies one value per named parameter.
    3. The test function receives those parameters and uses them.

    This produces four independent tests, each with its own pass/fail result. pytest reports them separately:

    test_parse_price[$25.00-expected0] PASSED
test_parse_price[US $1,234.56-expected1] PASSED
test_parse_price[$25.00 to $30.00-expected2] PASSED
test_parse_price[Subtotal (3 items) $50.00-expected3] PASSED

    Why generate separate tests instead of looping?

    You could write for text, expected in cases: assert parse_price(text) == expected inside one test. But then the first failing case stops the loop, hiding the rest, and the report shows a single test rather than telling you which input broke. Parametrization runs every case independently and pinpoints exactly which one failed. Always prefer it to an in-test loop.

    From TypeScript

    @pytest.mark.parametrize ≈ Jest's test.each([...]) / it.each. Same payoff: one body, many cases, each reported separately.

    14.2 Readable test IDs¶

    By default pytest builds an ID for each case from its values (expected0, expected1, …), which can be cryptic. Supply your own with ids= to make the report self-documenting:

    @pytest.mark.parametrize(
    "text, expected",
    [("$25.00", Decimal("25.00")), ("US $1,234.56", Decimal("1234.56"))],
    ids=["plain-dollars", "us-prefixed-thousands"],
)
def test_parse_price(text, expected): ...

    test_parse_price[plain-dollars] PASSED
test_parse_price[us-prefixed-thousands] PASSED

    Now a failure report reads like documentation: you know instantly which kind of input broke.

    14.3 Stacking parametrize (a test matrix)¶

    Two parametrize decorators on the same test multiply together into every combination:

    @pytest.mark.parametrize("query", ["shoes", "books"])
@pytest.mark.parametrize("limit", [3, 5])
def test_search(query, limit): ...
# runs 2 × 2 = 4 combinations: (shoes,3) (shoes,5) (books,3) (books,5)

    Useful for small matrices, but combinations multiply fast — keep them intentional and small, or you'll generate hundreds of slow tests by accident.

    14.4 The real thing: data from an external file¶

    Inline lists are perfect for a pure function like the price parser. But richer scenarios — "search for X, cap the price at $Y, expect at least N results" — belong in an external, editable file, so that the data lives apart from the logic and even non-programmers can add cases. The reference project uses YAML:

    # db/data.yaml
scenarios:
  regression-bluetooth-speakers:
    query: bluetooth speaker
    max_price: "50.00"
    limit: 10
    min_results: 10
    allow_partial: false
    tags: [regression]

    To turn external rows into tests, pytest gives you a hook called pytest_generate_tests, which runs during test collection and can parametrize any test that requests a particular fixture. Put it in conftest.py:

    def pytest_generate_tests(metafunc):
    if "scenario" in metafunc.fixturenames:        # only tests that ask for a `scenario`
        db = TestDatabase("db")
        scenarios = db.scenarios.where(tag="regression")
        metafunc.parametrize("scenario", scenarios, ids=lambda s: s.id)

    Now any test with a scenario parameter runs once per regression row in the file:

    @pytest.mark.regression
def test_scenario(scenario, search_service, cart_service):
    urls = search_service.search_items_by_name_under_price(
        scenario.query, scenario.max_price, scenario.limit
    )
    ...

    The payoff is the property that earns "data-driven" marks: adding a test is now a data edit, not a code edit. Drop a new scenario into data.yaml and a new parametrized test appears automatically, with no change to the test body.

    From TypeScript

    pytest_generate_tests is dynamic test.each whose cases are loaded from a file at collection time — like reading a JSON fixture and calling it.each(rows), except pytest wires it directly into discovery so each row becomes a first-class, separately-reported test.

    Visualised, the flow from a YAML row to many parametrized tests:

    flowchart LR
    YAML["data.yaml<br/>(scenarios)"]
    Load["TestDatabase loader<br/>(typed dataclasses;<br/>money → Decimal)"]
    Hook["pytest_generate_tests<br/>(filter by tag)"]
    T1["test_scenario[bluetooth-speakers]"]
    T2["test_scenario[vintage-postcards]"]
    T3["test_scenario[leather-wallets]"]
    YAML --> Load --> Hook
    Hook --> T1
    Hook --> T2
    Hook --> T3

    14.5 Why parse data into typed objects, not raw dicts¶

    Look closely at the test above: it uses scenario.query and scenario.max_price — attribute access on a typed Scenario object — not scenario["query"] on a raw dictionary. That's deliberate. The loader (Chapter 21) parses each YAML row into a frozen dataclass, converting max_price into a Decimal at load time. The benefits:

    • Typos fail loudly and early. scenario.qurey raises an AttributeError immediately; scenario["qurey"] on a dict raises a KeyError only if you're lucky, or silently returns None if you used .get().
