    • Money is a Decimal everywhere downstream, because the conversion happens once, at the boundary where the data enters the system — not sprinkled through the test code.
    • Editor autocomplete and type-checking work on scenario. — the editor knows the fields.

    Interview lens

    "How is your suite data-driven?" → "Scenario rows live in an external YAML file, loaded into typed, frozen dataclasses with money parsed to Decimal at load time. A pytest_generate_tests hook parametrizes the end-to-end test from those rows, filtered by tag — so adding a scenario is a one-line YAML edit with zero code change. For pure functions like the price parser, I use inline parametrize for their many format cases." That answer covers both flavours and the typing discipline behind them.

    Exercise 14.1 — data-driven from a file

    Create a small cases.yaml with three login scenarios (username, password, expect_ok). In conftest.py, load it and use pytest_generate_tests to parametrize a test_login(scenario) that just asserts on the fields (no real login needed). Run pytest -v and confirm three separately-named tests appear. Then add a fourth row, re-run, and confirm a fourth test appears with no code change. You've just built a data-driven suite.

    Key idea

    Separate logic from data. Use parametrize for inline cases (one body, many separately- reported tests), and pytest_generate_tests to generate tests from an external file at collection time. Parse each external row into a typed dataclass at the boundary, so the rest of the suite enjoys type safety, Decimal-correct money, and autocomplete — and adding a scenario becomes a data edit, not a code change.

    Chapter 15 — Markers, Parallelism & the pytest-playwright Plugin¶

    This chapter covers the operational layer of pytest: how to tag tests so you can run subsets of them, how to run them in parallel for speed, and the plugin that manages Playwright's lifecycle so you never have to. These are the tools that turn a pile of tests into a suite you can actually operate day to day.

    15.1 Markers: tagging tests¶

    A marker is a label you attach to a test with a decorator. It lets you group and select tests later:

    import pytest

@pytest.mark.smoke
def test_home_loads(page): ...

@pytest.mark.regression
def test_full_e2e(...): ...

    You should register your markers in pyproject.toml so pytest doesn't warn about "unknown markers" (and so there's a documented list of what each means):

    [tool.pytest.ini_options]
markers = [
    "smoke: fast critical-path tests — run before every deploy",
    "regression: the full regression suite — run nightly",
    "slow: long-running tests — run in a dedicated pipeline",
]

    Then you select tests by marker with the -m flag, which accepts a boolean expression:

    uv run pytest -m smoke                 # only tests marked smoke
uv run pytest -m regression            # only regression
uv run pytest -m "not slow"            # everything except slow tests
uv run pytest -m "smoke or regression" # either

    Interview lens

    "How do you organise which tests run when?" → "By marker, not by directory. smoke for the fast critical path on every push, regression nightly, slow in a dedicated pipeline. CI runs -m regression; locally I run -m smoke for quick feedback. Organising by marker means a test's speed and role is a property of the test itself, not of where its file happens to live — and a single test can carry several tags." (This is, incidentally, why a suite organised this way doesn't need separate smoke/ and regression/ folders — selection is by marker.)

    15.2 Parallelism with pytest-xdist¶

    By default pytest runs tests one after another. The pytest-xdist plugin runs them across several worker processes at once, which can cut a multi-minute suite dramatically:

    uv run pytest -m regression -n 4        # spread across 4 worker processes
uv run pytest -n auto                   # one worker per CPU core

    The crucial requirement: because each worker is a separate process with its own browser and its own contexts, your tests must be independent — no shared mutable state, no assumptions about the order tests run in. This is exactly where the function-scoped, isolated context from Chapter 6 and Chapter 13 pays off: because every test already gets its own clean session, your tests parallelise safely with no extra work.

    Gotcha — parallelism exposes hidden coupling

    Running with -n 4 is unforgiving of hidden dependencies between tests. If two tests both write to the same file, share a session, or rely on running in a particular order, parallel execution will surface it as seemingly-random failures. The fix is never "turn off parallelism" — it's "remove the shared state." Process-level isolation (a separate browser context per worker) is precisely what makes safe parallelism possible.

    From TypeScript

    -n auto ≈ Jest's default parallel workers, or Playwright Test's workers setting. Same contract everywhere: tests must be independent. Python parallelises across processes (which also sidesteps the Global Interpreter Lock), so each worker launches its own browser.

    15.3 The pytest-playwright plugin: lifecycle for free¶

    Installing the pytest-playwright plugin gives you a set of fixtures that own Playwright's entire lifecycle, so you never write sync_playwright(), launch(), or close() in a test:

    Fixture Scope What it provides
    playwright session the Playwright runtime
    browser session one launched browser, shared across the run
    context function a fresh, isolated context per test
    page function a fresh page inside that context 
    def test_home(page):          # a fresh page + context, automatically torn down afterwards
    page.goto("https://www.ebay.com")

    It also adds command-line flags for the things you'd otherwise have to wire by hand:

    uv run pytest --headed                 # show the browser window
uv run pytest --browser firefox        # chromium | firefox | webkit
uv run pytest --slowmo 200
uv run pytest --tracing retain-on-failure
uv run pytest --video retain-on-failure
uv run pytest --screenshot only-on-failure

    Interview lens

    "Why use the plugin instead of launching Playwright yourself inside the test?" → "The plugin owns the runtime/browser/context/page lifecycle, gives every test a fresh isolated context, and wires up trace/video/screenshot capture and xdist parallelism for free. Launching Playwright by hand inside a test throws all of that away — no automatic trace on failure, no isolation, no parallel safety. It's literally one of the bugs in the AI-generated-code review in Chapter 26."

    15.4 Overriding the plugin's defaults¶

    The plugin's launch and context settings are themselves fixtures, which you can override in conftest.py to inject your own configuration. The pattern is: request the plugin's fixture by the same name, spread its existing value, and add your overrides:

    @pytest.fixture(scope="session")
def browser_type_launch_args(browser_type_launch_args, env):
    return {**browser_type_launch_args, "headless": env.headless, "slow_mo": env.slow_mo_ms}

@pytest.fixture(scope="session")
def browser_context_args(browser_context_args, env):
    return {
        **browser_context_args,
        "base_url": env.base_url,
        "locale": f"en-{env.region}",
        "viewport": {"width": 1440, "height": 900},
    }

    This is how the reference project drives headless/slow-mo/base-url from its Environment configuration without forking the plugin. The {**existing, "key": value} syntax is a dict merge — it starts from the plugin's defaults and layers your settings on top. (Dict merge is covered in Appendix C; it's the same idea as JS object spread {...existing, key: value}.)

    From TypeScript

    Overriding browser_context_args ≈ extending Playwright Test's use: {} config block — baseURL, locale, viewport, trace. Same knobs, surfaced here as fixtures you compose rather than a static config object.

    15.5 Configure capture once, in addopts¶

    The flags you always want can live in pyproject.toml under addopts, so every run captures diagnostics without you remembering the flags:

    [tool.pytest.ini_options]
addopts = "--tracing=retain-on-failure --video=retain-on-failure --screenshot=only-on-failure"

    The magic value is retain-on-failure: it keeps the trace and video only for tests that fail. So you get rich debugging artifacts exactly where you need them — failures — without filling your disk with recordings of the 99% of tests that pass. Configure it once; it applies to the whole suite.

    Exercise 15.1 — markers and selection

    Take any project with a few tests. Mark two of them @pytest.mark.smoke and register the marker in pyproject.toml. Run pytest -m smoke and confirm only those two run. Then run pytest -m "not smoke" and confirm the rest run. You've just built selectable test suites with no folders.

    Key idea

    Markers tag tests for selection with -m (organise by role, not by folder). pytest-xdist runs tests across parallel processes — safe precisely because each test's context is isolated. The pytest-playwright plugin owns the browser lifecycle and adds trace/video/screenshot capture; override browser_context_args / browser_type_launch_args to inject config without forking it. Put always-on capture in addopts with retain-on-failure.

    Chapter 16 — The Test Pyramid & Why Unit Tests¶

    Unit testing is the discipline that experienced end-to-end engineers most often skip, and the gap that most often makes an otherwise strong engineer look junior under questioning. It is also one of the easiest gaps to close. This chapter explains the economics of different test types, why a pure function is the unit-testing sweet spot, and how to write unit tests that pay for themselves many times over.

    16.1 The three layers of tests¶

    Tests come in layers, conventionally drawn as a pyramid:

            ╱╲          End-to-end (E2E / UI) tests
       ╱  ╲         few; slow (seconds); a real browser; high confidence;
      ╱────╲        brittle; expensive to maintain
     ╱      ╲       Integration tests
    ╱        ╲      some; medium speed; several units together (e.g. with a real DB)
   ╱──────────╲     Unit tests
  ╱            ╲    many; fast (milliseconds); one function in isolation; pinpoint failures
 ╱──────────────╲
    • A unit test exercises one function or class in isolation, in memory, with no I/O. It runs in milliseconds.
    • An integration test exercises several units together, possibly with a real dependency like a database or the filesystem. Medium speed.
    • An end-to-end test drives the whole stack through a real browser — the most realistic, but slow and prone to flakiness.

    The "pyramid" is a prescription about proportions: have many fast unit tests at the base, fewer integration tests, and a thin layer of end-to-end tests covering only the most important user journeys. The reasoning is economic, and worth understanding rather than memorising.

    16.2 Why not test everything end-to-end?¶

    End-to-end tests are the most convincing — they exercise the real product — but they are the worst on almost every other axis:

    Property Unit test End-to-end test
    Speed milliseconds seconds to minutes
    Flakiness essentially none network, timing, third-party site changes
    Diagnosing a failure points at the exact line "something in the flow broke"
    Setup cost none a browser, fixtures, a live site
    Confidence per test narrow but precise broad but vague

    Make it concrete. Suppose there's a bug in price parsing. An end-to-end test might catch it — but only if a product listing happens to use the problematic format — and when it does, the failure says "cart total assertion failed," pointing nowhere near the parser, after thirty seconds of running a browser. A unit test for the parser catches the same bug in two milliseconds and says parse_price("US $1,234.56") == 1234.56 failed. Same bug; roughly fifteen-thousand times faster to find and fix, with a message that names the culprit.

    Key idea

    Push correctness checks down the pyramid. Test logic at the unit level, where it's fast and precise; reserve end-to-end tests for proving the journey holds together. The opposite shape — mostly end-to-end tests, few or no unit tests — is the slow, flaky, expensive "ice-cream cone" anti-pattern that experienced UI engineers drift into.

    16.3 What makes code unit-testable: purity¶

    A pure function is one whose output depends only on its inputs, and which has no side effects — no network calls, no DOM access, no reading the clock, no global state. Pure functions are trivially unit-testable: you feed inputs and assert on the output, full stop.

    The reference project's parse_price was deliberately written this way:

    def parse_price(text: str) -> Decimal:      # a string in, a Decimal out — nothing else
    match = _DOLLAR_AMOUNT.search(text)
    if match is None:
        raise ValueError(...)
    return Decimal(match.group(1).replace(",", ""))

    No browser, no page, no I/O. So you can hammer it with edge cases instantly:

    @pytest.mark.parametrize("text, expected", [
    ("$25.00", Decimal("25.00")),
    ("US $1,234.56", Decimal("1234.56")),
    ("$25.00 to $30.00", Decimal("25.00")),           # a range → take the lower bound
    ("Subtotal (3 items) $50.00", Decimal("50.00")),  # the "3" must NOT win
])
def test_parse_price(text, expected):
    assert parse_price(text) == expected

@pytest.mark.parametrize("text", ["", "free shipping", "Time left: 3d 4h"])
def test_parse_price_rejects_garbage(text):
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        parse_price(text)

    That's around twenty cases, running in well under a tenth of a second, with no Chromium in sight. It is the part of the suite that is always green — the reliable demonstration you can show even when a live third-party site is having a bad day.

    Interview lens — the design insight, not just the technique

    The reason parse_price can be unit-tested is that it was deliberately extracted from the component into a pure utility. The senior framing is: "I isolate the tricky logic — price parsing, budget arithmetic, pagination decisions — into pure functions, so I can unit-test them exhaustively, and I keep the browser-dependent glue thin." That sentence shows you understand that testability is a design property you build in, not an afterthought.

    16.4 A worked example of the payoff¶

    The trickiest parsing case is "Subtotal (3 items) $50.00". A naive parser ("grab the first number you see") would return 3 — and then every budget comparison downstream would silently use the item count as if it were the price. That bug would:

    • pass most end-to-end runs (3 is less than nearly any budget),
    • occasionally cause inexplicable failures,
    • and never point a finger at the parser.

    The unit test pins it down in isolation:

    def test_dollar_anchor_beats_bare_integers():
    assert parse_price("Subtotal (3 items) $50.00") == Decimal("50.00")
    assert parse_price("Subtotal (99 items) $1.00") == Decimal("1.00")

    If someone later "simplifies" the regex and breaks the $ anchor, this test goes red immediately, naming the exact input. That is the entire value proposition of unit tests: they convert a future silent regression into a loud, located failure.

    16.5 Where each kind of test sits in the reference project¶

    Test Layer Why it lives there
    test_price_parser.py (≈22 cases) Unit a pure function, no browser
    test_smoke.py E2E (thin) "does search even work?" — the critical path
    test_search_under_price.py E2E the full journey, one canonical case
    test_scenario (data-driven) E2E the journey across many data rows

    Notice the shape: exactly one pure-logic module is heavily unit-tested, and the end-to-end layer stays focused on user journeys. Given the domain (browser automation against a live site) it's necessarily browser-heavy, but the principle still holds — the fragile, exact logic is pushed down to fast unit tests.

    Exercise 16.1 — write your first unit tests

    Write a pure function within_budget(prices: list[Decimal], budget: Decimal) -> bool that returns whether the sum of prices is within budget. Unit-test it with: an empty list; a sum exactly equal to the budget; a sum one cent over; and the float-trap case [Decimal("0.1"), Decimal("0.2")] against Decimal("0.3") (which must return True — and would break if you'd used floats). Run it and note that it's instant and needs no browser. You've just practised the most under-used skill in QA automation.

    Key idea

    Many fast unit tests at the base, few slow end-to-end tests at the top. Unit testing is possible because logic is extracted into pure functions; those tests catch regressions in milliseconds and name the exact failing input. Testability is a design choice — isolate logic from I/O and you can test it cheaply, exhaustively, and forever.

    Part IV — Test Architecture

    Chapter 17 — SOLID & SRP for Test Frameworks¶

    Architecture and clean code are, in almost any serious evaluation, the most heavily weighted area of all — and they're what an interviewer is probing when they say "walk me through your design" or "why is this in a service and not a component?" This chapter gives you the principles, in plain language and applied directly to test code. The next four chapters put them into practice. Don't skip this even if "SOLID" sounds like buzzword bingo — the one principle that actually earns the marks (Single Responsibility) is taught here on concrete cases you'll be asked about.

    17.1 Why a test suite needs architecture at all¶

    A twenty-line throwaway script needs no architecture. A suite of two hundred tests against a user interface that changes every week needs it desperately. The reason has a name: change amplification. A small change in one place should not force edits in fifty files.

    Picture the worst case. The site renames a CSS class. If that class string appears in eighty test files, you now have eighty edits to make, you'll miss three, and the suite goes red for a week. Good architecture localises the blast radius of change: a class rename touches one line, in one place. Every principle in this chapter is, ultimately, a different angle on that single goal — keeping changes small and contained.

    17.2 The layered design, as a picture¶

    The reference project (and most well-built suites) is organised into layers, each depending only on the one below it:

    flowchart TD
    T["tests/ — what to verify (assertions only)"]
    S["services/ — business flows & policy (the 'how')"]
    C["components/ — one UI region each (the markup)"]
    P["Playwright — browser / context / page"]
    U["utils/ — pure helpers (price parser, paginator)"]
    D["db/ — typed config & scenario data"]
    T --> S --> C --> P
    S -.uses.-> U
    T -.parametrized by.-> D

    The arrows point only downward — tests depend on services, services on components, components on Playwright. Nothing points back up. That one-directional, acyclic flow is the architecture, and the SOLID principles below explain why each boundary is drawn where it is.

    17.3 SOLID, translated into test-code terms¶

    SOLID is five principles. Here's each, stated plainly and shown in this domain:

    S — Single Responsibility: a class should have exactly one reason to change. : A ResultCardComponent changes only when the result-card markup changes. A SearchService changes only when the search flow changes. (Expanded in §17.4 — this is the one that matters most.)

    O — Open/Closed: open for extension, closed for modification. : Adding a new test scenario is a new row in the YAML data file (extension), not an edit to the test body (modification). Adding a new flow is a new method on a service, not surgery on existing methods.

    L — Liskov Substitution: any subtype must work wherever its base type is expected. : Every component extends BaseComponent and honours its contract, so anything written to work with a BaseComponent works with any specific component.

    I — Interface Segregation: don't force a client to depend on methods it doesn't use. : The paginator depends on _Pageable — just has_next_page() and go_to_next_page() — not on the whole SearchResultsPage. It needs two methods, so it asks for exactly two.

    D — Dependency Inversion: depend on abstractions, not concrete implementations. : The paginator depends on the _Pageable Protocol (Chapter 4), not on SearchResultsPage. The high-level paginator and the low-level page both depend on an abstraction, not on each other.

    From TypeScript

    These are the same SOLID principles you'd apply in a NestJS service or an Angular app. The translation to test code is direct: components are your "view" layer (markup), services are your "business" layer (flows), tests are the "callers" (assertions). If you've kept HTTP concerns out of business logic in application code, you already have the instinct.

    17.4 Single Responsibility is the one that earns the marks¶

    Of the five, Single Responsibility is the principle interviewers probe hardest, because violating it is the most common real-world failure. The test to apply is one question: "What is the one reason this class would change?"

    • ResultCardComponent → "the result-card markup changed." ✔ one reason.
    • SearchService → "the search flow changed — different filters, a different sort, a new pagination policy." ✔ one reason.
    • A hypothetical CartPage that also knew how to walk search results → it would change when the cart markup changes and when search pagination changes. ✘ two unrelated reasons → split it.

    The layered design from §17.2 enforces SRP physically, by giving each layer one category of reason-to-change:

    Layer Changes when…
    tests/ what we want to assert changes
    services/ a business flow changes
    components/ a page's markup changes
    utils/ a pure algorithm changes (price format, pagination rule)

    That clean separation of "reasons to change" is the architecture.

    Interview lens — the question you WILL be asked

    "Why is the price filtering in the service and not the component?" → "Because 'skip sponsored, skip auctions, drop anything over the max price' is a business decision — it changes when our selection policy changes, not when eBay's card markup changes. The component's job is only to report what's on a card — price_text(), is_sponsored(); deciding what to do with that is the service's job. Putting the policy in the component would give the component two reasons to change and couple business rules to markup." That is SRP, articulated on a concrete case, and it's the answer that scores the architecture marks.

    17.5 Mechanism versus policy¶

    A theme that threads through the whole codebase, worth naming explicitly because it makes the SRP boundary obvious in practice:

    • Mechanism = how to do a low-level thing. parse_price knows how to turn text into a Decimal. card.is_sponsored() knows how to detect the sponsored badge.
    • Policy = what to do about it. The service decides that sponsored cards are skipped and that an unparseable price means drop this listing.

    Keep them apart and each stays simple and reusable. The parser refuses to guess and raises; the caller decides whether to skip the listing or fail the test. The very same parser then serves a strict test and a lenient demo, because it has no policy baked into it. When you're unsure which layer something belongs in, ask: "is this how to do something (mechanism → lower layer) or what to do about it (policy → higher layer)?"

    17.6 DRY, and its limits¶

    "Don't Repeat Yourself" is why the three end-to-end suites (smoke, regression, data-driven) all call the same search → add → assert flow living once in the services, instead of copy-pasting it three times where the copies would drift apart.

    But beware premature DRY. Two pieces of code that merely look alike today, but would change for different reasons tomorrow, should not be merged — coupling them means a change for one forces a change on the other. The skill is to merge things that share a reason to change, not things that are superficially similar. (That's the SRP test again, viewed from the other side.)

    Gotcha — over-abstraction is as harmful as under-abstraction

    A five-level-deep page-object inheritance tree, or a "BaseTest" that everything extends, usually signals DRY applied to things that don't actually share a reason to change. Prefer composition and shallow hierarchies. A reliable smell test: if an abstraction makes a test harder to read, it's the wrong abstraction. Clever indirection that obscures what a test does costs more than the duplication it removed.

    Exercise 17.1 — apply the SRP question

    Take a method you've written (or imagine a LoginPage that both fills the login form and decides which user role to log in as based on the test environment). Ask "what are the reasons this would change?" If you find two unrelated reasons (the login markup changing vs. the policy of which role to use), describe how you'd split it into a component (markup) and a service or fixture (policy).

    Key idea

    Architecture exists to localise change. Of the SOLID five, Single Responsibility — one reason to change per class — is the one that earns the marks; be ready to articulate it on the concrete "why service, not component?" question. Separate mechanism (how to do something) from policy (what to do about it). Apply DRY to shared reasons to change, never to superficial resemblance — and never let an abstraction make a test harder to read.

    Chapter 18 — The Page Object Model¶

    Most engineers who adopt the Page Object Model quickly sense that it is cleaner than scattering raw Playwright calls through their tests. This chapter explains precisely why, and — just as importantly — what separates a good page object from a bad one, because POM done badly can be worse than no POM at all. We build from the problem it solves up to a catalogue of the mistakes to avoid.

    18.1 The problem POM solves¶

    Without POM, selectors get scattered through every test that touches a given screen:

    def test_a(page):
    page.fill("#gh-ac", "shoes")              # eBay's search input id
    page.click("#gh-btn")                      # eBay's search button id
    assert page.locator("ul.srp-results > li.s-item").count() > 0

def test_b(page):
    page.fill("#gh-ac", "books")              # the SAME selectors, copy-pasted
    page.click("#gh-btn")
    ...

    Now eBay renames #gh-ac. You must find and fix it in every test that searches. Across two hundred tests that's a day's work and a guaranteed missed occurrence — and the suite goes red until you find it. The deeper problem is conceptual: selectors are implementation detail, and they've leaked into the expression of test intent. A test should say "search for shoes," not "type into the element with id gh-ac."

    18.2 The core idea: hide selectors behind intent¶

    A Page Object is a class that wraps a page (or a region of one) and exposes intent-revealing methods, keeping the selectors hidden inside:

    class HeaderComponent(BaseComponent):
    _SEL_SEARCH_INPUT_NAME = "Search for anything"
    _SEL_SEARCH_SUBMIT_NAME = "Search"

    def search(self, query: str) -> None:
        self.root.get_by_role("combobox", name=self._SEL_SEARCH_INPUT_NAME).fill(query)
        self.root.get_by_role("button", name=self._SEL_SEARCH_SUBMIT_NAME).click()

    Now the tests speak the domain language and own zero selectors:

    def test_a(page):
    HomePage(page).header.search("shoes")     # WHAT to do, not HOW it's wired

def test_b(page):
    HomePage(page).header.search("books")

    When eBay renames its search input, you fix it in one method, and every test that searches keeps working untouched.

    Key idea

    A page object converts how the page is built (selectors, clicks, waits) into what you can do with it (search, add_to_cart, subtotal). Tests express intent; the page object owns the markup. That single inversion of responsibility is the entire point of POM.

    18.3 What a good page object SHOULD do¶

    • Expose intent-revealing methods: header.search("shoes"), item.add_to_cart(), cart.subtotal(). The method name describes a user-meaningful action or query.
    • Own its selectors, as _SEL_ constants (Chapter 8).
    • Return domain values, not Playwright objects: subtotal() returns a Decimal, price_text() returns a str, is_sponsored() returns a bool. (More on this in §18.5.)
    • Encapsulate one region's markup, and nothing else.

    18.4 What a good page object should NOT do¶

    This list is where most POM implementations go wrong. Each item is a real, common mistake:

    • It should not return raw Locators to the test. If cart.subtotal_locator() hands a locator back, the test will call .inner_text() on it and parse the result — and now selector-and-parsing knowledge has leaked back into the test, defeating the point. Return the parsed value instead.
    • It should not contain assertions. A page object reports state (subtotal() -> Decimal); the test asserts on it. Putting assert statements inside page objects scatters your verification logic across many classes and makes the page object unusable in non-test contexts (like a demo script or a monitoring tool).
    • It should not contain business logic or cross-page flow. "Search, paginate, filter by price, add the first five" is a flow across pages — it belongs in a service (Chapter 20), not on any single page object.
    • It should not know about test data or environments. Those are injected from above; a page object just drives whatever page it was handed.

    Interview lens — the most-tested boundary

    "Should a page object contain assertions?" → "No. Page objects report state as domain values; tests assert on those values. Keeping assertions out means the same page object works in a test, in a demo script, and in a monitoring tool — and all verification stays in one place (the test) instead of scattered across page classes." Many candidates get this wrong; getting it right is a strong signal.

    18.5 Returning domain values — a concrete before/after¶

    This is worth seeing side by side, because it's the most common subtle leak:

    # BAD — leaks a Locator; the test ends up knowing about markup AND parsing:
class CartPage:
    def subtotal_element(self) -> Locator:
        return self.page.get_by_text(re.compile(r"^Subtotal"))

# in the test:
text = cart.subtotal_element().inner_text()      # the test does the reading...
amount = Decimal(text.replace("$", ""))           # ...and the parsing. The leak is here.

    # GOOD — returns a parsed Decimal; the test knows nothing about markup or parsing:
class CartPage:
    def subtotal(self) -> Decimal:
        text = self.page.get_by_text(re.compile(r"^Subtotal")).first.inner_text()
        return parse_price(text)

# in the test:
assert cart.subtotal() <= budget                  # pure intent

    In the "good" version, all of the markup-and-parsing knowledge is sealed inside CartPage. The test reads like a requirement: "the subtotal must not exceed the budget."

    18.6 A catalogue of POM anti-patterns¶

    Anti-pattern Why it's bad The fix
    Selectors in test files change amplification move them to _SEL_ constants in a page object
    Page object with asserts scatters verification; can't reuse outside tests return values; assert in the test
    One "god" page object for the whole site a thousand reasons to change one class per region
    Returning Locators to tests selector knowledge leaks back into tests return parsed domain values
    Deep page-object inheritance rigid, hard to follow a shallow base + composition
    Business logic in page objects couples flow to markup extract a service

    18.7 When POM is not worth it¶

    Maturity means knowing when a pattern is overkill. Modern Playwright (especially in TypeScript) sometimes favours small fixtures over full page-object classes for simple apps. The trade-off: POM shines when the UI is large, shared across many tests, and volatile — an e-commerce site is the textbook case. For a tiny, stable app with a handful of tests, heavy POM is just indirection that costs more than it saves.

    Interview lens

    "When is POM not worth it?" → "For a small, stable surface with few tests, the indirection can cost more than it saves — a couple of role locators inline are fine. POM earns its keep when the UI is large, volatile, and shared across many tests, so the one-place-to-fix-a-selector payoff dominates. It's a judgment call, not dogma." Showing you know when not to apply a pattern is more senior than reciting that the pattern is good.

    Exercise 18.1 — refactor toward POM

    Take the scattered-selector test_a/test_b from §18.1. Write a small SearchPage class with _SEL_ constants and a search(query) method, plus a result_count() method that returns an int. Rewrite both tests to use it. Notice that the tests no longer contain a single selector, and that a class rename would now be a one-line fix.

    Key idea

    A page object hides selectors behind intent-revealing methods and returns domain values — never raw locators, never assertions, never business logic. One class per region; no test-data knowledge. POM's payoff scales with the size, churn, and reuse of the UI — apply it where that payoff is real, not reflexively.

    Chapter 19 — Component Objects & the Base Class¶

    Classic POM has one object per page. But real pages are built from repeating, reusable regions — a header, a result card, a filter panel — that show up across many pages. The component object pattern (the grown-up form of POM) models those regions as their own small classes. This chapter explains the pattern, and the one mechanic — scoped locators — that makes it work without elements colliding.

    19.1 Pages are composed of components¶

    A page object doesn't have to be one giant class. It can be assembled from smaller component objects, each owning one region:

    class HomePage(BaseComponent):
    def __init__(self, page: Page) -> None:
        super().__init__(page)
        self.header = HeaderComponent(page)          # reused on every page
        self.cookie_banner = CookieBannerComponent(page)

    Now home.header.search("shoes") reads exactly the way the page is structured: a home page has a header, and the header can search. And because HeaderComponent is its own class, the same header object is reused on the search-results page, the item page, and the cart — written once, composed everywhere. This is composition (Chapter 3) applied to UI structure:

    flowchart TD
    HP["HomePage"] --> HD["HeaderComponent"]
    HP --> CB["CookieBannerComponent"]
    SR["SearchResultsPage"] --> HD
    SR --> FP["FilterPanelComponent"]
    SR --> RC["ResultCardComponent (one per result)"]
    IP["ItemPage"] --> HD
    CP["CartPage"] --> HD

    Notice HeaderComponent is shared by every page — that reuse is the payoff of modelling regions as components rather than duplicating header selectors in each page class.

    19.2 The root locator and scoped queries — the key mechanic¶

    The defining feature of a component is that it can be scoped to a sub-tree of the page, so that its locators only ever match elements within its own region. This is what the BaseComponent provides:

    class BaseComponent:
    def __init__(self, page: Page, root: Locator | None = None) -> None:
        self.page = page
        self.root = root if root is not None else page.locator("body")   # default: whole page
        self.log = get_logger(self.__class__.__name__)
        self.screenshots = ScreenshotManager(page)

    def locator(self, selector: str) -> Locator:
        return self.root.locator(selector)      # ALWAYS resolves *within* this component's root
    • A component created without a root defaults to the whole body — appropriate for page-level objects like HomePage.
    • A component created with a root (say, scoped to one result card's <li>) finds elements only inside that subtree.

    Why does this matter so much? Consider a search-results page showing fifty result cards, each containing a .s-item__price. If a component used self.page.locator(".s-item__price"), it would match all fifty prices — a strict-mode disaster (Chapter 7). But because each ResultCardComponent is handed its own <li> as root, calling self.locator(".s-item__price") resolves to that card's price and no other:

    class ResultCardComponent(BaseComponent):
    _SEL_PRICE_CSS = ".s-item__price"

    def __init__(self, page: Page, root: Locator) -> None:
        super().__init__(page, root)             # root is MANDATORY for a card

    def price_text(self) -> str:
        return self.locator(self._SEL_PRICE_CSS).first.inner_text().strip()

    Key idea

    The root locator is what makes a component reusable and unambiguous. Scoped self.locator(...) queries are resolved relative to the component's own subtree, so N instances of the same component on one page never collide. This is the single most important implementation detail in component-style POM.

    From TypeScript

    root.locator(...) is identical to chaining locators in TS Playwright (card.locator(".price")). The component simply stores that root, so every method is automatically scoped — much like a React component receiving a ref to its own DOM subtree and querying only within it.

    19.3 The child-factory pattern¶

    A page often needs to hand back a list of components — one per repeated element. That's a child factory:

    class SearchResultsPage(BaseComponent):
    _SEL_CARDS_CSS = "ul.srp-results > li.s-item"

    @property
    def cards(self) -> Locator:
        return self.page.locator(self._SEL_CARDS_CSS)

    def get_visible_result_cards(self) -> list[ResultCardComponent]:
        cards = self.cards
        return [ResultCardComponent(self.page, cards.nth(i)) for i in range(cards.count())]

    get_visible_result_cards() walks the matched <li> elements and wraps each one as its own typed ResultCardComponent, scoped to its nth(i) locator. The caller can then ask each card domain questions (card.is_sponsored(), card.price_text()) without ever touching a selector.

    Gotcha — is the comprehension 'business logic in a component'?

    A reviewer might object that the list comprehension is logic inside a component. It isn't business logic — it's a structural child factory: it produces typed wrappers and makes no decisions about which cards matter (that's the service's job). Be ready to name that distinction. Selecting or filtering cards by price or sponsorship would be business logic, and it lives in the service (Chapter 20), not here.

    19.4 What belongs in the base class — and what doesn't¶

    A BaseComponent should hold only cross-cutting plumbing that every component genuinely needs:

    • the page and root references,
    • the scoped locator() factory,
    • a logger automatically labelled with the subclass name (via self.__class__.__name__, Chapter 3),
    • a screenshot helper.

    Resist the temptation to put page-specific methods on the base — that's a "god object" creeping in by the back door, and it violates Single Responsibility. The base stays thin; everything specific lives in the subclasses.

    19.5 The component catalogue, at a glance¶

    Component Root Single responsibility
    HomePage body the entry point; composes header + cookie banner
    HeaderComponent the banner role search box + submit, cart link
    CookieBannerComponent body detect and dismiss the consent banner (idempotently)
    SearchResultsPage body the card factory, pagination, composes the filter panel
    FilterPanelComponent the results region price range, Buy-It-Now filter, sort
    ResultCardComponent one <li> report one card's title, price, type, sponsored-ness
    ItemPage body title, price, variants, add-to-cart
    CartPage body subtotal, line items

    Every row has a crisp single responsibility (Chapter 17), and the one that's repeated on the page (ResultCardComponent) is precisely the one that takes a mandatory root.

    Interview lens

    "How do you stop selector collisions when a page has many identical cards?" → "Each card is its own component scoped to a root locator (cards.nth(i)), and all queries go through a self.locator() factory that resolves relative to that root. So fifty cards' fifty price nodes never collide — each component only ever sees its own subtree. The base class provides that scoped factory plus logging and screenshots, and holds no page-specific behaviour." That answer demonstrates you've actually built component POM, not just read about it.

    Exercise 19.1 — scope a repeated component

    On any page with a repeated card/row (a search result list, a table), write a tiny RowComponent(BaseComponent) that takes a root and exposes one method returning some text from within that row. Then write a factory method that returns a list of them, one per row, each scoped with .nth(i). Confirm that calling the method on row 3 returns row 3's text, not row 1's — that's scoping working.

    Key idea

    Components model reusable regions; pages compose them. The root locator plus the scoped locator() factory make many instances of the same component unambiguous. A child factory wraps repeated elements as typed components (structural, not business logic). The base class holds only thin cross-cutting plumbing — never page-specific behaviour.

    Chapter 20 — The Service Layer¶

    This is the chapter that lifts a suite from "fine" to "architected," and it contains the single most valuable thing you can articulate in an interview: why there is a layer above the page objects at all. Many candidates build page objects and stop there; being able to explain the service layer — what it's for, what goes in it, and what stays out — is what marks senior design judgment. We'll build the motivation carefully, then state the rules.

    20.1 The gap that page objects alone leave¶

    Page objects model regions of the UI. But a real test goal isn't about one region — it spans several. Consider the headline flow:

    "Search for shoes under $220, add the first five Buy-It-Now items to the cart, then assert the cart total."

    That single sentence touches the home page, the search-results page, multiple item pages, and the cart — and it carries real logic: pagination bounds, filtering out sponsored and auction listings, picking random variants, and money arithmetic. Where does all of that go?

    Two tempting-but-wrong answers:

    • Put it in the test. Then it gets duplicated across the smoke, regression, and data-driven suites — three copies that drift apart over time.
    • Put it in a page object. Then a CartPage ends up knowing how to walk search results, which gives it two unrelated reasons to change — a Single Responsibility violation (Chapter 17).

    Neither fits. The flow needs a home of its own. That home is a service.

    flowchart LR
    Test["test (asserts)"] --> Svc["SearchService.search_items_by_name_under_price()"]
    Svc --> Home["HomePage"]
    Svc --> Results["SearchResultsPage"]
    Svc --> Filter["FilterPanelComponent"]
    Svc --> Pag["collect_until() paginator"]

    20.2 What a service is¶

    A service owns the flows and policy of one business domain. It composes calls to several components into a meaningful, multi-step action, holding the what to do (policy) while the components hold the how (mechanism):

    class SearchService(BaseService):
    def __init__(self, page: Page, env: Environment) -> None:
        super().__init__(page)
        self.env = env
        self._home = HomePage(page)
        self._results = SearchResultsPage(page)

    def search_items_by_name_under_price(
        self, query: str, max_price: Decimal, limit: int = 5
    ) -> list[str]:
        self._home.load()
        self._home.header.search(query)
        self._results.apply_price_filter(max_price)
        self._results.filter_panel.apply_buy_it_now()
        self._results.filter_panel.sort_by_price_plus_shipping_lowest()
        return collect_until(
            component=self._results,
            collect_fn=lambda r: self._collect_card_urls(r, max_price),
            target_count=limit,
            env=self.env,
        )

    Read that method top to bottom: it's a recipe — load, search, filter, sort, paginate-and-collect. Each step delegates to a component; the service decides the sequence and the rules. The components execute the clicks; the service decides what the clicks add up to.

    20.3 Policy lives in the service; mechanism lives in the component¶

    The filtering rules are private service methods, and that placement is deliberate:

        def _qualify_card(self, card: ResultCardComponent, max_price: Decimal) -> str | None:
        if card.is_sponsored():            # the component REPORTS; the service DECIDES
            return None
        if card.item_type() != "buy_it_now":
            return None
        try:
            price = parse_price(card.price_text())
        except ValueError:
            return None                    # unparseable price → skip (a policy decision)
        if price > max_price:
            return None
        return card.url() or None

    card.is_sponsored() is mechanism — it knows how to detect the sponsored badge. "Skip sponsored cards" is policy — and policy is the service's job. If the selection rules change tomorrow (say, "allow auctions after all"), you edit the service; the component is untouched, because the markup didn't change. That's Single Responsibility paying off in practice.

    Interview lens — THE architecture question

    "Why have a service layer on top of your page objects?" → "The flows I'm testing span multiple pages and own business logic — pagination bounds, price filtering, variant selection, money math. Put that in a test and it's duplicated across suites; put it in a page object and the object grows a second reason to change. A service is the single home for cross-page flow and policy, so components stay markup-only and tests stay assertion-only. Each tier ends up with exactly one job." This is the highest-value answer in the whole interview — internalise its shape and say it in your own words.

    20.4 The rules services follow¶

    The reference services follow a tight contract worth stating as explicit rules:

    1. One service per domain. auth, search, cart, variants — not one giant EbayService doing everything.
    2. Receive page / context / env at construction (injected by a fixture). A service never reaches for globals.
    3. Never import another service. Services compose components, not each other — importing one service into another creates coupling and risks circular imports. (The cart service uses a variant service, but it's injected as a dependency, not imported and constructed internally — see §20.5.)
    4. Return domain values, not Locators. search_items_by_name_under_price returns list[str] (URLs); a subtotal getter returns Decimal. The test asserts on plain values.
    5. No assertions scattered through flows (with one deliberate, named exception — §20.6). Services do the flow and return results; tests assert.

    20.5 Dependency injection between services¶

    The cart service needs the variant service. Rather than constructing one internally (which would hard-couple them), it receives one:

    class CartService(BaseService):
    def __init__(self, page, context, variant_service: VariantService) -> None:
        super().__init__(page)
        self.context = context
        self.variant_service = variant_service     # INJECTED, not newed up internally

    And the fixture wires the two together:

    @pytest.fixture
def cart_service(page, context, variant_service):   # variant_service is itself a fixture
    return CartService(page, context, variant_service)

    This keeps the cart service decoupled from how variants get chosen — you could inject a different variant-selection strategy without touching the cart service at all. It's the same dependency injection you saw with fixtures (Chapter 13) and with the Protocol (Chapter 4), now applied between services.

    20.6 The one nuance: where the budget assertion lives¶

    There is one place a service does raise: assert_cart_total_not_exceeds.

        def assert_cart_total_not_exceeds(self, budget_per_item: Decimal, items_count: int) -> None:
        self._cart.open()
        subtotal = self._cart.subtotal()
        budget = budget_per_item * items_count
        if subtotal > budget:
            raise AssertionError(f"cart subtotal exceeds budget ... over_by {subtotal - budget}")

    Doesn't that violate rule #5 ("no assertions in services")? This is a named spec function — the reference project's spec defines assertCartTotalNotExceeds as a reusable assertion primitive, so encapsulating the comparison (with a rich, structured failure message) and reusing it across all the suites is exactly right. The general rule still holds — services don't litter ad-hoc asserts through their flow logic — but a deliberately named, reusable assertion method is a reasonable, defensible exception. The point is to be able to explain the distinction, not to follow the rule blindly.

    Interview lens

    If an interviewer says "you told me no assertions in services, but here's one" — don't get flustered. "General flows return values and let tests assert. But the spec defined assertCartTotalNotExceeds as a named, reusable assertion primitive, so I encapsulated it with a structured failure message and reuse it across suites. It's a deliberate, named exception — not assertions sprinkled through business logic." Being able to defend a considered deviation is more impressive than rigidly insisting a rule has no exceptions.

    Exercise 20.1 — find the seam

    Take a flow you know (e.g. "log in, open settings, change the theme, confirm it saved"). List which steps are component mechanics (fill, click, read text) and which are policy / sequencing (which order, what counts as success, what to do if a step is missing). The mechanics belong in components; the policy and sequencing belong in a service. Sketch the service method signature and the component calls it would make.

    Key idea

    Services own cross-page flows and policy; components own markup; tests own assertions. One service per domain, dependencies injected (never imported between services), returning domain values. The answer to "why a service layer?" is your single most valuable interview sentence — know it cold.

    Chapter 21 — Configuration & Environments¶

    Configuration — data-driven config, environment variables, profiles — is its own area of evaluation, because it is what separates a one-off script from a maintainable suite. The goals of this chapter: zero hardcoded URLs or magic values anywhere in the code, switching between environments with a single variable, and one typed source of truth for everything structural. We build it from the two-axis distinction up to a small typed loader.

    21.1 Two independent axes of "configuration"¶

    People lump "configuration" into one bucket, but there are really two independent questions, and conflating them causes real problems:

    1. Is it secret, or structural? A password is secret — it differs per person, must never be committed to git. A base URL is structural — it's shared by the whole team and should be committed. (We covered this in Chapter 1; secrets go in a gitignored .env, structural config in a committed file.)
    2. Does it vary by environment, or stay constant? headless differs between your laptop and CI; the result-card CSS selector is the same everywhere.

    A clean design answers both: secrets in .env, structural config in a committed typed file, and an environment profile that bundles the structural values that vary by environment.

    21.2 Profiles: a named bundle of environment settings¶

    A profile is a named set of environment-specific settings. The reference project defines two — dev (your laptop) and ci:

    # db/data.yaml
environments:
  dev:
    base_url: https://www.ebay.com
    region: US
    currency: USD
    headless: false        # show the browser locally
    slow_mo_ms: 100        # slow it down so you can watch
    max_pages_to_paginate: 5
  ci:
    base_url: https://www.ebay.com
    region: US
    currency: USD
    headless: true         # no display in CI; run fast
    slow_mo_ms: 0
    max_pages_to_paginate: 3

    You choose the active profile with a single environment variable, read once in a fixture:

    @pytest.fixture(scope="session")
def profile() -> str:
    return os.getenv("PROFILE", "dev")     # default to "dev" if PROFILE isn't set

@pytest.fixture(scope="session")
def env(db, profile) -> Environment:
    return db.environments.get(profile)

    uv run pytest -m smoke                          # PROFILE unset → "dev" (headed, slow-mo)
PROFILE=ci uv run pytest -m regression -n 4     # "ci" (headless, tighter pagination cap)

    The same code runs differently in the two environments, and the difference is driven entirely by which profile is selected — not by if running_in_ci: checks scattered through the code. The profile is the switch.

    From TypeScript

    os.getenv("PROFILE", "dev") ≈ process.env.PROFILE ?? "dev". Profiles are like Playwright Test projects, or a config.{env}.ts chosen by an env var — the same "one knob picks a whole bundle of settings" idea.

    21.3 Why YAML, and not .env, for structural config¶

    .env files are flat KEY=value strings. That's fine for a handful of secrets, but wrong for structured, typed, queryable data:

    • Scenarios have nested fields, lists (tags: [regression]), and real types (Decimal, bool, int).
    • The same data feeds the regression suite, the data-driven runner, and a standalone demo script.
    • You want to query it — "give me all the regression-tagged scenarios."

    A flat .env can't express any of that without ugly conventions like SCENARIO_1_QUERY=.... YAML gives you nesting, lists, comments, and types, and it parses cleanly into structured objects.

    Interview lens

    "Why a YAML 'database' instead of .env or a Python config module?" → "Secrets go in .env because they're per-person and gitignored. But structural test data is nested, typed, and shared across suites and a demo script, so it lives in one committed YAML file loaded into typed dataclasses, queryable by tag. .env is a flat string map — the wrong shape for scenarios. And money fields are stored as quoted strings so they parse to Decimal, never float." That single answer covers configuration, secrets, data-driven design, and the Decimal rule.

    21.4 Parse into typed objects at the boundary¶

    Raw YAML loads as nested dictionaries of strings, ints, and lists. The professional move is to convert it once, right at the edge, into typed frozen dataclasses, so the rest of the code works with real types:

    @dataclass(frozen=True)
class Environment:
    id: str
    base_url: str
    region: str
    currency: str
    headless: bool
    slow_mo_ms: int
    max_pages_to_paginate: int

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Scenario:
    id: str
    query: str
    max_price: Decimal      # parsed from a quoted string, at load time
    limit: int
    allow_partial: bool
    min_results: int = 1
    tags: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)

    The loader does the conversion, including the critical money step:

    _DECIMAL_FIELDS = frozenset({"max_price"})

def _load_model(model, id_, payload):
    kwargs = {"id": id_}
    for f in fields(model):
        if f.name == "id" or f.name not in payload:
            continue
        value = payload[f.name]
        if f.name in _DECIMAL_FIELDS:
            value = Decimal(str(value))     # str → Decimal: exact, never via float
        kwargs[f.name] = value
    return model(**kwargs)

    After this boundary, every scenario.max_price is a Decimal and every env.headless is a real bool — no string-to-type juggling anywhere downstream.

    Key idea — convert at the boundary

    Parse and type external data once, at the point it enters the system, into immutable typed objects. The rest of the codebase then trusts those types. This is the same principle as validating untrusted input at a system's edge — and it's where the "string → Decimal, never float" money rule (Chapter 5) gets enforced exactly once.

    21.5 Accessor objects: a small query API¶

    Rather than passing raw dictionaries around, wrap each table in an accessor with a small, intention-revealing API:

    class ScenarioAccessor:
    def __init__(self, items: dict[str, Scenario]) -> None:
        self._items = items
    def get(self, id: str) -> Scenario:
        if id not in self._items:
            raise KeyError(f"scenario '{id}' not found. Available: {sorted(self._items)}")
        return self._items[id]
    def all(self) -> list[Scenario]:
        return list(self._items.values())
    def where(self, tag: str) -> list[Scenario]:
        return [s for s in self._items.values() if tag in s.tags]

    Now db.scenarios.where(tag="regression") reads like a query and hides the underlying dict. Notice that get lists the available keys in its error message — a small touch that turns a cryptic KeyError into a helpful "here's what you could have meant." This is the difference between data that merely sits in a file and data that's a first-class part of your system.

    21.6 Validate at load, fail clearly¶

    The loader rejects malformed config loudly and immediately, rather than letting it cause a confusing failure three layers deep later:

    unknown = set(raw) - set(_EXPECTED_TABLES)
if unknown:
    raise ValueError(
        f"unknown top-level keys: {sorted(unknown)}. Expected: {sorted(_EXPECTED_TABLES)}"
    )

    Mistype a top-level key as scenrios: and you get an immediate, clear error at load time — not a baffling empty result far away from the cause. Fail fast, fail clearly is a quiet hallmark of well-built infrastructure.

    Interview lens

    "How do you keep environment URLs out of the code?" → "There are none in the code. The base_url lives in the profile and is set on the browser context, so tests navigate with paths (/sch/i.html). Switching environments is one PROFILE env var. All structural config loads into typed, frozen dataclasses with validation at the boundary, exposed through accessor objects with a small query API." Zero hardcoded URLs is an explicit evaluation point — this is how you satisfy it.

    Exercise 21.1 — a tiny typed loader

    Create a settings.yaml with two profiles (local, ci) each having a base_url and a timeout (int). Write a frozen @dataclass Settings, a loader that reads the YAML and returns the right Settings for a profile chosen by os.getenv("PROFILE", "local"), and a line that prints settings.base_url. Then mistype a field in the YAML and confirm you get a clear error rather than a silent wrong value.

    Key idea

    Keep secrets in .env and structural config in one committed YAML file, loaded into frozen typed dataclasses (with money parsed to Decimal at the boundary). Profiles bundle the environment-varying settings, switched by a single PROFILE variable. Accessor objects give a clean query API, and validation at load makes mistakes fail fast and clearly. The result: no hardcoded URLs, one source of truth, one knob to switch environments.

    Part V — Robustness, Reporting, Review

    Chapter 22 — Smart Locators & Resilience¶

    Robustness and smart locators are typically the second most heavily weighted area of an automation evaluation, right after architecture. This chapter is about one thing: surviving a hostile, changing, dynamic website without your tests flaking. We'll start with the mindset, then work through each concrete technique with examples, and end with a checklist you can recite when asked "how do you make tests robust?"

    22.1 The resilience mindset¶

    A real commercial site like eBay is, from an automation standpoint, actively hostile in ways a tidy demo app never is:

    • the markup changes between visits (A/B tests, personalization);
    • result order is shuffled per visitor, so "the third item" is meaningless;
    • sponsored listings and ads are injected into the middle of lists;
    • some elements load late or only conditionally (cookie banners, lazy images);
    • the same logical thing appears in multiple markup variants (a price as a single value, or a range, or with a "US $" prefix).

    Resilience means your locators and flows tolerate all of this without breaking. None of the techniques below is complicated; together they're the difference between a suite that runs green for months and one that needs babysitting every morning.

    22.2 Locate by identity, never by position¶

    This is the number-one rule, stated already in Chapter 8 and worth repeating because positional locators are the single most common cause of "worked yesterday, broke today":

    # FRAGILE — breaks the moment an ad is injected or the order shuffles:
page.locator("li.s-item:nth-child(3)")

# RESILIENT — finds the thing by WHAT IT IS:
page.get_by_role("link", name="Nike Air Max")
card.filter(has_text="In stock")

    eBay reorders its results per visitor, so "the third card" doesn't identify anything stable. The XPath in the reference project was written specifically without positional indices for exactly this reason (Chapter 9).

    22.3 Fallback selectors with the CSS comma¶

    When a site exposes the same element two different ways across markup variants, list both and let Playwright try them in order — the comma means "match any of these":

    _SEL_PRICE_CSS = '[data-testid="x-price-primary"], .x-price-primary'
_SEL_LINE_ITEM_CSS = "[data-testid='cart-item'], li.cart-item, [data-listitemid]"

    This one trick absorbs a whole category of "eBay rolled out a new header variant overnight" failures: prefer the stable data-testid, and fall back to the class if it's absent. It costs nothing and buys real resilience on volatile pages.

    22.4 Regex names for fuzzy-but-anchored matching¶

    Accessible names sometimes carry a dynamic part — a count, a suffix. A regular expression lets you match the stable part while ignoring the variable part:

    import re
page.get_by_role("link", name=re.compile(r"^Cart"))          # "Cart", "Cart (3)", "Cart (12)"
page.get_by_text(re.compile(r"^Subtotal"))                    # "Subtotal (3 items) $50.00"
self._SEL_ACCEPT_NAME = re.compile(r"^Accept(?:\s+all)?$", re.I)   # "Accept" OR "Accept all"

    The anchors (^, $) keep the match tight so you don't accidentally match a longer unrelated label, and re.I makes it case-insensitive. This is how the cookie-banner component handles the two common button labels ("Accept" and "Accept all") with a single locator. (Regex itself is covered in Appendix B.)

    22.5 Idempotent, conditional steps for maybe-present elements¶

    Some elements appear only sometimes — a cookie banner, a promo modal. Don't assume one is there; probe for it with a bounded wait, then branch:

    class CookieBannerComponent(BaseComponent):
    _SEL_ACCEPT_NAME = re.compile(r"^Accept(?:\s+all)?$", re.I)

    def is_visible(self) -> bool:
        try:
            self._accept_button().wait_for(state="visible", timeout=2000)
        except PlaywrightTimeoutError:
            return False                     # not here within 2s → there's no banner
        return True

    def accept(self) -> None:
        if self.is_visible():                # no banner present? this is a no-op
            self._accept_button().click()

    accept() is idempotent — safe to call whether or not a banner is present, so you can call it unconditionally in a fixture and not worry. The bounded wait_for(..., timeout=2000) is a legitimate explicit wait (a 2-second "is it here? if not, move on" probe with a branch), not a blind sleep. Dismissing the banner once in a fixture then handles it for the whole suite.

    Interview lens

    "How do you handle elements that only sometimes appear, like cookie banners or modals?" → "A bounded probe plus a branch: wait_for(state='visible', timeout=2s) inside a try/except, and I act only if it's present — so the step is idempotent and safe to call unconditionally. I dismiss the banner once in a fixture, not in every test. The bounded timeout means a missing banner costs two seconds once, never a hang." This shows you distinguish a conditional wait from a sleep.

    22.6 Parse defensively; refuse to guess¶

    Dynamic text is unreliable, and a parser that invents a value spreads bugs downstream. The price parser (Chapter 5) anchors on $ and raises on anything ambiguous, so the caller gets to decide the policy (skip this listing) rather than silently receiving a misleading 0. Resilience here means "fail in a way the caller can handle," not "return something and hope."

    22.7 Skip-and-continue for non-fatal anomalies¶

    A robust collection flow tolerates an individual bad item without aborting the entire run:

    def add_items_to_cart(self, urls: list[str]) -> None:
    for url in urls:
        tab = self.context.new_page()
        try:
            tab.goto(url)
            item = ItemPage(tab)
            if not item.is_buy_it_now():
                self.log.warning("skipping auction-only listing: %s", url)
                continue                      # one bad item is not a failed run
            if item.required_variant_selects():
                self.variant_service.pick_random_variants(item)
            item.add_to_cart()
        finally:
            tab.close()                       # always clean up the tab

    An auction listing (which has no Add-to-Cart button) is logged and skipped, not treated as fatal — and the caller later decides, via the scenario's allow_partial flag, whether a short result set is acceptable. This is policy-driven robustness: the mechanism tolerates the anomaly, and the data (allow_partial, min_results) sets the tolerance.

    Gotcha — robust is not the same as permissive

    "Skip and continue" must always be logged (self.log.warning(...)) — silent skipping hides real problems. And it must be bounded by a policy (allow_partial, min_results) so you don't quietly pass a run that actually collected zero usable items. Tolerating individual anomalies is good; tolerating a completely empty result without noticing is a bug.

    22.8 The robustness checklist¶

    When asked "how do you make tests robust?", walk this list — it's a complete answer:

    1. Locate by identity (role/label/text), never by position.
    2. Auto-wait; never time.sleep; use a bounded wait_for only for genuine probes.
    3. Fallback selectors (data-testid, .class) for volatile markup.
    4. Regex names, anchored tight, for labels with dynamic parts.
    5. Idempotent conditional steps for maybe-present elements.
    6. Defensive parsing that raises on ambiguity.
    7. Skip-and-log non-fatal anomalies, bounded by a data-driven tolerance.
    8. Isolated contexts per test so parallel runs don't interfere.

    Exercise 22.1 — make a brittle locator resilient

    Find (or write) a locator like page.locator("div.card:nth-child(2) .price"). Rewrite it to locate by identity instead — by the card's visible product name (filter(has_text=...)) then the price within it. Then add a comma-fallback for the price selector. Explain which of the two versions survives (a) an injected ad row above the card and (b) a price-class rename.

    Key idea

    Robustness is designing for a site that changes under you: identity over position; fallback selectors for volatile markup; tight, anchored regex names for dynamic labels; idempotent probes for conditional UI; parsers that refuse to guess; and logged skip-and-continue bounded by data-driven tolerances. Memorise the eight-point checklist — it is the robustness answer.

    Chapter 23 — Three Dynamics: Pagination, Variants & Prices¶

    Real e-commerce automation has to handle three recurring dynamic challenges: paginating to collect enough items, selecting product variants, and parsing messy prices. Each is a small, self-contained algorithm, and "how did you handle pagination / variants?" is a direct interview question. We'll work through all three in full, drawing out the reusable design ideas in each.

    23.1 Pagination — a generic, reusable collector¶

    The requirement. Collect up to limit qualifying items. If the current page has fewer than needed, go to the next page and keep collecting. Stop when you have enough, when you run out of pages, or when you hit a safety cap.

    The elegant solution is a generic paginator that knows nothing about eBay, search, or URLs — only "a thing I can advance through pages." That capability is captured by the _Pageable Protocol from Chapter 4:

    def collect_until(component, collect_fn, target_count, max_pages=None, *, env=None):
    if max_pages is None:
        if env is None:
            raise ValueError("collect_until needs max_pages or env")
        max_pages = env.max_pages_to_paginate

    collected = []
    for page_index in range(1, max_pages + 1):
        batch = collect_fn(component)              # collect this page's qualifying items
        collected.extend(batch)
        if len(collected) >= target_count:         # got enough?
            return collected[:target_count]        # trim any overshoot to exactly the target
        if not component.has_next_page():           # no more pages?
            break
        component.go_to_next_page()                 # advance and loop
    return collected                                # may be fewer than target — that's allowed

    The control flow, as a picture:

    flowchart TD
    Start([start, collected=empty]) --> Collect["collect this page → add to collected"]
    Collect --> Enough{"collected >= target?"}
    Enough -- yes --> Trim["return collected, trimmed to target"]
    Enough -- no --> Next{"has next page?"}
    Next -- no --> Return["return what we have"]
    Next -- yes --> Cap{"under max_pages?"}
    Cap -- no --> Return
    Cap -- yes --> Advance["go to next page"] --> Collect

    Design points worth naming in an interview:

    • Bounded by max_pages. Without a cap, a query that never yields limit items would paginate forever. The cap (5 for dev, 3 for ci) comes from the environment profile — a data-driven safety limit, not a magic number.
    • Returns up to the target. collected[:target_count] trims any overshoot, and returning fewer than the target is valid — the caller decides via allow_partial what to do with a short result. The paginator imposes no policy of its own.
    • Generic over the item type and the page. It works for any paginated list and any item type (Chapter 4), so it's reusable far beyond search results — dependency inversion in action.
    • The collector is injected (collect_fn), so what counts as a qualifying item (the price / sponsored / Buy-It-Now rules) stays in the service, not in the paginator.

    Interview lens

    "Walk me through your pagination." → "A generic collect_until that accepts anything satisfying a _Pageable Protocol — has_next_page and go_to_next_page — plus an injected collector function. It accumulates across pages until it has the target count, runs out of pages, or hits a config-driven max_pages safety cap, then trims to the target. Returning fewer is valid; the caller's allow_partial decides if that's fatal. The eBay-specific filtering lives in the injected collector, so the paginator itself is reusable for any list." That one answer demonstrates pagination, generics, and dependency inversion at once.

    A spec nuance worth owning

    The original spec said "paginate until you have 5 or pages run out." The max_pages cap means we might stop before pages truly run out. That's a deliberate safety trade-off — be ready to say "I bounded it to avoid an unbounded walk on a sparse query, and the cap is configuration, so it's trivial to raise." Owning a deliberate trade-off beats pretending it doesn't exist.

    23.2 Variants — random in-stock selection¶

    The requirement. If an item has variant pickers (size, colour), choose random in-stock values before adding it to the cart. The challenge is filtering out the junk options — placeholders like "Select…" and entries that are out of stock:

    class VariantService(BaseService):
    _PLACEHOLDER_PATTERN = re.compile(r"^\s*(?:-+|select|choose|please select|--)", re.I)
    _OUT_OF_STOCK_PATTERN = re.compile(r"(?:out of stock|sold out|unavailable)", re.I)

    def pick_random_variants(self, item: ItemPage) -> None:
        for combo in item.required_variant_selects():
            in_stock = combo.locator("option:not([disabled])")    # 1. skip disabled options
            labels = [label.strip() for label in in_stock.all_text_contents()]
            valid = [
                label for label in labels
                if label
                and not self._PLACEHOLDER_PATTERN.match(label)     # 2. skip "Select…" placeholders
                and not self._OUT_OF_STOCK_PATTERN.search(label)   # 3. skip out-of-stock labels
            ]
            if not valid:
                self.log.warning("no in-stock option; skipping")   # log + continue
                continue
            choice = random.choice(valid)
            combo.select_option(label=choice)
            self.log.info("variant: picked %r", choice)

    The design points:

    • Three layers of filtering, defence in depth: the CSS :not([disabled]) drops disabled options at the DOM level; the placeholder regex drops "Select…"-style prompts; the out-of-stock regex drops unavailable labels. Any one might miss a case; together they're robust.
    • Skip-and-log when a combobox has no valid option, rather than crashing — the caller decides whether the item is still usable (the §22.7 pattern).
    • It's a service, not a component. Choosing a variant at random is a business decision (the policy "pick any in-stock option"); the item page's job is only to expose the variant comboboxes. Putting random.choice in the ItemPage component would be business logic in a component — a real Single Responsibility violation. (This is exactly the kind of dead, duplicated method worth removing in a cleanup pass.)

    Interview lens

    "Why is variant selection in a service and not on the item page object?" → "Choosing which variant is a policy decision — we pick any in-stock one at random — while the item page's job is only to expose the variant comboboxes. Random choice is business logic, so it belongs in a service: the component reports, the service decides." Same SRP refrain as Chapter 20, on a fresh example.

    23.3 Prices — parse defensively (the robustness view)¶

    Price parsing is covered in depth in Chapter 5; here is the robustness framing. The parser must survive every format the site throws at it:

    Input Output Why it's tricky
    "$25.00" 25.00 the baseline
    "US $1,234.56" 1234.56 currency prefix + thousands comma
    "$25.00 to $30.00" 25.00 a range — take the lower bound
    "Subtotal (3 items) $50.00" 50.00 the "3" must NOT win — anchor on $
    "Time left: 3d 4h" ValueError not a price at all — refuse to guess

    The two robustness principles embodied:

    1. Anchor on intent ($), not on position. A "take the first number" parser would return 3 for the subtotal line — a silent, corrupting bug. Anchoring on $ makes the price win.
    2. Raise on ambiguity. Garbage in → ValueError out, so the caller skips the listing. A parser that returned 0 for "Auction ended" would silently pass budget checks it should fail.

    And because the parser is pure (text in, Decimal out, no I/O), all of this is verified by ~22 unit tests in well under a tenth of a second, with no browser (Chapter 16) — the part of the suite that's always green.

    Exercise 23.1 — generalise the paginator

    The collect_until paginator is generic. On paper (or in code), describe how you'd reuse it, unchanged, to collect the first 20 rows of an order-history page that paginates. What two methods must the order-history page expose to satisfy _Pageable, and what would its injected collect_fn return? (Answer: has_next_page() and go_to_next_page(); the collect_fn returns that page's order rows — and nothing in the paginator changes.)

    Key idea

    Pagination: a generic, Protocol-based, bounded collector with the filtering policy injected. Variants: defence-in-depth filtering with a random in-stock choice, living in a service because choosing is policy. Prices: anchor on $, take the lower bound of ranges, raise on garbage, and stay pure so it's exhaustively unit-tested. These three are the concrete robustness that evaluators reward.

    Chapter 24 — Flakiness & Debugging¶

    A flaky test is one that passes and fails without any change to the code. Flakiness is the single fastest way to destroy trust in a suite: once people start re-running red builds "to see if it passes this time," the suite has stopped doing its job — a red result no longer means anything. This chapter covers where flakiness comes from, how to prevent it, and — when it happens anyway — how to diagnose it with Playwright's tooling.

    24.1 The root causes of flakiness¶

    Almost all flakiness traces back to one of these five causes. Knowing the list lets you diagnose by elimination:

    1. Timing / race conditions — acting before the page is ready. Cure: auto-waiting and expect() (Chapter 7); never time.sleep.
    2. Brittle, positional locators — order shuffled, an ad injected. Cure: locate by identity (Chapter 22).
    3. Shared state between tests — order dependence, a leaked session. Cure: isolated contexts per test, function-scoped fixtures (Chapters 6, 13).
    4. External dependence — the live site is slow, down, or changed. Cure: push logic down to unit tests (Chapter 16); accept that end-to-end tests against a third-party site carry some irreducible flakiness, and design for fast diagnosis rather than perfect prevention.
    5. Animations / transitions — clicking mid-animation. Cure: Playwright's "stable" actionability check already waits for the bounding box to stop moving (Chapter 7).

    Key idea

    Flakiness is almost never truly random — it's a hidden assumption about timing, ordering, or markup. Playwright's defaults (auto-waiting, isolated contexts, strict mode) eliminate most of it by construction; the rest comes down to your locator and state-isolation choices. When a test flakes, don't shrug — find which of the five causes it is.

    24.2 The Trace Viewer — your primary debugging tool¶

    This is the tool that makes Playwright debugging genuinely pleasant, and it's a frequent interview topic. Playwright can record a trace: a complete timeline of a test, with a snapshot of the DOM before and after every single action, plus network logs, console output, and screenshots. When a test fails in CI, you download its trace and replay it on your laptop — time-travel debugging, without having to reproduce the failure yourself.

    Turn it on (keeping traces only for failures, to avoid filling the disk):

    # pyproject.toml
[tool.pytest.ini_options]
addopts = "--tracing=retain-on-failure"

    uv run pytest -m regression           # failures leave a trace.zip under test-results/
uv run playwright show-trace test-results/<...>/trace.zip

    In the viewer you get:
