    • a timeline of every action with its duration;
    • before/after DOM snapshots you can hover and inspect — you literally see what the page looked like at the instant a locator failed;
    • the exact locator each action used, and whether it matched;
    • network and console panels for the same moment.

    Interview lens — a very common question

    "How do you debug a flaky CI failure you can't reproduce locally?" → "I capture a trace on failure (--tracing=retain-on-failure), download the trace.zip artifact from the CI run, and open it with playwright show-trace. It gives me before/after DOM snapshots for every action, plus the network and console logs, so I can see the exact page state at the moment the locator failed and tell whether it was timing, a markup change, or missing data. I don't just re-run and hope it passes." That answer alone signals real production experience.

    24.3 Video and screenshots¶

    Cheaper, complementary artifacts:

    addopts = "--video=retain-on-failure --screenshot=only-on-failure"
    • Video — a recording of the run; the fastest way to eyeball "what on earth happened."
    • Screenshot on failure — the final frame at the moment of death; the quickest "what did it look like when it broke."

    The reference project also takes explicit step screenshots (screenshots.capture("cart")) and attaches them to the Allure report, so even a passing run documents each stage visually — useful for demos and for any evaluation that asks for reports or screenshots.

    24.4 Interactive debugging while developing¶

    When you're writing or fixing a test, these put you in the driver's seat:

    uv run pytest --headed --slowmo 500            # watch it run, slowly
PWDEBUG=1 uv run pytest tests/test_x.py        # open the Playwright Inspector: step + pick locators
uv run pytest -k test_search --headed -s       # -s lets print()/log output stream live
    • --headed + --slowmo — watch the browser drive itself and spot where it goes wrong.
    • PWDEBUG=1 opens the Inspector: you can pause, step through actions one at a time, and use the locator picker to test selectors against the live page.
    • -s disables pytest's output capture so your log.info(...) lines appear in real time.

    Gotcha — slow-mo is a magnifying glass, not a fix

    --slowmo and --headed are debugging aids, not solutions. If a test only passes with slow-mo, it has a genuine waiting bug — find the missing expect(); don't ship the slow-mo. Slowing the clock to mask a race condition is the exact same mistake as time.sleep.

    24.5 Retries — a controlled last resort¶

    pytest can be told to retry failed tests:

    uv run pytest --retries 2          # via pytest-playwright / pytest-rerunfailures

    Retries can paper over irreducible third-party flakiness (a CDN hiccup, a transient network blip), so one external glitch doesn't fail an entire build. But they are a last resort, never a substitute for fixing a real bug.

    Interview lens

    "Do you use retries?" → "Sparingly, and only for irreducible external flakiness — a third-party site we don't control. A retry on a test that's flaky because of our own timing or locator bug just hides the defect and erodes trust in the suite. First I fix the root cause with proper waits and stable locators; retries are the seatbelt, not the engine." The nuance — fine for external, not for your own bugs — is the senior take.

    24.6 Logging as a first-class diagnostic¶

    The suite logs each meaningful step — search start: query=… max_price=…, paginator: page=2 collected=4 target=5, cart: subtotal=… budget=…. When a run fails, that log reads as a narrative of what the flow believed it was doing, and it often pinpoints the failure before you even open the trace. Structured, levelled logging — info for flow milestones, debug for skips, warning for tolerated anomalies — is a quiet professional habit that reviewers notice (see Appendix C for the logging mechanics).

    Exercise 24.1 — make a trace and read it

    Write a tiny test that navigates somewhere and clicks a link. Run it with --tracing=on. Open the produced trace with playwright show-trace. Click through the timeline; hover an action and inspect the before/after DOM snapshots. Now you'll recognise the viewer instantly the day a CI failure hands you a trace.zip.

    Key idea

    Flakiness comes from timing, brittle locators, shared state, externals, or animations — and Playwright's defaults prevent most of it. When it strikes, the Trace Viewer (before/after DOM snapshots, captured on failure in CI) is your primary tool; video, screenshots, and PWDEBUG help while developing. Use retries only for irreducible external flakiness, never to mask your own bugs — and let levelled logging narrate each run.

    Chapter 25 — Reporting & Continuous Integration¶

    The last major area of evaluation: clear reports and a working CI pipeline. A suite nobody can read the results of, or that only runs on one person's laptop, is half a suite. This chapter covers the reporting options (with a focus on Allure), how to make a report tell a story a non-author can follow, and how to wire the whole thing into GitHub Actions so it runs automatically and leaves behind everything you need to debug a failure.

    25.1 The reporting options, and when to use each¶

    Tool Output Best for
    JUnit XML machine-readable XML CI dashboards that ingest results to track history and flaky tests
    HTML (pytest-html / Playwright) a single self-contained HTML page quick local sharing
    Allure a rich, interactive dashboard suites: timeline, steps, attachments, trends over time

    Allure is the richest, and it's what the reference project uses, so we focus there. But know the others exist and why: if an interviewer asks "what about JUnit XML?", the answer is "for CI tooling that ingests XML to track pass/fail history and identify flaky tests over time."

    25.2 How Allure works¶

    Allure runs in two stages. During the test run, the allure-pytest plugin writes raw result data (JSON) into a folder. Afterwards, the Allure command-line tool renders that data into an HTML dashboard:

    uv run pytest -m regression --alluredir=allure-results    # 1. tests emit raw JSON results
uv run allure serve allure-results                         # 2. render + open the dashboard locally
# or, for CI: generate static HTML into a folder
uv run allure generate allure-results -o allure-report --clean

    Out of the box, the plugin captures each test's status, duration, and output. You make the report genuinely useful by enriching it with steps and attachments.

    25.3 Steps — turning a test into a readable narrative¶

    allure.step is a context manager (Chapter 5) that groups actions into labelled, collapsible phases in the report:

    import allure

with allure.step("SETUP_GUEST"):
    auth_service.start_guest_session()

with allure.step("SEARCH"):
    urls = search_service.search_items_by_name_under_price("shoes", Decimal("220"), 5)
    assert len(urls) > 0

with allure.step("ADD_TO_CART"):
    cart_service.add_items_to_cart(urls)

with allure.step("ASSERT_TOTAL"):
    cart_service.assert_cart_total_not_exceeds(Decimal("220"), len(urls))

    In the rendered report, a failure is pinned to the step where it happened ("failed in ASSERT_TOTAL"), so a reader sees the user journey and exactly where it broke — without reading any code. That readability is the whole point of steps.

    25.4 Attachments — screenshots in the report¶

    You can attach files — screenshots, traces — to a step, and they render inline:

    path = screenshots.capture("cart")
allure.attach.file(str(path), name="cart", attachment_type=allure.attachment_type.PNG)

    Now the cart screenshot appears right under the ASSERT_TOTAL step. This is what satisfies the common "reports and screenshots" requirement and makes the report a self-contained record of what actually happened on screen.

    25.5 The Environment panel¶

    Allure shows an "Environment" panel if you drop an environment.properties file into the results folder. The reference project writes one from a session fixture, so every report records how it ran:

    @pytest.fixture(scope="session", autouse=True)
def _allure_environment(env, profile):
    _ALLURE_RESULTS.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    lines = [
        f"python.version={'.'.join(map(str, sys.version_info[:3]))}",
        f"playwright.version={_pkg_version('playwright')}",
        f"profile={profile}",
        f"base_url={env.base_url}",
        f"headless={env.headless}",
    ]
    (_ALLURE_RESULTS / "environment.properties").write_text("\n".join(lines) + "\n")

    A reviewer opening the report immediately sees it ran on Python 3.11, profile ci, headless — context that makes the results trustworthy and reproducible.

    Interview lens

    "What makes a good test report?" → "It tells a reader who didn't write the code what ran, in what environment, and exactly where any failure occurred — without their reading the source. So: Allure with labelled steps so failures pin to a phase, screenshots and traces attached, and an Environment panel recording the profile, base URL, and versions. The report is the artifact stakeholders actually look at." Framing the report as something for other people is the mature answer.

    25.6 Continuous Integration with GitHub Actions¶

    CI runs the suite automatically on every push and pull request, so regressions are caught before merge — not days later on someone's laptop. A GitHub Actions workflow is a YAML file under .github/workflows/:

    name: regression
on:
  push: { branches: [main] }
  pull_request: { branches: [main] }
  workflow_dispatch:            # also lets you trigger it manually from the GitHub UI

jobs:
  regression-chromium-headless:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with: { python-version: "3.11" }
      - name: Install uv
        run: curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
      - name: Sync deps
        run: ~/.local/bin/uv sync
      - name: Install browsers
        run: ~/.local/bin/uv run playwright install --with-deps chromium   # (1)
      - name: Run regression
        env: { PROFILE: ci }                                                # (2)
        run: ~/.local/bin/uv run pytest -m regression -n 4 --alluredir=allure-results
        continue-on-error: true                                            # (3)
      - name: Generate Allure report
        run: allure generate allure-results --clean -o allure-report
      - name: Upload artifacts
        if: always()                                                       # (4)
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with: { name: allure-report, path: allure-report/ }

    The four numbered details are exactly the ones that separate a working pipeline from a broken one:

    1. --with-deps installs the Linux system libraries headless Chromium needs on a bare runner (Chapter 1) — omit it and the browser won't launch.
    2. PROFILE: ci selects the headless, tighter-pagination profile — the same code, different configuration (Chapter 21).
    3. continue-on-error: true lets the later steps run even if tests failed, so the report and artifacts are still produced for failed runs — which is exactly when you need them.
    4. if: always() uploads the artifacts regardless of the test outcome. A failed run is the moment you want the trace, video, and report downloadable.

    Interview lens

    "Why upload CI artifacts even when tests fail?" → "Failed runs are when you most need the evidence. So I let the test step continue-on-error and gate the upload on if: always(), which produces the Allure report, traces, videos, and failure screenshots for red builds too. Otherwise a CI failure gives you a red X and nothing to debug with." A small detail that signals you've actually operated CI, not just written a workflow file once.

    25.7 The status badge¶

    A README badge (![regression](…/badge.svg)) shows the latest CI status at a glance. It must point at the correct owner/repo — a leftover <USERNAME_PLACEHOLDER> is a tell-tale sign of an unfinished project, so fixing it is a basic pre-publish step.

    Exercise 25.1 — enrich a report

    Take any small test and wrap its phases in two or three allure.step(...) blocks; attach a screenshot to one of them with allure.attach.file(...). Run with --alluredir=allure-results and allure serve. Click into the test and confirm you can see the steps and the inline screenshot. Then make a step fail and observe how the report pins the failure to that step.

    Key idea

    Reports are for other people: use Allure with labelled steps (so failures pin to a phase), attached screenshots/traces, and an Environment panel. CI runs the suite on every push with the ci profile and uploads artifacts on every run (continue-on-error + if: always()) so even red builds are debuggable. Know JUnit XML and HTML exist as alternatives, and why.

    Chapter 26 — Reviewing AI-Generated Test Code¶

    A common exercise — in interviews and in everyday code review — goes like this: a teammate used an AI assistant to draft a Playwright test, it doesn't behave as expected, and you must find and explain the bugs by reading the code statically. This is a skill, and it is exactly the skill this whole course has been building, applied backwards: where the earlier chapters taught you what correct looks like, here you use that knowledge to spot what's wrong. Every bug below maps to a chapter you've read, so this chapter also doubles as a review of the whole book.

    26.1 The code under review¶

    from playwright.sync_api import sync_playwright
from selenium import webdriver       # ← already suspicious
import time                          # ← already suspicious

def test_search_functionality():
    browser = sync_playwright().start().chromium.launch()
    page = browser.new_page()
    page.goto("https://example.com")

    time.sleep(2)

    search_box = page.locator("#search")
    search_box.fill("playwright testing")

    page.locator(".button").click()

    time.sleep(3)

    results = page.locator(".result-item")

    browser.close()

    It runs (more or less) and it looks like a test — imports, a test_ function, a browser, page actions. That's the trap. AI-generated code is very good at producing the shape of correct code without the substance. Reviewing it means checking, line by line, whether each statement actually does the thing its shape implies. Here, five things don't. We'll take them in order of impact — which is also how you should present them in an interview: lead with the worst.

    26.2 Bug 1 — the test has no assertions¶

    results = page.locator(".result-item")

    This constructs a lazy locator (Chapter 7) — it queries nothing, counts nothing, and verifies nothing. The function then ends with no assert and no expect(). A test that cannot fail is not a test. This one "passes" whether search returned results, returned zero results, redirected to an error page, or loaded an entirely different site — as long as nothing throws an exception. This is the most serious bug, because it means the test provides no signal at all.

    # Fix — verify something real:
results = page.locator(".result-item")
expect(results.first).to_be_visible()
assert results.count() > 0, f"expected results, got {results.count()}"

    Maps to: Chapter 7 (locators are lazy), Chapter 10 (expect vs the locator object).

    26.3 Bug 2 — brittle CSS locators (#search, .button)¶

    #search is a fragile ID, and .button is almost certainly not unique on the page — so the click either triggers a strict-mode violation (Chapter 7) or clicks the wrong element. Neither locator communicates intent: a reviewer can't tell which button is being clicked. These are precisely the position/class-based locators Chapter 8 warns against.

    # Fix — semantic, intent-revealing, stable:
page.get_by_role("searchbox", name="Search").fill("playwright testing")
page.get_by_role("button", name="Search").click()

    Maps to: Chapter 8 (locator strategy), Chapter 22 (resilience).

    26.4 Bug 3 — time.sleep() instead of auto-waiting¶

    Two hardcoded sleeps — the canonical Playwright anti-pattern (Chapter 7). They are simultaneously too slow (always burning the full 2 and 3 seconds even when the page is ready in 100ms) and too flaky (failing when a busy CI runner needs 3.2 seconds). Playwright already auto-waits on actions and offers expect() for state.

    # Fix — wait on observable state, never the clock:
page.goto("https://example.com", wait_until="domcontentloaded")
expect(search_box).to_be_visible()                          # replaces sleep(2)
# ...click...
expect(page.locator(".result-item").first).to_be_visible()  # replaces sleep(3)

    Maps to: Chapter 7 (auto-waiting), Chapter 11 (named conditions vs the clock).

    26.5 Bug 4 — stray Selenium import + leaked Playwright runtime¶

    Two distinct mistakes that, together, betray an AI hallucination:

    1. from selenium import webdriver is imported and never used. Selenium and Playwright are different frameworks; mixing them in one file suggests the generator stitched together fragments from its training data without understanding either. It will also crash on import in any environment where selenium isn't installed — breaking the test before it even starts.
    2. sync_playwright().start() starts a runtime that owns a background process. The code calls browser.close() but never .stop() on the runtime — leaking the process. Repeated across a CI suite, the runner exhausts its handles and starts failing in baffling ways.
    # Fix — drop Selenium; wrap the runtime in a context manager so it's always stopped:
from playwright.sync_api import sync_playwright, expect

def test_search_functionality():
    with sync_playwright() as p:          # __exit__ calls .stop() for you — no leak
        browser = p.chromium.launch()
        context = browser.new_context()   # isolate cookies/storage
        page = context.new_page()
        # ... test body ...
        context.close()
        browser.close()

    Maps to: Chapter 5 (context managers), Chapter 6 (the object model).

    26.6 Bug 5 — not a real pytest test (mixed paradigms)¶

    The function is named test_search_functionality — signalling pytest — but its body manually launches Playwright instead of accepting the page fixture. pytest will discover and run it, but it bypasses everything the pytest-playwright plugin provides (Chapter 15): automatic trace-on-failure, video, screenshots, per-test isolation, and xdist parallelism. It's the worst of both worlds — a pytest test that throws away pytest's entire value.

    # Fix — accept the fixture and let the plugin own the lifecycle:
import re
from playwright.sync_api import Page, expect

def test_search_functionality(page: Page):           # ← the plugin injects a fresh page
    page.goto("https://example.com", wait_until="domcontentloaded")
    page.get_by_role("searchbox", name="Search").fill("playwright testing")
    page.get_by_role("button", name="Search").click()
    results = page.locator(".result-item")
    expect(results.first).to_be_visible()
    assert results.count() > 0

    Maps to: Chapter 13 (fixtures), Chapter 15 (the plugin).

    26.7 The summary table (what you'd actually write in the review)¶

    # Bug Why it matters Chapters
    1 No assertions the test cannot fail on a real bug 7, 10
    2 #search, .button locators brittle, ambiguous, opaque 8, 22
    3 time.sleep() slow and flaky 7, 11
    4 Selenium import + leaked runtime dead code + a process leak 5, 6
    5 Manual Playwright in a pytest function discards trace, isolation, parallelism 13, 15

    26.8 The meta-lesson — how to review any AI-generated test code¶

    Key idea

    AI-generated test code looks like a test because it has the shape of one — imports, a test_* function, a browser launch, page actions. Reviewing it means checking, line by line, whether each statement actually does the thing its shape implies. In this snippet the assertions are missing, the locators are ornamental, the waits are wishful, the imports are hallucinated, and the framework is bypassed. Your value as a reviewer is knowing what correct looks like — which is the entire point of this course.

    Interview lens

    This kind of exercise tests judgment, not trivia. Lead with impact: "First and worst, it has no assertions, so it can't fail." Then group the rest — locators, waits, lifecycle, paradigm — and for each, explain why it matters (flaky CI, leaked processes, lost traces) rather than just naming it. Close with the meta-point: AI-generated tests fail by having the right shape and the wrong behaviour, which is precisely why a human who knows the craft has to review them.

    Exercise 26.1 — review it cold

    Before re-reading this chapter, copy the buggy snippet from §26.1 onto paper and find as many issues as you can in five minutes, writing one sentence on why each matters. Then check yourself against the table in §26.7. The goal isn't to memorise these five bugs — it's to build the habit of asking, of every line, "does this do what its shape implies?"

    Key idea (recap)

    Reviewing AI test code is the inverse of writing good test code: you apply everything from Parts I–V to spot where shape and substance diverge. Lead with the highest-impact problem (no assertions), explain the why of each, and remember the deeper point — looking like a test is not the same as being one.

    Part VI — Capstone & Interview

    Chapter 27 — Capstone: The Reference Suite End to End¶

    This chapter assembles everything into the full architecture. Read it as a guided tour from the test at the top down to the browser at the bottom and back up again, naming the chapter behind each decision. If you can narrate this walkthrough out loud, you genuinely understand the system — which is also the surest way to be able to defend a suite like it under questioning.

    27.1 The reference project, restated¶

    The worked example implements an end-to-end flow on eBay with clean architecture (POM, OOP, data-driven). It provides four functions:

    1. guest auth — establish a session;
    2. searchItemsByNameUnderPrice(query, maxPrice, limit) → URLs — search, filter by price, and collect up to limit qualifying item URLs;
    3. addItemsToCart(urls) — open each item, pick variants if required, add it to the cart;
    4. assertCartTotalNotExceeds(budgetPerItem, itemsCount) — verify the cart subtotal.

    Plus a static review of buggy AI-generated code, a README, and a run report.

    27.2 The layer map (with the chapter behind each layer)¶

    flowchart TD
    T["tests/  — assertions only  (Ch 18, 20)"]
    CF["conftest.py  — DI: db, env, services  (Ch 13, 21)"]
    SV["services/  — auth · search · cart · variants  (Ch 17, 20, 23)"]
    CO["components/  — home · header · results · card · filter · item · cart  (Ch 18, 19)"]
    PW["Playwright sync API  — browser · context · page  (Ch 6, 7)"]
    UT["utils/  — price_parser · paginator · screenshot · logger  (Ch 5, 16, 23)"]
    DB["db/  — data.yaml + typed loaders  (Ch 14, 21)"]
    T --> CF --> SV --> CO --> PW
    SV -.uses.-> UT
    T -.parametrized by.-> DB

    Every arrow points downward: tests depend on services, services on components, components on Playwright. Nothing points back up. That acyclic, downward dependency flow is the architecture — and each boundary is drawn where it is for the SOLID reasons from Chapter 17.

    27.3 Tracing one test from top to bottom¶

    Here is the canonical end-to-end test:

    @pytest.mark.regression
def test_full_e2e_search_add_assert(auth_service, search_service, cart_service, screenshots):
    with allure.step("SETUP_GUEST"):
        auth_service.start_guest_session()

    with allure.step("SEARCH"):
        urls = search_service.search_items_by_name_under_price("shoes", Decimal("220"), 5)
        assert len(urls) > 0

    with allure.step("ADD_TO_CART"):
        cart_service.add_items_to_cart(urls)

    with allure.step("ASSERT_TOTAL"):
        cart_service.assert_cart_total_not_exceeds(Decimal("220"), len(urls))

    Now walk through what happens, layer by layer, naming the chapter that explains each piece:

    1. Fixtures resolve (Chapter 13). Requesting search_service pulls in page → env → (db, profile). The test receives fully-wired services with no new in sight. The money values are Decimal literals — never floats (Chapter 5).
    2. start_guest_session() (auth service): seeds region/currency cookies on the context (Chapter 11), loads the home page, and dismisses the cookie banner idempotently (Chapter 22). No login — a guest can reach every flow under test, and the real login is captcha-gated and out of scope.
    3. search_items_by_name_under_price("shoes", 220, 5) (search service): orchestrates home.load() → header.search() → apply_price_filter() → apply_buy_it_now() → sort_by_price_plus_shipping_lowest(), then calls the generic collect_until paginator (Chapter 23) with an injected collector. The collector qualifies each card — skip sponsored, skip auctions, drop price > max, with parse_price raising on garbage (Chapters 5 and 20). It returns up to five URLs.
    4. assert len(urls) > 0 — a plain assert on an in-memory value (Chapter 10).
    5. add_items_to_cart(urls) (cart service): each URL opens in a new tab sharing the context session (Chapter 11); auctions are logged and skipped (Chapter 22); variants are chosen by the injected variant service (Chapter 23); add-to-cart fires; a screenshot is taken; the tab is closed in finally.
    6. assert_cart_total_not_exceeds(220, len(urls)) (cart service): opens the cart, parses the subtotal as a Decimal (Chapter 5), compares it against budget_per_item * items_count, and raises a structured message on failure (Chapter 20).
    7. Throughout, allure.step labels each phase and screenshots attach to the report (Chapter 25); on failure, the trace is retained (Chapter 24).

    27.4 How the data-driven variant reuses all of it¶

    @pytest.mark.regression
def test_scenario(scenario, auth_service, search_service, cart_service, screenshots):
    auth_service.start_guest_session()
    urls = search_service.search_items_by_name_under_price(
        scenario.query, scenario.max_price, scenario.limit
    )
    if len(urls) < scenario.limit and not scenario.allow_partial:
        raise AssertionError(...)
    assert len(urls) >= scenario.min_results
    if not urls:
        return
    cart_service.add_items_to_cart(urls)
    cart_service.assert_cart_total_not_exceeds(scenario.max_price, len(urls))

    It's the identical flow, but query/max_price/limit come from a Scenario dataclass that pytest_generate_tests parametrized from data.yaml (Chapter 14). Adding a scenario is a YAML edit. The allow_partial / min_results fields encode each scenario's tolerance (Chapter 22). Same services, different data — that's DRY across the smoke, regression, and data-driven suites (Chapter 17).

    27.5 The same services power a non-test demo¶

    A standalone simulate_usage.py script drives the exact same services outside pytest, headed, over a demos table — proving the framework is library-quality, not test-only glue. This is the real test of clean layering: if your services needed pytest fixtures to function, they'd be too coupled to the test harness. That they don't is the proof the boundaries are real.

    Interview lens — the whole-architecture narration

    Practise saying this in about sixty seconds: "Tests assert and are data-driven from YAML. They request services via fixture dependency injection. Services own the cross-page flows and policy — search composes home/header/results/filter plus a generic paginator; cart opens tabs, handles variants and auctions, and asserts the subtotal in Decimal. Components own one markup region each, scoped by a root locator so repeated cards don't collide. Pure utilities — the price parser, the paginator — are unit-tested in milliseconds. Config is typed, profile-switched by one env var, with no hardcoded URLs. And the same services run a headed demo outside pytest, which proves the layering holds." That narration touches every major area of evaluation.

    27.6 If you rebuilt it from scratch — a sensible order¶

    A bottom-up sequence, where each layer is testable before the next is built:

    1. Config + models (db/) — load YAML into typed dataclasses; unit-testable immediately.
    2. Pure utils (price_parser, paginator) — write them with their unit tests.
    3. BaseComponent — the scoped-locator plumbing.
    4. Components — one region at a time, against the live pages.
    5. Services — compose components into the four flows.
    6. conftest fixtures — wire the services together via DI.
    7. Tests — smoke first ("does search work?"), then the full e2e, then data-driven.
    8. Reporting + CI — Allure steps, the workflow, artifact upload.

    Exercise 27.1 — narrate it

    Without looking, narrate the path of test_full_e2e_search_add_assert out loud, from fixture resolution down to the browser and back to the assertion, naming the responsibility of each layer. Time yourself; aim for under ninety seconds. If you get stuck at a layer, that's the chapter to revisit.

    Key idea

    The whole suite is one downward dependency flow: tests → services → components → Playwright, with pure utilities and typed config on the side. Each layer has one job and one reason to change. The data-driven test and the demo script reuse the same services, proving the boundaries are real. Being able to narrate this tour is the same skill as being able to defend the design.

    Part VII — Beyond the Basics

    Chapter 29 — Network Interception & Mocking¶

    So far every test has driven the real application against whatever the network returned. Sometimes that's not what you want. Sometimes you need to control what the network returns — to test how the UI handles an error, an empty result, or a slow response, none of which you can reliably produce against a live backend. Playwright lets you intercept any request the page makes and decide what happens to it. This chapter teaches that capability from scratch, with the exact Python sync-API methods, and — just as importantly — when you should and shouldn't reach for it.

    29.1 Why intercept the network at all?¶

    Three motivations cover almost every real use:

    1. Test states you can't easily produce for real. How does the UI render when the search API returns zero results? When it returns a 500 error? When it's slow? Forcing the live backend into those states is hard or impossible; mocking the response makes them trivial and deterministic.
    2. Speed and determinism. A test that mocks the API doesn't depend on a real server being up, fast, or returning stable data — so it's faster and far less flaky.
    3. Block noise. You can abort requests for ads, analytics, or third-party widgets that slow tests down and add flakiness, without changing the app.

    The mechanism for all three is the same: page.route().

    29.2 page.route — intercept matching requests¶

    page.route(url_pattern, handler) registers a handler that runs for every request whose URL matches the pattern. The handler receives a Route object, and it must do exactly one of three things with it: fulfill it (provide a response), let it continue, or abort it.

    from playwright.sync_api import Page, Route, expect

def test_mock_the_fruit_api(page: Page):
    def handle(route: Route):
        mock = [{"name": "Strawberry", "id": 21}]
        route.fulfill(json=mock)              # respond with our own JSON, no real request made

    page.route("*/**/api/v1/fruits", handle)   # intercept any request to that path
    page.goto("https://demo.playwright.dev/api-mocking")
    expect(page.get_by_text("Strawberry")).to_be_visible()

    The URL pattern uses glob syntax: * matches within a path segment, ** matches across segments, so "*/**/api/v1/fruits" matches that endpoint on any host. The handler above calls route.fulfill(json=...), which makes Playwright return your JSON to the page — the real backend is never contacted. The page renders exactly as if the API had returned one strawberry, deterministically, every time.

    29.3 The three things a route handler can do¶

    route.fulfill(json=[...])               # 1. respond with a mock body (status defaults to 200)
route.fulfill(status=500, json={"error": "boom"})   # ...or a mock ERROR
route.abort()                           # 2. block the request entirely (good for ads/analytics)
route.continue_()                       # 3. let it proceed unchanged (note the trailing underscore)

    A few details that matter:

    • fulfill can set status, headers, body, or json — so you can simulate a 404, a 500, a malformed payload, anything.
    • abort simulates a failed request — useful for testing offline/error handling, or for silencing third-party noise.
    • continue_ has a trailing underscore because continue is a Python keyword (you can't name a method continue). It lets the request proceed, optionally with modified headers or post data.

    Gotcha — continue_, not continue

    continue is a reserved word in Python, so the method is spelled route.continue_(). This trips up people copying patterns from the JavaScript docs, where it's route.continue().

    29.4 Modifying a real response¶

    You can also let the real request happen, then edit the response before the page sees it. This is the route.fetch() pattern — fetch the genuine response, modify it, and fulfill with the result:

    def test_adds_a_fruit(page: Page):
    def handle(route: Route):
        response = route.fetch()              # perform the REAL request
        data = response.json()                # parse the real JSON
        data.append({"name": "Loquat", "id": 100})   # add one item
        route.fulfill(response=response, json=data)   # return the modified version

    page.route("https://demo.playwright.dev/api-mocking/api/v1/fruits", handle)
    page.goto("https://demo.playwright.dev/api-mocking")
    expect(page.get_by_text("Loquat", exact=True)).to_be_visible()

    This is the middle ground between "fully real" and "fully mocked": let the backend do its thing, but inject the one condition you want to test (an extra item, a flipped flag, a tweaked field).

    29.5 Replaying recorded traffic with HAR files¶

    For larger or more complex APIs, hand-writing mock JSON gets tedious. Playwright can record all network traffic to a HAR file (HTTP Archive) once, then replay it on later runs so the test never touches the network:

    # Replay responses from a previously-recorded HAR for matching requests:
page.route_from_har("./hars/fruit.har", url="*/**/api/v1/fruits", update=False)

    With update=True you record (or refresh) the HAR; with update=False you replay it. This gives you a deterministic, offline snapshot of a real API's behaviour — excellent for stable, fast tests against a backend you don't control, with the trade-off that the snapshot can drift from reality over time (so you re-record periodically).

    29.6 When NOT to mock¶

    Mocking is powerful, and therefore easy to overuse. The cardinal risk: a fully-mocked end-to-end test can pass while the real integration is broken. If you mock the search API and the cart API and the checkout API, your "end-to-end" test is really just testing your mocks against your UI — it would stay green even if the real backend changed its contract.

    A sound rule of thumb:

    • Mock at the edges and for hard-to-produce states — error responses, empty results, slow responses, third-party noise. These are things real backends won't reliably give you.
    • Don't mock the very thing you're trying to verify end-to-end. If the point of the test is "search really returns results from the real service," mocking that service defeats the purpose.
    • The reference project's flow is deliberately unmocked: it exercises the real eBay search and cart, because the whole point is to prove the real journey works. Mocking would be appropriate there only for a separate test like "show the empty-state message when search returns nothing."

    Interview lens

    "When do you mock the network in an end-to-end test?" → "For states the real backend can't easily produce — errors, empty results, timeouts — and to block third-party noise. I'm careful not to mock the integration the test is meant to verify, because a fully-mocked 'e2e' test can pass while the real system is broken; at that point it's a UI-against-mocks test, which is fine but should be labelled honestly. So I mock at the edges, not at the core of what I'm proving." That answer shows you understand the risk of mocking, which is more valuable than knowing the API.

    Exercise 29.1 — mock an error state

    Pick any page that calls a JSON API (the Playwright demo at https://demo.playwright.dev/api-mocking works). Write one test that uses route.fulfill to return an empty list and asserts the UI shows an empty state, and a second test that returns status=500 and asserts the UI shows an error message. Notice you just tested two states that would be very hard to trigger against a real server.

    Key idea

    page.route(pattern, handler) intercepts requests; the handler must fulfill (mock a response, including errors via status), abort (block it), or continue_ (let it pass — note the underscore). Use route.fetch() to modify a real response, and route_from_har to replay recorded traffic. Mock for hard-to-produce states and noise, never for the integration you're actually trying to verify end-to-end.

    Chapter 30 — API Testing with Playwright¶

    Playwright is best known for driving browsers, but it ships a full HTTP client too, and it's a genuinely useful one for test engineers. This chapter covers two things: testing a REST API directly (no browser at all), and — more powerfully — combining API calls with UI tests to set up state quickly. Both come up in interviews, and the second is a technique that separates slow, fragile suites from fast, focused ones.

    30.1 Why a browser-automation tool has an HTTP client¶

    Two reasons you'll actually use it:

    1. Pure API tests. Sometimes the thing under test is the API — you want to assert that POST /issues creates an issue and returns 201, with no UI involved. Playwright's request client does this without launching a browser, so it's fast.
    2. API as a setup shortcut for UI tests. This is the high-value pattern. Suppose a UI test needs "a user with three items already in their cart." Driving the UI to create that state is slow and flaky. Instead, you call the API to set it up in milliseconds, then point the browser at the already-prepared state and test only the part you care about.

    30.2 The APIRequestContext¶

    The HTTP client is an APIRequestContext. You create a standalone one through playwright.request.new_context(...), typically in a session-scoped fixture so it's shared and configured once:

    import pytest
from playwright.sync_api import Playwright

@pytest.fixture(scope="session")
def api_request_context(playwright: Playwright):
    request_context = playwright.request.new_context(
        base_url="https://api.github.com",
        extra_http_headers={
            "Accept": "application/vnd.github.v3+json",
            "Authorization": f"token {GITHUB_API_TOKEN}",
        },
    )
    yield request_context
    request_context.dispose()        # clean up after the session (the yield/teardown pattern)

    Note the familiar shapes: a base_url so calls use short paths (Chapter 21), extra_http_headers for things like auth, the yield fixture pattern for guaranteed teardown (Chapter 13), and dispose() to release resources.

    30.3 Making requests and asserting on responses¶

    The context has a method per HTTP verb, and the response object exposes status and body:

    def test_create_issue(api_request_context):
    new_issue = api_request_context.post(
        f"/repos/{USER}/{REPO}/issues",
        data={"title": "Bug report", "body": "Something is broken"},
    )
    assert new_issue.ok                       # True for any 2xx status
    created = new_issue.json()                # parse the JSON response body
    assert created["title"] == "Bug report"

def test_list_issues(api_request_context):
    issues = api_request_context.get(f"/repos/{USER}/{REPO}/issues")
    assert issues.ok
    titles = [i["title"] for i in issues.json()]
    assert "Bug report" in titles

    The vocabulary:

    • .get(url), .post(url, data=...), .put(url, data=...), .delete(url) — one method per verb. data= sends a JSON body.
    • .ok — a boolean, True for any 2xx status. (For a specific code, there's .status.)
    • .json() — parses the response body as JSON, giving you ordinary Python dicts/lists you can assert on with plain assert (Chapter 10 — these are in-memory values, so assert, not expect).

    From TypeScript

    This is the same APIRequestContext as in TS Playwright (request.newContext, .get, .post, response.ok(), response.json()), minus the awaits. If you've used supertest or axios in JS tests, the request client fills the same role, but shares Playwright's networking and cookie handling.

    30.4 The killer pattern: API setup, UI assertion¶

    This is the technique worth internalising. Use the API to arrange state quickly, then use the browser only to assert the part you actually want to verify:

    def test_issue_appears_in_ui(api_request_context, page):
    # ARRANGE via API — fast, reliable, no clicking through forms:
    api_request_context.post(f"/repos/{USER}/{REPO}/issues",
                             data={"title": "Shows in UI", "body": "..."})

    # ASSERT via UI — only the thing under test:
    page.goto(f"https://github.com/{USER}/{REPO}/issues")
    expect(page.get_by_role("link", name="Shows in UI")).to_be_visible()

    Compare this to creating the issue through the UI (open the new-issue form, fill the title, fill the body, submit, wait for redirect) just to then check it appears in the list. That setup is slow, involves many fragile selectors, and isn't even the thing you're testing. Doing setup via the API makes the test faster, more robust, and focused — it fails only when the thing it's actually verifying breaks.

    Interview lens

    "How do you set up complex preconditions for a UI test efficiently?" → "Through the API, not the UI. Driving the UI to create state is slow and brittle and isn't what the test is verifying. I use Playwright's APIRequestContext (or any HTTP client) to arrange the state — create the user, seed the cart — in milliseconds, then point the browser at the prepared state and assert only the behaviour under test. It makes tests faster, more reliable, and more focused." This is a strong, practical answer that many candidates miss.

    30.5 Sharing authentication between the API and the browser¶

    Because both the API client and the browser context speak Playwright's networking, you can authenticate once via the API and hand the resulting session to the browser (Chapter 11's storage state):

    state = api_request_context.storage_state()       # capture cookies/tokens from the API session
context = browser.new_context(storage_state=state) # start the browser ALREADY logged in

    So a fast API login can replace a slow, captcha-prone UI login for the entire suite — log in through the API once, reuse the session everywhere.

    Exercise 30.1 — API setup, UI check

    Against any public API + UI you have access to (or a local app), write one test that creates a record via api_request_context.post(...), asserts the response .ok, then navigates the browser to a page that should display it and asserts it's visible. Time it, then imagine how much slower the same test would be if you created the record by filling out the UI form. That delta is the value of the pattern.

    Key idea

    Playwright includes a real HTTP client, the APIRequestContext (playwright.request. new_context, .get/.post/.put/.delete, .ok, .json(), .dispose()). Use it for pure API tests, and — more powerfully — to arrange state via the API and assert via the UI, which makes UI tests faster, more reliable, and focused on what they actually verify. You can even authenticate via the API once and share the session with the browser.

    Chapter 31 — Accessibility & Visual Testing¶

    Two kinds of testing go beyond "does the button work?" to ask "is the page structured correctly?" and "does it look right?" Playwright Python supports the first natively, through aria snapshots, and the second through a mix of built-in screenshots and third-party tooling. This chapter is careful to tell you exactly what's built in versus what needs a plugin — because being honest about that distinction is itself an interview signal.

    31.1 Accessibility, and why your role locators already help¶

    Recall from Chapter 8 that the browser builds an accessibility tree — a semantic description of the page (roles and names) that assistive technology navigates. Because the whole course has you locating elements by role and name, your tests have already been exercising that tree: if get_by_role("button", name="Search") can't find the button, that's often a sign the page has an accessibility problem (a clickable <div> with no role). So good locator hygiene gives you a free, partial accessibility check.

    But you can test the accessibility structure explicitly, two ways.

    31.2 Aria snapshots — asserting the accessibility tree¶

    An aria snapshot is a YAML representation of an element's accessibility tree: its roles, names, and hierarchy. Playwright Python lets you assert that a region matches an expected structure with expect(...).to_match_aria_snapshot(...):

    from playwright.sync_api import Page, expect

def test_header_structure(page: Page):
    page.goto("https://playwright.dev")
    expect(page.get_by_role("banner")).to_match_aria_snapshot("""
        - banner:
          - link "Playwright"
          - navigation:
            - link "Docs"
            - link "API"
    """)

    This asserts that the header contains, in order, a "Playwright" link and a navigation region with "Docs" and "API" links — by their accessible roles and names, not by markup. Key features:

    • Partial matching by default: you list only the structure you care about; extra elements are allowed. (Use /children: equal or /children: deep-equal to require an exact set of children.)
    • Regex for dynamic text: write /pattern/ in place of a fixed name to match changing text.

    You can also generate the YAML programmatically to see the current tree or to capture a baseline:

    print(page.get_by_role("banner").aria_snapshot())   # prints the YAML for that region

    Aria snapshots are a powerful middle ground: more holistic than asserting one element at a time, but — unlike a pixel screenshot — stable against cosmetic restyling, because they assert meaning, not appearance.

    Interview lens

    "How would you test accessibility / page structure?" → "Two levels. First, my locators are role- and name-based, so the suite already fails if key controls aren't in the accessibility tree. Second, for structural assertions I use Playwright's aria snapshots (to_match_aria_snapshot), which assert the roles, names, and hierarchy as YAML — holistic but stable against restyling, because they check meaning, not pixels. For full WCAG rule auditing I'd add an axe-core integration (next section)." That layered answer shows real depth.

    31.3 Full accessibility auditing with axe¶

    Aria snapshots assert structure you specify. To audit a page against the actual WCAG ruleset (colour contrast, missing alt text, form labels, ARIA misuse, and dozens more), the industry standard is axe-core, integrated via a third-party library such as axe-playwright-python:

    # pip/uv add: axe-playwright-python
from axe_playwright_python.sync_playwright import Axe

def test_no_accessibility_violations(page: Page):
    page.goto("https://example.com")
    results = Axe().run(page)
    assert results.violations_count == 0, results.generate_report()

    Be honest about the boundary: axe is not part of Playwright — it's a separate, well-established library you add. Knowing that distinction (Playwright gives you aria snapshots and role locators; axe gives you rule-based auditing) is exactly the kind of accurate, non-hand-wavy answer interviewers value.

    31.4 Visual testing — and an honest caveat about Python¶

    "Visual regression testing" means capturing a screenshot and failing if it differs from an approved baseline by more than a threshold — catching unintended layout/CSS changes that functional tests miss.

    Important — to_have_screenshot is NOT in Playwright Python

    Playwright's built-in visual snapshot assertion, expect(page).to_have_screenshot(), is a feature of Playwright Test (the JavaScript/TypeScript test runner), not of the Python pytest-playwright integration. If you claim "I use to_have_screenshot in Python," an informed interviewer will know that's wrong. Be precise.

    What you can do in Python:

    # 1. Capture a screenshot (this IS built in):
page.screenshot(path="cart.png")
page.get_by_role("main").screenshot(path="cart-main.png")   # just one region

    To turn screenshots into assertions, you use a third-party pytest plugin (for example pytest-playwright-visual, or pytest-image-diff) that compares a freshly-captured image against a committed baseline and fails on a diff beyond a tolerance — or you write that comparison yourself with an image library. Either way, the capture is Playwright; the diffing is an add-on.

    A practical caution worth voicing: pixel-perfect visual tests are notoriously flaky across operating systems and browser versions (font rendering and anti-aliasing differ), so teams usually run them in a fixed container, mask dynamic regions, and allow a small pixel tolerance. Many teams deliberately prefer aria snapshots over pixel diffs precisely because structural assertions don't flake on a font-rendering difference.

    Interview lens

    "Do you do visual regression testing?" → "Playwright's built-in to_have_screenshot is a JavaScript-runner feature, not available in Python pytest-playwright. In Python I capture screenshots with page.screenshot() and compare them against baselines using a plugin like pytest-playwright-visual. But pixel diffs flake across OS/browser font rendering, so I pin them to a container, mask dynamic regions, and allow a tolerance — and where I just need structural correctness, I prefer aria snapshots, which don't flake on rendering differences." Naming the Python/JS distinction and the flakiness trade-off is a strong, precise answer.

    31.5 Attaching these to your reports¶

    Both kinds of artifact slot into the reporting you built in Chapter 25: attach screenshots to Allure steps, and attach an axe report (or the aria-snapshot YAML) on failure, so a reviewer can see what was wrong without re-running anything.

    Exercise 31.1 — assert structure, then audit

    On any page: (a) generate an aria snapshot of a region with locator.aria_snapshot(), paste the YAML into a to_match_aria_snapshot(...) assertion, then trim it to just the structure you care about and confirm partial matching still passes. (b) If you can, add axe-playwright-python and run Axe().run(page) against a deliberately-broken page (an image with no alt text) and read the violation report.

    Key idea

    Role-based locators already give partial accessibility coverage. For explicit structure, use Playwright's native aria snapshots (to_match_aria_snapshot, aria_snapshot()) — stable because they assert meaning, not pixels. For full WCAG auditing, add axe (a separate library). For visual regression, remember to_have_screenshot is JS-only; in Python you capture with page.screenshot() and diff via a plugin — and pixel diffs are flaky, so prefer structural checks where they suffice.

    Chapter 32 — Authoring Tools & Advanced Debugging¶

    This chapter covers the tooling that makes writing and fixing tests faster: the code generator that writes a first draft for you, the Inspector for stepping through and picking locators, and a few expect refinements (with an honest note about one feature Python doesn't have). These are the day-to-day productivity tools that distinguish someone who's actually lived in Playwright from someone who's only read about it.

    32.1 playwright codegen — record actions into code¶

    You don't have to write a test from a blank file. playwright codegen opens a browser and the Playwright Inspector side by side; as you click and type in the browser, it writes the corresponding Playwright code — using good role-based locators by default:

    playwright codegen demo.playwright.dev/todomvc

    Two windows appear: the browser you interact with, and the Inspector showing generated code that you can copy into a test. Useful options:

    playwright codegen --target python-pytest playwright.dev   # emit pytest-style Python
playwright codegen --viewport-size="800,600" playwright.dev # set the viewport
playwright codegen --device="iPhone 13" playwright.dev      # emulate a device
playwright codegen --color-scheme=dark playwright.dev
playwright codegen --timezone="Europe/Rome" --geolocation="41.89,12.49" --lang="it-IT" bing.com/maps

    How to use codegen well

    Treat codegen's output as a first draft, not a finished test. It produces solid locators and correct actions, but it doesn't know your architecture — it won't put selectors into a component or extract a service. The professional workflow is: record the happy path with codegen to get correct locators quickly, then refactor that draft into your Page Object / service structure (Part IV). Codegen saves you the tedious locator-hunting; you supply the architecture.

    32.2 Capturing and reusing login with codegen¶

    Codegen can record an authenticated session and save it, so you don't have to log in by hand every time you record:

    playwright codegen github.com/microsoft/playwright --save-storage=auth.json   # log in once, save it
playwright codegen --load-storage=auth.json github.com/...                     # resume already logged in

    This is the storage-state pattern from Chapter 11, surfaced as codegen flags — handy for authoring tests on pages that sit behind a login.

    32.3 The Inspector and page.pause()¶

    For debugging (rather than recording), the Inspector lets you pause execution and step through actions one at a time. You can launch it for a whole run with an environment variable, or drop into it at a specific point in your own code with page.pause():

    PWDEBUG=1 uv run pytest tests/test_search.py      # open the Inspector for the run

    def test_something(page):
    page.goto("https://example.com")
    page.pause()                  # execution stops here; the Inspector opens with your context loaded
    page.get_by_role("button", name="Search").click()

    page.pause() is especially valuable when you've built up custom state (cookies, a logged-in session, a mid-flow page) and want the codegen/pick-locator tools available in that exact state — something a fresh codegen launch can't reproduce. While paused you can step forward, and use the Pick Locator button to hover any element and have the Inspector show you the best locator for it.

    32.4 The Trace Viewer (recap, in context)¶

    For failures you can't reproduce interactively — especially in CI — the Trace Viewer from Chapter 24 is the tool: it replays a recorded run with before/after DOM snapshots for every action. The mental split is worth stating plainly:

    • Inspector / page.pause() / --headed --slowmo — for debugging while you develop, live and interactive.
    • Trace Viewer — for debugging after the fact, especially a CI failure you can't reproduce.

    Reach for the right one based on whether you can make the failure happen again on demand.

    32.5 Tuning expect timeouts¶

    expect() assertions retry up to a default timeout (5 seconds for assertions; navigation/actions have their own 30-second default). When a specific assertion legitimately needs longer — a slow report that takes a while to generate, say — set a per-assertion timeout rather than slowing the whole suite:

    expect(slow_widget).to_be_visible(timeout=15_000)   # wait up to 15s for THIS assertion only

    You can also raise the global expectation timeout in configuration if your application is uniformly slow, but prefer per-assertion overrides — a single slow spot shouldn't make every assertion in the suite wait longer before failing.

    Honest note — Python has no built-in soft assertions

    Playwright's soft assertions (expect.soft(...), which record a failure but let the test continue so you can collect several failures in one run) are a feature of Playwright Test (the JavaScript runner), not the Python pytest-playwright integration — just like to_have_screenshot (Chapter 31). In Python, an expect failure raises immediately and stops the test. If you genuinely need to collect multiple soft-failures in one pytest run, you reach for a third-party helper such as pytest-check. Don't claim expect.soft in a Python interview — knowing it's JS-only is the precise answer.

    Interview lens

    "How do you write tests faster, and debug them?" → "I draft with playwright codegen to get correct role-based locators quickly, then refactor that into my component/service structure — I never ship raw codegen output. For debugging I use page.pause() and the Inspector's pick-locator while developing, and the Trace Viewer for CI failures I can't reproduce. And I tune timeouts per-assertion rather than globally so one slow spot doesn't slow the whole suite." That's a complete, lived-in workflow.

    Exercise 32.1 — codegen, then refactor

    Run playwright codegen --target python-pytest <some site> and record a short flow (search for something, click a result). Copy the generated test and run it. Then refactor it: move the selectors into a small Page Object with a method or two, so the test body contains no selectors. You've just done the real codegen workflow — generate, then architect.

    Key idea

    playwright codegen records a first draft with good locators (use --target python-pytest, --device, --save-storage) — then refactor it into your architecture. page.pause() + the Inspector (pick-locator) debug live; the Trace Viewer debugs after the fact. Tune expect timeouts per-assertion. And remember the honest boundaries: soft assertions and to_have_screenshot are JavaScript-runner features, not available in Python pytest-playwright.

    Part VIII — Practice

    Chapter 33 — Hands-On Labs¶

    Reading teaches recognition; building teaches understanding. These labs take you from a single passing test to a small, properly-layered framework, using free public practice sites. Do them in order — each builds on the last. Every lab states a goal, gives staged hints, and hides a solution sketch you should only open after attempting it.

    Practice sites used here

    • https://playwright.dev — stable docs site, good for locators and assertions.
    • https://www.saucedemo.com — a demo shop with login, products, and a cart (great for POM).
    • https://demo.playwright.dev/api-mocking — a tiny app that calls a JSON API (for mocking).
    • https://the-internet.herokuapp.com — many isolated UI challenge pages.

    Set up a fresh project first (uv init, uv add playwright, uv add --dev pytest pytest-playwright, uv run playwright install chromium) as in Chapter 1.

    Lab 1 — Your first robust test (Chapters 7, 8, 10)¶

    Goal. Write a test that searches playwright.dev and verifies results appear, using only role/text locators and web-first assertions — no time.sleep, no CSS classes.

    Steps. 1. Navigate to https://playwright.dev. 2. Open the search (press the search button/icon), type "locator". 3. Assert that a results listbox becomes visible and that the first result contains "locator".

    Hints
    • The search trigger is a button; the input is a searchbox/textbox. Use get_by_role.
    • For the results, assert with expect(...).to_be_visible() — never assert is_visible().
    Solution sketch 

    from playwright.sync_api import Page, expect

def test_search_docs(page: Page):
    page.goto("https://playwright.dev")
    page.get_by_role("button", name="Search").click()
    page.get_by_role("searchbox").fill("locator")
    results = page.get_by_role("listbox")
    expect(results).to_be_visible()
    expect(results.get_by_role("option").first).to_contain_text("locator", ignore_case=True)
    What you practised: role locators, auto-waiting, web-first assertions. If a site's exact roles differ, use playwright codegen (Chapter 32) to discover them — then keep the role-based result.

    Lab 2 — A pure function and its unit tests (Chapters 5, 16)¶

    Goal. Write and exhaustively unit-test a pure parse_price function — no browser at all.

    Steps. 1. Write parse_price(text: str) -> Decimal that anchors on $, handles thousands commas, takes the lower bound of a range, and raises ValueError on garbage. 2. Write parametrized tests covering: plain, US-prefixed, thousands, a range, the "(3 items) $50" trap, and several unparseable inputs.

    Hints
    • Reuse the regex from Chapter 5: re.compile(r"\$\s*(-?\d{1,3}(?:,\d{3})*(?:\.\d+)?)").
    • Build the Decimal from a string (match.group(1).replace(",", "")), never a float.
    • Use @pytest.mark.parametrize for the valid cases and pytest.raises for the garbage.
    Solution sketch

    See Chapter 16 §16.3 for the parser and the full parametrized test. What you practised: purity, Decimal correctness, parametrization, and the test-pyramid principle — these ~20 tests run in well under a tenth of a second with no browser.

    Lab 3 — Refactor into a Page Object (Chapters 18, 19)¶

    Goal. Log in to saucedemo.com and assert you reach the products page — first as a scrappy test, then refactored into a LoginPage component owning the selectors.

    Steps. 1. Write a working but "ugly" test: raw page.fill/page.click with selectors inline. 2. Create a LoginPage(BaseComponent) with _SEL_ constants and a login(username, password) method; add an is_logged_in() query returning a bool. 3. Rewrite the test to use it. Confirm the test body now contains zero selectors.

    Hints
    • Standard saucedemo creds are shown on its login page (e.g. standard_user / secret_sauce).
    • login() should do (fill + click); a separate method should report state (return a bool) — keep doing and reporting separate.
    Solution sketch 

    class LoginPage(BaseComponent):
    _SEL_USER = "Username"
    _SEL_PASS = "Password"
    _SEL_SUBMIT = "Login"
    def login(self, username: str, password: str) -> None:
        self.page.get_by_placeholder(self._SEL_USER).fill(username)
        self.page.get_by_placeholder(self._SEL_PASS).fill(password)
        self.page.get_by_role("button", name=self._SEL_SUBMIT).click()
    def is_on_products(self) -> bool:
        return self.page.get_by_text("Products").is_visible()
    What you practised: hiding selectors behind intent, _SEL_ constants, separating action (login) from query (is_on_products). Note the page object has no assertions — the test asserts on is_on_products().

    Lab 4 — Add a service layer (Chapters 17, 20)¶

    Goal. On saucedemo, build a flow that spans pages — log in, add the two cheapest products to the cart, and return the cart count — and put that flow in a service, not a page object.

    Steps. 1. Add a ProductsPage component that can list product (name, price) pairs and add a product to the cart by name. 2. Write a ShoppingService whose constructor takes the page, composes LoginPage and ProductsPage, and has add_cheapest(n) returning the names added. 3. Write a test that logs in, calls add_cheapest(2), and asserts the cart badge shows 2.

    Hints
    • "The two cheapest" is a policy decision (sort by price, take the first two) — that belongs in the service, not in ProductsPage. The page object only reports prices.
    • Parse prices into Decimal (Lab 2's function) before sorting.
    Solution sketch

    The service sorts the page's reported (name, Decimal) pairs, slices the cheapest n, and calls products.add_to_cart(name) for each. What you practised: the mechanism/policy split — the component reports prices (mechanism), the service decides which to add (policy) — and a service composing multiple components. This is the Chapter 20 pattern in miniature.

    Lab 5 — Data-drive it (Chapters 13, 14)¶

    Goal. Turn Lab 4's test into a data-driven one, with login credentials and the expected outcome loaded from a YAML file via fixtures.

    Steps. 1. Create users.yaml with a few users (standard_user should succeed; locked_out_user should be blocked). 2. Load it in conftest.py and use pytest_generate_tests to parametrize a test_login(scenario). 3. Each case asserts success or the expected error, per its expect_ok field.

    Hints
    • Model each row as a frozen dataclass; parse it at load (Chapter 21 pattern).
    • pytest_generate_tests(metafunc) should check if "scenario" in metafunc.fixturenames.
    Solution sketch

    See Chapter 14 §14.4 for the pytest_generate_tests shape. What you practised: external data, typed loading, and generating one test per row — adding a user becomes a YAML edit, not a code change.

    Lab 6 — Mock an error state (Chapter 29)¶

    Goal. On demo.playwright.dev/api-mocking, force the fruit API to return an empty list and an error, and assert the UI handles each.

    Steps. 1. Use page.route("*/**/api/v1/fruits", handler) to route.fulfill(json=[]) and assert the UI shows no fruit. 2. In a second test, route.fulfill(status=500, json={"error": "boom"}) and assert the UI's error handling (or simply that the known fruit does not appear).

    Solution sketch

    See Chapter 29 §29.2. What you practised: controlling the network to test states a real backend won't reliably produce — and doing so deterministically.

    Lab 7 — Mock three states of a real API (Chapter 29)¶

    Goal. Against https://demo.playwright.dev/api-mocking, write three tests that force the fruit API into three different states and assert how the UI handles each: empty, server error, and a slow response.

    Steps. 1. Test A — fulfil with an empty JSON array; assert no fruit names appear. 2. Test B — fulfil with status=500; assert an error region/message becomes visible. 3. Test C — use a real route.fetch() then call time.sleep(0.0) inside the handler (or use page.route with a delayed response via a separate technique) — at minimum, log how long the page took to render with the slow mock. (For a true delay you can implement it in the handler.)

    Hints
    • Use route.fulfill(json=[]) for the empty case and route.fulfill(status=500, json={"error": "boom"}) for the error case.
    • For "slow," your handler can import time; time.sleep(2) inside the handler — Playwright will simply not respond to the page until the handler returns. (Beware: this slows the test by ~2s too; that's the point of exercising the slow case in isolation.)
    Solution sketch

    Each test installs a page.route("*/**/api/v1/fruits", handler) before page.goto(...), then asserts the UI state with expect(). Same locators, three different controlled backends. What you practised: deterministic testing of states the live backend won't reliably produce.

    Lab 8 — Use the API client (Chapter 30)¶

    Goal. Use playwright.request.new_context to exercise a public REST API directly — no browser.

    Steps. 1. Build an APIRequestContext for https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com in a session-scoped fixture, with extra_http_headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"}. 2. Write a test that POSTs {"title": "lab", "body": "hi", "userId": 1} to /posts and asserts response.ok and that the parsed json() echoes back the title. 3. Write a second test that GETs /posts/1 and asserts the JSON has a non-empty title.

    Hints
    • JSONPlaceholder is a sandbox — it doesn't really persist anything, but it responds correctly, which is what you need to practise the API client.
    • request_context.dispose() after the yield in your fixture.
    Solution sketch 

    @pytest.fixture(scope="session")
def api(playwright):
    ctx = playwright.request.new_context(base_url="https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com")
    yield ctx
    ctx.dispose()

def test_create_post(api):
    r = api.post("/posts", data={"title": "lab", "body": "hi", "userId": 1})
    assert r.ok
    assert r.json()["title"] == "lab"
    What you practised: the standalone API client. The next step in real work — covered in Chapter 30 — is to combine an API setup with a UI assertion on an app you own, where the API actually persists.

    Lab 9 — Assert structure with an aria snapshot (Chapter 31)¶

    Goal. On playwright.dev, capture an aria snapshot of the page header and use it as an assertion.

    Steps. 1. Navigate to https://playwright.dev. 2. Print page.get_by_role("banner").aria_snapshot() to see the YAML structure. 3. Trim that YAML to just the structural elements you care about (a couple of nav links) and feed it into expect(...).to_match_aria_snapshot(...). Confirm the test passes (partial matching is the default). 4. Add a deliberately wrong line (a link that doesn't exist) and watch the assertion fail.

    Solution sketch 

    expect(page.get_by_role("banner")).to_match_aria_snapshot("""
  - banner:
    - link "Playwright"
    - navigation:
      - link "Docs"
""")
    What you practised: asserting page structure (meaning) rather than appearance — far more stable than pixel-diffing.

    Lab 10 — Codegen, then refactor (Chapter 32)¶

    Goal. Use the recorder to draft a test quickly, then refactor it into a Page Object — the correct codegen workflow.

    Steps. 1. Run playwright codegen --target python-pytest https://www.saucedemo.com. In the browser, log in (e.g. standard_user / secret_sauce) and click a product. 2. Copy the generated Python into a new test file and run it; confirm it passes. 3. Refactor: move every selector into LoginPage/ProductsPage components with _SEL_ constants; keep the test body free of selectors. Re-run; still passes.

    Solution sketch

    The point isn't the specific selectors codegen produced — they'll vary — it's the refactor. Your final test should look like LoginPage(page).login("standard_user", "secret_sauce"); ProductsPage(page).click("Sauce Labs Backpack"); expect(...).to_be_visible(). What you practised: using codegen as a first draft, then applying architecture. Never ship raw codegen output.

    Lab 11 — Drive the Trace Viewer (Chapter 24)¶

    Goal. Capture and replay a trace, so the tool isn't unfamiliar the first time a CI failure hands you one.

    Steps. 1. Write any small test that navigates and clicks. Force a failure by changing one locator to something that doesn't exist (e.g. page.get_by_role("button", name="Does Not Exist").click()). 2. Run it with uv run pytest --tracing=on. Locate the produced trace.zip under test-results/. 3. Open it: uv run playwright show-trace test-results/.../trace.zip. Step through the timeline, hover an action, and inspect the before/after DOM snapshot. Read the network and console panels.

    What to notice

    The before/after snapshots are the magic — they let you see the DOM state at the exact moment the locator failed, so you can tell whether it was a timing problem, a markup change, or just-wrong text. That capability is why "capture a trace on failure in CI" is the senior debugging answer.

    Lab 12 — Review the AI snippet cold (Chapter 26)¶

    Goal. Practise the static-review skill before an interview asks you to.

    Steps. 1. Without re-reading Chapter 26, copy this snippet onto paper: 

    from playwright.sync_api import sync_playwright
from selenium import webdriver
import time
def test_search_functionality():
    browser = sync_playwright().start().chromium.launch()
    page = browser.new_page()
    page.goto("https://example.com")
    time.sleep(2)
    page.locator("#search").fill("playwright testing")
    page.locator(".button").click()
    time.sleep(3)
    results = page.locator(".result-item")
    browser.close()
    2. In five minutes, list every problem you can find and why each matters (not just what it is). 3. Check yourself against Chapter 26 §26.7. Lead your answer with the highest-impact issue (the one that makes the test unable to fail).

    What you practised

    The reviewer's instinct — for every line, ask "does this do the thing its shape implies?" AI-generated tests fail by looking right and behaving wrong; spotting that gap is the entire point of being a senior reviewer.

    Capstone lab — your own miniature suite¶

    Goal. Combine Labs 3–6 into a small, properly-layered project: components/ (LoginPage, ProductsPage, CartPage), services/ (ShoppingService), db/data.yaml (users + scenarios), tests/ (a unit test for price parsing, a smoke test, a data-driven e2e), and a GitHub Actions workflow (Chapter 25). Add an Allure report with allure.step phases.

    When it builds green and you can narrate the path of one test from fixture to browser and back (Chapter 27), you have built — and can defend — a real framework.

    Key idea

    You learn this craft by building it. These labs walk the same arc as the whole book: a robust single test → a unit-tested pure function → a Page Object → a service → data-driven → mocking → a complete layered suite. Do them in order, attempt before peeking, and refactor as you go — that refactoring is the learning.

    Chapter 34 — Self-Check Quizzes¶

    Use these to test recall and to rehearse interview answers out loud. Try to answer before expanding each solution. If an answer doesn't come quickly, that's the chapter to revisit — each answer links back to it. Aim to answer in your own words, not verbatim.

    Part I — Python¶

    1. Why must money be a Decimal, and what's the one rule when constructing one?

    Floats are binary and can't represent most decimal fractions exactly, so 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3, which causes false pass/fail on budget comparisons. Decimal is exact base-10 — but only if you build it from a string (Decimal("0.1")), never a float (Decimal(0.1) preserves the float error). (Chapter 5)

    2. What is a Protocol, and why does the paginator use one?

    A Protocol is structural typing: a class satisfies it by having the right shape (methods), not by inheriting from it. The paginator depends on _Pageable (just has_next_page and go_to_next_page), so it's decoupled from any concrete page — that's dependency inversion, and it makes the paginator reusable for any paginated list. (Chapter 4)

    3. is vs ==, and when does if x: differ from if x is not None:?

    is checks identity (same object); == checks value equality. Use is only for None/True/False. They differ when x could be 0 or "": if x: is False for those, but if x is not None: is True. So when zero/empty is a valid value, test is None explicitly. (Chapter 2)

    4. Explain a decorator in one sentence, and what @d desugars to.

    A decorator is a function that takes a function (or class) and returns a replacement; @d above a definition means name = d(name). (Appendix A)

    Part II — Playwright core¶

    5. Why is time.sleep an anti-pattern, and what replaces it?

    It's simultaneously too slow (always burns the full duration) and too flaky (fails when a slow runner needs longer). Actions auto-wait for actionability; expect() retries assertions; bounded wait_for(state=...) handles genuine probes. (Chapter 7)

    6. What's the difference between a browser, a context, and a page — and which is the isolation boundary?

    A browser is one expensive launched process (reused). A context is a cheap, isolated session (own cookies/storage) — the isolation and parallelism boundary. A page is a tab within a context. (Chapter 6)

    7. What is strict mode, and how should you resolve a violation?

    If a locator matches more than one element, an action throws instead of guessing — turning a silent wrong-click into an immediate error. Resolve it by making the locator more specific (add an accessible name), not by reflexively appending .first. (Chapter 7)

    8. State the locator priority order and the principle behind it.

    Role/label → text/placeholder → test-id → CSS (with comma fallbacks) → XPath last. The principle: locate the way a user perceives the page (roles, labels, text), not the way a developer built it (classes, positions), because the former is stable and the latter is implementation detail. (Chapter 8)

    9. Name the two things XPath can do that CSS can't, and one thing to never put in an XPath.

    XPath can match by text and walk to a parent/ancestor/sibling. Never put positional indices (li[3]) in it, because sites reorder elements per visitor. (Chapter 9)

    Part III — pytest¶

    10. What is a fixture, and what does 'scope' control?

    A fixture is a function that provides a dependency, requested by naming it as a parameter (dependency injection); fixtures compose into a graph pytest resolves. Scope controls how often it's built — function (default, per test) up to session (once per run) — trading isolation for speed. (Chapter 13)

    11. How would you make a suite data-driven from an external file?

    Store rows in YAML, load them into typed (frozen) dataclasses at the boundary (money → Decimal), and use pytest_generate_tests to parametrize the test from those rows filtered by tag — so adding a case is a YAML edit with no code change. (Chapter 14)

    12. Why have unit tests if you already have end-to-end tests?

    Unit tests are fast (milliseconds), precise (name the exact failing input), and not flaky. They catch logic regressions an e2e test would either miss or report vaguely after 30 seconds. They're possible because logic is extracted into pure functions. Many fast unit tests, few slow e2e — the pyramid. (Chapter 16)

    13. Why organise tests by marker rather than by folder, and how does parallelism stay safe?

    A marker makes a test's role/speed a property of the test itself (and a test can carry several), selectable with -m. Parallelism (xdist) is safe because each test gets its own isolated context, so there's no shared mutable state to corrupt. (Chapter 15)

    Part IV — Architecture¶

    14. THE big one: why have a service layer on top of page objects?

    Flows span multiple pages and own business logic (pagination, filtering, money math). In a test that logic duplicates across suites; in a page object it gives the object a second reason to change (SRP violation). A service is the single home for cross-page flow and policy, so components stay markup-only and tests stay assertion-only. (Chapter 20)

    15. Why is 'skip sponsored listings' in the service, not the component?

    It's policy (what to do), which changes for different reasons than the markup the component owns. The component only reports (is_sponsored()); the service decides to skip. Mechanism in the component, policy in the service. (Chapter 17)

    16. How do you stop fifty identical result cards from colliding in locators?

    Each card is its own component scoped to a root locator (cards.nth(i)), and all its queries go through self.locator(), which resolves relative to that root — so each component only ever sees its own subtree. (Chapter 19)
