    17. Should a page object contain assertions? Where do hardcoded URLs live?

    No — page objects return domain values; tests assert. There are no hardcoded URLs: base_url lives in the profile and is set on the context, so tests navigate by path, and PROFILE switches environments. (Chapter 18, Chapter 21)

    Part V — Robustness, reporting, review¶

    18. Give three techniques for making locators resilient on a volatile site.

    Locate by identity not position; use CSS comma-fallbacks ([data-testid=x], .x) for markup variants; use anchored regex names for labels with dynamic parts (re.compile(r"^Cart")). (Also: idempotent probes for conditional UI, defensive parsing, logged skip-and-continue.) (Chapter 22)

    19. How do you debug a flaky CI failure you can't reproduce locally?

    Capture a trace on failure (--tracing=retain-on-failure), download the trace.zip artifact, and open it with playwright show-trace — it gives before/after DOM snapshots, network, and console for every action, so you see the exact state when the locator failed. (Chapter 24)

    20. Why upload CI artifacts even on failed runs, and how?

    A failed run is when you most need the evidence. Let the test step continue-on-error: true and gate the artifact upload on if: always(), so the report, traces, and screenshots are produced for red builds too. (Chapter 25)

    21. The buggy AI snippet 'passes' — what's its single worst problem?

    It has no assertions — it builds a locator and verifies nothing, so it can't fail on a real bug. (Then: brittle locators, time.sleep, a stray Selenium import + leaked runtime, and manual Playwright in a pytest function.) Lead with impact: no assertions first. (Chapter 26)

    Part VII — Beyond the basics¶

    22. When should you mock the network, and when should you NOT?

    Mock for states the real backend can't easily produce (errors, empty results, slow responses) and to block third-party noise. Don't mock the integration the test is meant to verify — a fully-mocked 'e2e' test can pass while the real system is broken. (Chapter 29)

    23. What's the high-value pattern for setting up complex UI-test preconditions?

    Arrange state via the API (APIRequestContext), not by driving the UI — it's faster, more reliable, and keeps the test focused on what it's actually verifying. Then assert via the UI. You can even authenticate via API once and share the session with the browser. (Chapter 30)

    24. Which 'visual/structural' assertions exist in Python, and which is JS-only?

    Python has aria snapshots (to_match_aria_snapshot) for asserting the accessibility tree, and role-based locators give partial a11y coverage; full WCAG auditing needs axe (a separate library). Pixel to_have_screenshot is JavaScript-runner-only — in Python you capture with page.screenshot() and diff via a plugin. (Soft assertions are likewise JS-only.) (Chapter 31, Chapter 32)

    25. What's the right way to use playwright codegen?

    As a first draft generator: record a flow to get correct role-based locators quickly, then refactor that into your component/service architecture. Never ship raw codegen output as your test. (Chapter 32)

    Key idea

    If you can answer all 25 of these in your own words, you can hold your own in a senior Playwright/Python interview. The ones to over-prepare: #14 (why a service layer), #9/the XPath defence, #19 (trace viewer), and #22 (when not to mock) — these are where judgment shows. Anything you stumbled on points straight at the chapter to re-read.

    Appendices — The Little Things

    Appendix A — Decorators, In Depth¶

    Decorators are the Python feature most likely to be asked about in a "do you really know Python?" moment, and they're everywhere in this stack (@property, @dataclass, @pytest.fixture, @pytest.mark.*). This appendix takes you from "I use them" to "I can explain and write them."

    A.1 The prerequisite: functions are objects¶

    In Python a function is a first-class value — you can assign it to a variable, pass it as an argument, return it, and store it in a list:

    def shout(text):
    return text.upper()

f = shout              # assign the function itself (no parentheses!)
f("hi")                # "HI" — call it through the new name

def apply(fn, value):  # pass a function as an argument
    return fn(value)
apply(shout, "hi")     # "HI"

    Gotcha

    f = shout stores the function; f = shout("hi") calls it and stores the result ("HI"). The presence or absence of () is the entire difference. Decorators rely on passing the function itself, so this distinction matters.

    From TypeScript

    Identical to JS/TS — functions are values you can pass around. If you've written arr.map(fn) or passed a callback, you already have the prerequisite.

    A.2 A decorator is a function that takes a function and returns a function¶

    That's the whole definition. Here's the simplest useful one — a logger that wraps any function to announce its calls:

    import functools

def logged(fn):                              # (1) takes the original function
    @functools.wraps(fn)                     # (4) preserve fn's name/docstring
    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):            # (2) a replacement function
        print(f"calling {fn.__name__}")
        result = fn(*args, **kwargs)         # (3) call the original
        print(f"{fn.__name__} returned {result!r}")
        return result
    return wrapper                           # (5) hand back the replacement

def add(a, b):
    return a + b

add = logged(add)        # wrap it manually
add(2, 3)
# calling add
# add returned 5
    1. logged receives the function to decorate.
    2. It defines wrapper, which has the same calling convention via *args, **kwargs (so it works for any signature).
    3. wrapper does its extra work, then calls the original fn.
    4. functools.wraps(fn) copies fn's name and docstring onto wrapper (without it, add.__name__ would become "wrapper" — confusing in tracebacks).
    5. logged returns wrapper, which now stands in for add.

    A.3 The @ syntax is just sugar¶

    add = logged(add) is exactly what the @ does. These two are identical:

    def add(a, b):
    return a + b
add = logged(add)        # explicit form

    @logged                  # sugar — runs `add = logged(add)` for you
def add(a, b):
    return a + b

    Key idea

    @decorator above a definition means name = decorator(name). Read every @ you see as "replace this function with whatever decorator returns when given it." That single sentence demystifies all of them.

    A.4 Decorators that take arguments (one more layer)¶

    @pytest.fixture(scope="session") and @dataclass(frozen=True) take arguments. That needs a third layer: a function that takes the arguments and returns a decorator. Reading outward-in:

    import functools

def retry(times):                            # (1) takes the ARGUMENT, returns a decorator
    def decorator(fn):                       # (2) the actual decorator
        @functools.wraps(fn)
        def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):        # (3) the replacement function
            last = None
            for _ in range(times):
                try:
                    return fn(*args, **kwargs)
                except Exception as e:
                    last = e
            raise last
        return wrapper
    return decorator

@retry(times=3)                              # retry(3) returns `decorator`, applied to flaky
def flaky():
    ...

    So @retry(times=3) first calls retry(3) (returning decorator), then applies that to flaky. Three nested functions: configure → decorate → wrap. This is the shape behind every parameterized decorator you use.

    Interview lens

    "How does a decorator with arguments work?" → "Three layers: the outer function takes the arguments and returns a decorator; the decorator takes the function and returns a wrapper; the wrapper takes the call's args and adds behavior. @retry(3) calls the outer to get a decorator, then applies it. That's why @pytest.fixture(scope='session') has parentheses but @pytest.fixture doesn't — one is called to produce a decorator, the other is the decorator."

    A.5 The decorators you use in this course — decoded¶

    Decorator What it does Chapter
    @property turns a method into a read-only getter (access without ()) 3
    @staticmethod a method with no self — a plain function namespaced in the class C
    @classmethod a method receiving the class (cls) instead of an instance C
    @dataclass(frozen=True) generates __init__/__eq__/__repr__; frozen makes it immutable 3
    @pytest.fixture marks a function as a dependency provider for tests 13
    @pytest.fixture(scope="session") same, built once per run 13
    @pytest.mark.smoke / .regression tags a test for selection with -m 15
    @pytest.mark.parametrize(...) generates one test per data row 14
    @pytest.hookimpl(hookwrapper=True) wraps a pytest hook (used to capture test reports) 13

    Notice @property, @staticmethod, and @classmethod are built-in decorators; @dataclass is from the stdlib; the @pytest.* ones come from pytest. They're all just functions following the rule in A.3.

    A.6 Class decorators¶

    A decorator can also wrap a class (it receives the class and returns one). @dataclass is the canonical example: it takes your class with its field annotations and returns the same class with an auto-generated __init__, __eq__, and __repr__:

    @dataclass(frozen=True)
class Environment:
    id: str
    headless: bool
# dataclass added __init__(self, id, headless), __eq__, __repr__, and froze it

    You almost never write class decorators, but knowing @dataclass is "a class decorator that generates boilerplate from annotations" is a strong, precise answer.

    A.7 Why decorators matter for clean test code¶

    Decorators let a framework add cross-cutting behavior without you changing your functions: pytest discovers and parametrizes your plain test function because @parametrize wrapped it; @property lets results.cards read as a noun; @dataclass removes a dozen lines of self.x = x. They're how Python keeps your code declarative — you say what (this is a fixture, this is parametrized) and the decorator supplies the how.

    Exercise A

    1. Write a @timed decorator that prints how long the wrapped function took (use time.perf_counter()), with functools.wraps.
    2. Apply it to a function and confirm fn.__name__ is preserved.
    3. Extend it to @timed(label="search") (the three-layer form) so the printout includes a custom label.
    4. Explain out loud why @timed has no parentheses but @timed(label="x") does.

    Key idea

    A decorator is a function that takes a function (or class) and returns a replacement; @d means name = d(name). Parameterized decorators add a third nesting layer (@d(arg) calls d(arg) to get the decorator). Every @property, @dataclass, and @pytest.fixture you use is just that rule in action — and you can now write your own.

    Next: Appendix B — Regular Expressions. Back to the homepage.

    Appendix B — Regular Expressions You Actually Need¶

    Regex shows up in two places in this stack: price parsing (Chapter 5) and fuzzy locator names (get_by_role("link", name=re.compile(r"^Cart")), Chapter 22). You don't need to be a regex wizard — you need the dozen tokens below and the Python API.

    B.1 The Python re API¶

    import re

pattern = re.compile(r"\$\d+\.\d{2}")     # compile once, reuse (used as a class constant)

pattern.search("price: $25.00")           # finds FIRST match anywhere → Match or None
pattern.match("$25.00 total")             # match only at the START → Match or None
pattern.fullmatch("$25.00")               # must match the ENTIRE string
pattern.findall("$1.00 $2.00")            # list of ALL matches → ['$1.00', '$2.00']
re.search(r"\d+", "abc123")               # one-shot without compiling
    Function Matches Returns
    search anywhere in the string (first) Match or None
    match at the start only Match or None
    fullmatch the entire string Match or None
    findall every occurrence list[str]

    Gotcha — search vs match

    re.match anchors at the start of the string — re.match(r"\d+", "abc123") returns None. re.search scans the whole string. The price parser uses search because the $ may not be at the very start ("US $25.00"). Picking match when you meant search is the most common regex bug.

    B.2 Raw strings: always use r"..."¶

    re.compile(r"\d+")     # CORRECT — raw string, backslashes are literal
re.compile("\d+")      # works but Python warns; "\d" isn't a valid string escape

    A backslash means something to both Python strings and regex. The r"..." prefix ("raw string") tells Python "don't interpret backslashes," so the regex engine sees them intact. Always prefix regex patterns with r — it's a habit, not a case-by-case decision.

    From TypeScript

    JS regex literals (/\d+/) avoid this because the syntax is built into the language. Python has no regex literal, so patterns are strings — and r"..." is how you stop the string layer from eating your backslashes. JS new RegExp("\\d+") has the same double-escaping problem r"..." saves you from.

    B.3 The tokens that cover 95% of cases¶

    Token Means Example
    . any single character a.c → "abc", "axc"
    \d a digit [0-9] \d{4} → "2026"
    \w word char [A-Za-z0-9_]
    \s whitespace \s* = optional spaces
    [abc] one of a, b, c [$£€]
    [^abc] NOT a, b, or c
    [a-z] a range [0-9]
    * 0 or more \d*
    + 1 or more \d+
    ? 0 or 1 (optional) -? = optional minus
    {n} / {n,m} exactly n / between n and m \d{1,3}
    ^ / $ start / end anchor ^Cart$
    \| OR (alternation) cat\|dog
    ( ) capturing group extracts a piece
    (?: ) non-capturing group groups without capturing
    \$ \. a literal $ / . (escaped)

    Gotcha — escape the literals

    $ and . are special (end-anchor and any-char). To match a literal dollar sign or dot, escape them: \$, \.. "$25.00" matched by r"\$\d+\.\d{2}" — the \$ and \. are literals, the \d are digits.

    B.4 Groups and extracting values¶

    Parentheses capture the matched substring so you can pull it out:

    m = re.search(r"\$(\d+\.\d{2})", "Total: $25.00")
m.group(0)     # "$25.00" — the whole match
m.group(1)     # "25.00"  — the first ( ) group → the part you actually want

    That's exactly how the price parser extracts the number from the surrounding text: Decimal(match.group(1).replace(",", "")).

    A (?:...) group bundles tokens without capturing — used when you need grouping for */?/| but don't want it cluttering your group numbers:

    r"-?\d{1,3}(?:,\d{3})*(?:\.\d+)?"
#          └── repeat ",234" groups ──┘└─ optional ".56" ─┘

    B.5 Flags¶

    re.compile(r"^accept(?:\s+all)?$", re.I)     # re.I = case-INsensitive

    re.I (or re.IGNORECASE) is the one you'll use — it makes "Accept", "accept", and "ACCEPT" all match, which is why the cookie-banner locator uses it. Combine flags with |: re.I | re.MULTILINE.

    B.6 Greedy vs lazy¶

    * and + are greedy — they match as much as possible. Add ? to make them lazy (as little as possible):

    re.search(r"\$.*\d", "$5 to $9")    # greedy: ".*" eats up to the LAST digit
re.search(r"\$.*?\d", "$5 to $9")   # lazy:  ".*?" stops at the FIRST digit

    This rarely bites in this codebase (the price pattern is specific), but it's a classic interview "gotcha" — know that greedy is the default.

    B.7 Regex in Playwright locators¶

    Playwright's get_by_role, get_by_text, etc. accept a compiled regex for the name/text, enabling fuzzy-but-anchored matching against dynamic labels:

    page.get_by_role("link", name=re.compile(r"^Cart"))          # "Cart", "Cart (3)"
page.get_by_text(re.compile(r"^Subtotal"))                    # "Subtotal (3 items) $50.00"
page.get_by_role("button", name=re.compile(r"^Buy It Now$", re.I))

    Anchor with ^/$ to keep matches tight — ^Cart matches "Cart (3)" but not "My Cart Settings". This is the resilience technique from Chapter 22: match the stable part of a label that has a dynamic suffix.

    Interview lens

    "How do you locate an element whose label includes a dynamic count, like 'Cart (3)'?" → "A regex name anchored on the stable prefix: get_by_role('link', name=re.compile(r'^Cart')). The ^ anchor keeps it from matching unrelated 'Cart'-containing labels, and the regex absorbs the changing count." Short, concrete, and shows you combine two tools (roles + regex).

    Exercise B

    Without running it, predict what each returns, then verify in a Python REPL: 1. re.search(r"\$(\d+)", "Subtotal (3 items) $50").group(1) 2. re.match(r"\d+", "id: 42") 3. re.compile(r"^accept$", re.I).search("Accept All") 4. re.findall(r"\$\d+", "$5 $10 $15") (Answers: "50"; None — match anchors at start; None — $ requires the string to end at "accept"; ['$5', '$10', '$15'].)

    Key idea

    re.compile + search (not match!) for "anywhere"; always r"..."; () to capture and .group(1) to extract; re.I for case-insensitive; escape \$ and \.. In Playwright, a regex name anchored with ^/$ matches labels with dynamic parts. That's all the regex this job needs.

    Next: Appendix C — Python Odds & Ends. Previous: Appendix A — Decorators.

    Appendix C — Python Odds & Ends¶

    The grab-bag of smaller Python features that appear in the codebase or come up in interviews. Each is short; together they close the long tail of "wait, what does that do?"

    C.1 staticmethod and classmethod¶

    A normal method takes self (the instance). Two decorators change that:

    class TestDatabase:
    __test__ = False                    # tell pytest "I'm not a test class"

    @staticmethod
    def _safe(name):                    # no self — a plain function living in the class
        return re.sub(r"[^A-Za-z0-9_-]+", "_", name)

    @classmethod
    def from_default(cls):              # receives the CLASS (cls), not an instance
        return cls("db")                # alternative constructor
    • @staticmethod — no self, no cls. It's a plain function namespaced inside the class because it logically belongs there. Use for helpers that don't touch instance state.
    • @classmethod — receives the class as cls. The classic use is an alternative constructor (TestDatabase.from_default() returns a configured instance). cls(...) calls the constructor.

    From TypeScript

    @staticmethod/@classmethod ≈ TS static methods. classmethod's cls parameter (the class itself, so subclasses construct the right type) is the one twist — it's like static from(): InstanceType<typeof this>.

    C.2 Generators and yield¶

    A function with yield is a generator — it produces values lazily, one at a time, pausing between them instead of building a whole list in memory:

    def first_n_squares(n):
    for i in range(n):
        yield i * i              # pause here, hand out i*i, resume on next request

for sq in first_n_squares(5):    # 0, 1, 4, 9, 16 — computed one at a time
    print(sq)

    You met yield in a different role in fixtures (Chapter 13), where pytest uses the pause point to inject the value and run teardown after. Same mechanism — execution suspends at yield — applied to setup/teardown rather than iteration.

    From TypeScript

    yield ≈ JS generator functions (function*). Lazy, suspendable iteration. Python leans on it more (it's the basis of range, file iteration, and fixtures).

    C.3 *args and **kwargs, and dict/list spread¶

    def f(*args, **kwargs):       # args = tuple of positional; kwargs = dict of named
    ...
f(1, 2, x=3)                  # args=(1, 2), kwargs={"x": 3}

    The same */** also unpack when calling or merging:

    nums = [1, 2, 3]
print(*nums)                  # unpacks → print(1, 2, 3)

base = {"headless": True}
merged = {**base, "slow_mo": 100}     # dict merge → {"headless": True, "slow_mo": 100}

    That {**a, "k": v} dict-merge is exactly how the suite overrides the plugin's browser_context_args (Chapter 15): spread the defaults, add your keys.

    From TypeScript

    {**a, k: v} ≈ object spread {...a, k: v}. *args/**kwargs ≈ rest params (...args) plus an options object. print(*nums) ≈ fn(...nums).

    C.4 Dunder methods worth knowing¶

    "Dunder" (double-underscore) methods are hooks Python calls for you. You rarely write them by hand (@dataclass generates the common ones), but recognizing them helps:

    Dunder Called when Note
    __init__ constructing the constructor
    __repr__ repr(x), debugger, failed asserts dataclass generates a useful one
    __eq__ x == y dataclass generates value equality
    __len__ len(x)
    __enter__ / __exit__ with x: defines a context manager (Chapter 5)
    __call__ x() makes an instance callable

    The reason a frozen dataclass prints nicely in a failure log and compares by value is that @dataclass wrote __repr__ and __eq__ for you.

    C.5 pathlib.Path — modern file paths¶

    The suite builds file paths with pathlib, not string concatenation:

    from pathlib import Path

root = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent   # the project root
db_path = root / "db"                            # `/` joins paths (cross-platform)
results = root / "allure-results"
results.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)       # create dir, no error if it exists
(results / "environment.properties").write_text("...")   # write a file
db_path.is_dir()                                 # checks

    The / operator joins path segments correctly on any OS (no manual "/" vs "\\"), and Path objects carry handy methods (.exists(), .read_text(), .mkdir()). Prefer it to os.path.join string juggling.

    C.6 Logging (not print)¶

    Production code logs through the logging module, not print, so output has levels, timestamps, and a source label and can be routed/filtered:

    import logging
log = logging.getLogger("search")

log.debug("card price unparseable; skipping")     # noisy detail
log.info("search done: collected=%d target=%d", len(urls), limit)   # normal flow
log.warning("skipping auction-only listing: %s", url)               # anomaly
log.error("...")                                                    # failure

    Two habits the suite follows:

    • Use levels deliberately: info for flow milestones, debug for skip details, warning for tolerated anomalies (auctions, missing variants).
    • Use %s/%d lazy formatting, not f-strings, in log calls: log.info("x=%d", n) defers the string building until the message is actually emitted (skipped if that level is disabled). A small efficiency and a convention reviewers notice.

    Interview lens

    "Why log instead of print in tests?" → "Levels (debug/info/warning), a source label, and routing — so the failure log reads as a narrative of what the flow did, and I can dial verbosity per environment. print has none of that. I log flow at info, skips at debug, anomalies at warning, which makes a failed run self-explanatory before I even open the trace." (Ties to Chapter 24.)

    C.7 Handy builtins you'll use¶

    enumerate(items)            # → (0, item0), (1, item1), ...  (index + value)
zip(a, b)                   # → pairs: (a0, b0), (a1, b1), ...
any(c.is_sponsored() for c in cards)    # True if ANY is truthy
all(p > 0 for p in prices)              # True if ALL are truthy
sum(prices)                             # adds (works with Decimal — stays exact)
sorted(cards, key=lambda c: c.price)    # sort by a computed key
min(prices), max(prices)
len(urls)

    any/all with a generator are the Pythonic way to express "is there a sponsored card?" / "are all prices positive?" — concise and readable.

    C.8 The ternary expression¶

    self.root = root if root is not None else page.locator("body")
#           └─ value if ─┘ └─ condition ─┘     └─ value else ─┘

    Python's conditional expression reads value-first: X if cond else Y. This is the exact line in BaseComponent.__init__ (Chapter 19) that defaults the root.

    From TypeScript

    X if cond else Y ≈ cond ? X : Y, but ordered differently (value first). The root or page.locator("body") shortcut also exists but differs subtly — or treats any falsy value (including a legitimately empty one) as "use the default", whereas if root is not None only defaults on actual None. (See the truthiness gotcha in Chapter 2.)

    C.9 f-string format specifiers¶

    f-strings can format, not just interpolate:

    f"{price:.2f}"        # "25.00" — 2 decimal places
f"{count:03d}"        # "007"   — zero-padded to width 3 (used in screenshot filenames)
f"{value!r}"          # repr() of value — quotes strings, useful in logs/errors
f"{ratio:.1%}"        # "45.0%" — percentage

    The {step_counter:02d} in the screenshot manager pads the step number so files sort correctly (01_, 02_, …, 10_). !r (used in the parser's error message) shows the repr, so text!r prints ' ' with visible quotes rather than blank space.

    Key idea

    staticmethod/classmethod for non-instance methods; yield for lazy sequences and fixture teardown; */** for variadic params and {**a} merge; dunders are hooks @dataclass writes for you; pathlib for paths; logging with levels over print; any/all/enumerate/sorted(key=...) for clean iteration; X if c else Y ternary; f-string specs like :.2f and :02d.

    Appendix D — Cheat Sheet & Glossary¶

    The night-before reference. Skim it; click through to the chapter behind anything that isn't instant.

    D.1 Command cheat sheet¶

    # Environment
uv sync                                   # install deps
uv run playwright install chromium        # install browser
uv run <anything>                         # run a command inside the venv

# Running tests
uv run pytest                             # everything
uv run pytest -m smoke                    # by marker
uv run pytest -m "not slow"               # boolean marker expr
uv run pytest tests/unit -v               # one folder, verbose
uv run pytest path::test_name             # one test
uv run pytest -k "price"                  # name substring
uv run pytest -x                          # stop on first failure
uv run pytest -n 4                        # 4 parallel workers (xdist)
uv run pytest --headed --slowmo 500       # watch it
PWDEBUG=1 uv run pytest path              # Playwright Inspector

# Profiles & reports
PROFILE=ci uv run pytest -m regression    # switch environment
uv run pytest --alluredir=allure-results
uv run allure serve allure-results
uv run playwright show-trace test-results/<...>/trace.zip

# Quality gates
uv run ruff check .                       # lint
uv run black --check .                    # formatting check
uv run black .                            # auto-format
uv run mypy src/                          # type check

    D.2 Locator cheat sheet (priority order)¶

    page.get_by_role("button", name="Search")      # 1. role + accessible name  ← default
page.get_by_label("Maximum Value")             # 2. form fields
page.get_by_text(re.compile(r"^Subtotal"))     # 3. content-anchored
page.get_by_test_id("x-price-primary")         # 4. data-testid when present
page.locator('[data-testid="x"], .x-class')    # 5. CSS, with comma-fallback
page.locator("xpath=//li[contains(@class,'s-item')]//a")   # 6. XPath, last resort

loc.first / loc.nth(2)                          # disambiguate (nth is 0-indexed)
loc.filter(has_text="In stock")                 # filter by content
root.locator(".price")                          # scope within a component root

    D.3 Assertion cheat sheet¶

    # Page state → expect() (RETRIES, waits):
expect(loc).to_be_visible()
expect(loc).to_have_text("...")        / .to_contain_text("...")
expect(loc).to_have_count(5)
expect(loc).to_have_value("shoes")
expect(page).to_have_url(re.compile(r"/sch/"))
expect(loc).not_.to_be_visible()

# In-memory value → plain assert (one-shot):
assert len(urls) > 0
assert subtotal <= budget, "helpful message"

# Error path:
with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="no numeric value"):
    parse_price("garbage")

    D.4 The one-sentence concept list (rehearse aloud)¶

    • POM — classes that hide selectors behind intent-revealing methods; tests speak the domain, not markup. (18)
    • Component object — POM for a reusable region, scoped to a root locator so repeated elements don't collide. (19)
    • Service layer — owns cross-page flows and policy above the page objects; the single home for logic that would otherwise duplicate in tests or bloat a page object. (20)
    • SRP — one reason to change per class: component changes on markup, service on flow, test on assertions. (17)
    • Fixture — dependency injection by parameter name; composes into a graph pytest resolves. (13)
    • Fixture scope — how often it's built (function default → session); wider = faster but less isolated. (13)
    • Data-driven — external YAML → typed dataclasses → pytest_generate_tests; adding a case is a data edit. (14)
    • Auto-waiting — actions wait for actionability; never time.sleep. (7)
    • expect() vs is_visible() — expect retries (waits); is_visible is a non-waiting snapshot. (10)
    • Strict mode — a locator matching >1 element throws instead of guessing. (7)
    • Locator vs ElementHandle — locator is a lazy, re-resolved recipe (no staleness); use it. (7)
    • Browser/context/page — expensive shared browser; cheap isolated context (test boundary); page = tab. (6)
    • Decimal — exact base-10 money, built from a string, never a float. (5)
    • Protocol — structural typing; the paginator depends on a shape, not a class = dependency inversion. (4)
    • Decorator — a function that takes a function and returns a replacement; @d means name = d(name). (A)
    • Test pyramid — many fast unit tests, few slow e2e; unit-testable because logic is extracted into pure functions. (16)
    • Trace viewer — before/after DOM snapshots captured on failure; primary debug tool. (24)
    • XPath — last-resort locator; only for text match and parent/ancestor traversal; never positional. (9)

    D.5 Glossary¶

    Term Meaning
    Actionability the checks (visible, stable, enabled, hittable) Playwright waits for before acting
    Allure a reporting tool that renders test results into an interactive dashboard
    Autouse fixture a fixture applied to every test in scope without being requested
    conftest.py a file whose fixtures/hooks are auto-shared with all tests below it
    Context (BrowserContext) an isolated browser session (own cookies/storage); the test/parallelism boundary
    Dataclass a class with auto-generated constructor/equality/repr from typed fields
    Dependency injection the framework supplies a component's dependencies rather than it constructing them
    Dunder a __double_underscore__ method Python calls implicitly (__init__, __eq__, …)
    Fixture a pytest function that provides a dependency to tests by name
    Flaky passes/fails without code change — usually a timing, ordering, or locator issue
    Headless running the browser with no visible window (CI default)
    Idempotent safe to call repeatedly with the same effect (e.g. cookie_banner.accept())
    Locator a lazy, re-evaluated recipe for finding element(s)
    Marker a @pytest.mark.* tag for selecting/grouping tests
    Parametrize generate one test per data row from one test function
    POM Page Object Model — encapsulate page markup behind intent methods
    Profile a named bundle of environment settings (dev, ci) chosen by PROFILE
    Protocol a structural-typing interface — matched by shape, not inheritance
    Pure function output depends only on input, no side effects → trivially unit-testable
    Service a class owning a business domain's cross-page flows and policy
    SRP Single Responsibility Principle — one reason to change per unit
    Storage state saved cookies + localStorage, reloaded to start tests authenticated
    Strict mode Playwright erroring when a locator matches more than one element
    Trace a recorded timeline (DOM snapshots, network, console) for replay debugging
    uv the Rust-based Python project/venv/dependency manager used here
    xdist the pytest plugin that runs tests across parallel worker processes
